At $x\in U$, choose a positive-definite SQP model matrix and solve the exact
quadratic subproblem by
[[alg-sqp-exhaustive-active-set-qp-solve]]. If it reports infeasibility or
failure, return that status. On a solution return, retain its step $p$, full
QP multiplier vectors $(\nu^{QP},\lambda^{QP})$, retained equality basis
$E$, and selected inequality support $J$. The stacked rows $Dh_E(x)$ and
$Dg_J(x)$ are independent, and the selected rows satisfy
$h_E(x)+Dh_E(x)p=0$ and $g_J(x)+Dg_J(x)p=0$. Given parameters $\rho_0>0$,
$\gamma>1$, $\beta\in(0,1)$, $\sigma\in(0,1)$ and finite integer caps
$R,J_{\max}\ge1$, keep the resulting step $p$ fixed, initialize flags
$P_{\rm pos}=\mathrm{false}$ and $P_{\rm dom}=\mathrm{false}$, and perform
attempts $r=0,\ldots,R-1$ with $\rho_r=\rho_0\gamma^r$:

1. Compute $D_r=D_{\rho_r}(x,p)$ from
   [[def-sqp-l1-exact-penalty-merit]]. If $D_r\le0$, go to the next penalty.
   Otherwise set $P_{\rm pos}=\mathrm{true}$.
2. If $x+p\in U$, call
   [[alg-sqp-second-order-correction]] with the specified map
   $c_A=(h_E,g_J)$. If it returns a correction $w$ and $x+p+w\in U$, set
   $P_{\rm dom}=\mathrm{true}$ and test
   $\psi_{\rho_r}(x+p+w)\le\psi_{\rho_r}(x)-\sigma D_r$. If it passes,
   return `accepted-soc` with $x+p+w$, $p$, $(\nu^{QP},\lambda^{QP})$, $E$,
   and $J$. If $x+p\notin U$, skip the correction call.
3. For $j=0,\ldots,J_{\max}-1$, set $t_j=\beta^j$. Whenever $x+t_jp\in U$,
   set $P_{\rm dom}=\mathrm{true}$ and test
   $$\psi_{\rho_r}(x+t_jp)\le\psi_{\rho_r}(x)-\sigma t_jD_r.$$
   On the first passing test, return `accepted` with $x+t_jp$, $t_j$,
   $p$, $(\nu^{QP},\lambda^{QP})$, $E$, and $J$.

After all attempts, if $P_{\rm pos}$ is false, return
`nonpositive-predicted-decrease-budget`. If $P_{\rm pos}$ is true but
$P_{\rm dom}$ is false, return `domain-exit`: no SOC or ordinary trial could
be evaluated in $U$. Otherwise return `line-search-budget-exhausted`. These
finite tests do not guarantee acceptance or convergence.

quadratic subproblem by

attempts $r=0,\ldots,R-1$ with $\rho_r=\rho_0\gamma^r$:

   [[def-sqp-l1-exact-penalty-merit]]. If $D_r\le0$, go to the next penalty.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $c_A:U\to\mathbb R^r$ collect the equality constraints and a specified
set of active inequality constraints, in that order. Given $x,x+p\in U$,
assume $A=Dc_A(x)$ has full row rank and the SQP step satisfies
$c_A(x)+Ap=0$. For $r>0$, compute
$$w=-A^T(AA^T)^{-1}c_A(x+p)$$
and return $p+w$ as the corrected displacement. If the rank test fails,
the inverse or evaluation fails, return `correction-failure`. If $r=0$,
return $p$ with $w=0$. This is a correction for the specified active
constraints; it does not certify feasibility of inactive constraints.

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Assume AC and the Brownian conventions of
[[def-locally-lipschitz-ito-sde-and-maximal-solution]] on $[0,T]$ with
$U=\mathbb R^d$. The input is an autonomous drift $b:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb
R^d$, diffusion $\sigma:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$, initial state
$\xi$, and integer $N\ge1$ with $h=T/N\le1$. Define $t_n=nh$ and
$$b_h(x)=\frac{b(x)}{1+h|b(x)|}.$$
Return the grid values, step process, continuous interpolation, and status as
follows.

Exact current Definition anchor: Input real endpoints $a,b,c,d$, integer panel counts $n_x,n_y$, and an exact evaluation oracle that, when queried at a point, returns either a value in $\mathbb R^2$ or evaluation-failure. First, if $a\ge b$ or $c\ge d$, return invalid-domain without querying the oracle. Next, if either panel count is odd or is less than two, return invalid-panel-count without querying the oracle. For the remaining inputs set $R=[a,b]\times[c,d]$, $h_x=(b-a)/n_x$, $h_y=(d-c)/n_y$, $x_i=a+ih_x$ for $0\le i\le n_x$, and $y_j=c+jh_y$ for $0\le j\le n_y$. Query the oracle at every grid point in lexicographic order with $i$ first and $j$ second, storing the returned values. If a query fails, stop at the first such point and return evaluation-failure with that point. Otherwise, for each $j$ form the continuous piecewise-linear interpolant through the stored values $F(x_i,y_j)$ and apply [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]] componentwise in $x$ to this interpolant, obtaining $G_j=Q_xF(\cdot,y_j)$. Form the continuous piecewise-linear interpolant through the stored $G_j$ and apply the same valid Simpson procedure componentwise in $y$ to obtain $Q_yG=Q_yQ_xF$. Each interpolant is queried only at its stored grid nodes, so no new oracle call is needed. Both calls to the supplier use strictly ordered endpoints and even panel counts at least two. This exact-real procedure makes finitely many evaluations and sums; it makes no floating-point roundoff or force-accuracy claim, and error control is a separate result.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ and
$g:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper closed convex, let
$K:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p$ and $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^p$ be linear,
let $c\in\mathbb R^p$, and let $\rho>0$. The primal problem is
$$\min_{x,z}\ f(x)+g(z)\quad\text{subject to }Kx+Lz=c,$$
and its Lagrangian is
$\mathcal L((x,z),y)=f(x)+g(z)+\langle y,Kx+Lz-c\rangle$.
A saddle point means a saddle pair in the sense of
[[def-saddle-point-for-convex-concave-lagrangian]].

For an exact outer sweep with scaled dual $u^k$, compute, in order,
$$x^{k+1}\in\arg\min_x\left(f(x)+\frac\rho2\|Kx+Lz^k-c+u^k\|_2^2\right),$$
$$z^{k+1}\in\arg\min_z\left(g(z)+\frac\rho2\|Kx^{k+1}+Lz-c+u^k\|_2^2\right),$$
then set $r^{k+1}=Kx^{k+1}+Lz^{k+1}-c$ and
$u^{k+1}=u^k+r^{k+1}$. Report also the unscaled dual
$y^k=\rho u^k$, objective $p_k=f(x^k)+g(z^k)$, and primal residual $r^k$.
If an exact subproblem has multiple minimizers, choose the unique minimum-norm
member of its nonempty closed convex minimizer set; existence and uniqueness of
that tie-break follow from [[thm-nearest-point-in-a-nonempty-closed-convex-set]].

A finite implementation supplies finite inner iteration caps for both solves.
A solve is accepted only with a certificate of an attained global minimizer
before its cap. Return **invalid-input** for invalid dimensions or $\rho\le0$;
return **x-solve-failed**, **x-cap-exhausted**, **z-solve-failed**, or
**z-cap-exhausted** if the corresponding solve fails, is uncertified, or reaches
its cap. A failed sweep does not change the outer state, even if its first
subproblem was solved. These statuses give no approximate convergence guarantee.

Thus the specified tie-break exists and is unique in every dimension, so exact outer sweeps are deterministic. A capped solver that does not certify this attained minimizer returns its stated failure status without changing $(x^k,z^k,u^k)$; hence the finite wrapper makes no claim that every cap will succeed. review_basis.full_actual_interface:
**Input:** an ODE field $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ on the open domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$, $(t_n,y_n)\in D$, $h>0$, a finite real state-Jacobian approximation $\widetilde J_n$, a finite approximation $\widetilde T_n$ to $\partial_t f(t_n,y_n)$, stage residual tolerances $\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2\ge0$, a unit roundoff $u>0$ with $du<1$, the selected stored finite set $\mathbb F$ of [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]], a terminating field-evaluation routine `evaluate_f` that returns either the exact value $f(t,y)$ or `evaluation-failure` for each requested $(t,y)\in D$, terminating `store` routine, and terminating certificate evaluator `evaluator` meeting the input contract of [[alg-rosenbrock-shifted-qr-solver-with-residual-certificate]]. The exact-storage check returns $v$ if every entry is in $\mathbb F$ and `unavailable` otherwise; it does not round. Put
$$\alpha:=\frac{1}{2+\sqrt2}=1-\frac{1}{\sqrt2},\qquad W:=I_d-\alpha h\widetilde J_n.$$
The two-stage method is
$$W k_1=f(t_n,y_n)+\alpha h\widetilde T_n,$$
$$F_1=f\!\left(t_n+\frac h2,y_n+\frac h2k_1\right),\qquad W q_2=F_1-k_1,\qquad k_2=q_2+k_1,$$
$$y_{n+1}=y_n+h k_2.$$

The residuals $Wk_1-[f(t_n,y_n)+\alpha h\widetilde T_n]$ and $Wq_2-(F_1-k_1)$ are update residuals of their linear stage equations in the sense of [[def-implicit-residual-and-algebraic-error-units]]. The coefficient $\alpha$ and the autonomous two-stage formula are the second-order Rosenbrock formula recorded for ode23s in WIAS Example 2.37. The first-stage $\alpha h\widetilde T_n$ term specifies the nonautonomous extension used here; its order is independently established under the stated boundedness hypotheses.

1. Form $W$ by exact outer arithmetic and set $W_s:=\operatorname{store}(W)$. If storage returns `unavailable`, return $(y_n,\texttt{representation-unavailable})$. Call `factor(W_s,u,evaluator)` of [[alg-rosenbrock-shifted-qr-solver-with-residual-certificate]]. If it returns a factorization failure status, return $(y_n,\texttt{factorization-failure})$; otherwise retain its factor object.
2. Call `evaluate_f(t_n,y_n)`. If it returns `evaluation-failure`, return $(y_n,\texttt{input-or-representation-failure})$. Otherwise denote its returned exact value by $f_0$, form $b_1=f_0+\alpha h\widetilde T_n$ by exact outer arithmetic, and set $b_{1,s}:=\operatorname{store}(b_1)$. If storage returns `unavailable`, return $(y_n,\texttt{input-or-representation-failure})$. Call the retained factor object's `solve(b_{1,s},\varepsilon_1)`. If it is not certified, return $(y_n,\text{stage-1 status})$. Otherwise set $k_1$ to its returned vector.
3. Check $(t_n+h/2,y_n+hk_1/2)\in D$. If not, return $(y_n,\texttt{invalid-stage-domain})$. Otherwise call `evaluate_f(t_n+h/2,y_n+hk_1/2)`. If it returns `evaluation-failure`, return $(y_n,\texttt{stage-2-input-or-representation-failure})$. Otherwise set $F_1$ to the returned exact value, form $b_2=F_1-k_1$ exactly, and set $b_{2,s}:=\operatorname{store}(b_2)$. If storage returns `unavailable`, return $(y_n,\texttt{stage-2-input-or-representation-failure})$. Call the same factor object's `solve(b_{2,s},\varepsilon_2)`. If this solve is not certified, return $(y_n,\text{stage-2 status})$.
4. Set $k_2=q_2+k_1$ and return $(y_n+h k_2,\texttt{success},\rho_1,\rho_2)$ with the two certified update-residual bounds.

The exact-J branch takes $\widetilde J_n=D_yf(t_n,y_n)$ and $\widetilde T_n=\partial_t f(t_n,y_n)$. The W-method branch permits any bounded matrix approximations satisfying the hypotheses of the local and global order results; it receives no scalar A/L-stability guarantee from the exact-J result. The factor matrix is the same in both stages, so the procedure performs one shifted-matrix factorization and two stage solves. For this mixed-arithmetic specification, field evaluations and outer affine combinations are exact real operations, and every matrix/RHS passed to factorization or solve must pass `store`; factorization, triangular solves, and residual dot products use the operationwise model, while residual-bound formation is delegated to the terminating certificate evaluator. A full hardware-rounding theorem for outer operations would need additional certified evaluation and update-error terms. A finite arithmetic residual is not a forward-error bound without an inverse estimate.

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
**Input:** an ODE field $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ on the open domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$, $(t_n,y_n)\in D$, $h>0$, a finite real state-Jacobian approximation $\widetilde J_n$, a finite approximation $\widetilde T_n$ to $\partial_t f(t_n,y_n)$, stage residual tolerances $\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2\ge0$, a unit roundoff $u>0$ with $du<1$, the selected stored finite set $\mathbb F$ of [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]], a terminating field-evaluation routine `evaluate_f` that returns either the exact value $f(t,y)$ or `evaluation-failure` for each requested $(t,y)\in D$, terminating `store` routine, and terminating certificate evaluator `evaluator` meeting the input contract of [[alg-rosenbrock-shifted-qr-solver-with-residual-certificate]]. The exact-storage check returns $v$ if every entry is in $\mathbb F$ and `unavailable` otherwise; it does not round. Put
$$\alpha:=\frac{1}{2+\sqrt2}=1-\frac{1}{\sqrt2},\qquad W:=I_d-\alpha h\widetilde J_n.$$
The two-stage method is
$$W k_1=f(t_n,y_n)+\alpha h\widetilde T_n,$$
$$F_1=f\!\left(t_n+\frac h2,y_n+\frac h2k_1\right),\qquad W q_2=F_1-k_1,\qquad k_2=q_2+k_1,$$
$$y_{n+1}=y_n+h k_2.$$

The residuals $Wk_1-[f(t_n,y_n)+\alpha h\widetilde T_n]$ and $Wq_2-(F_1-k_1)$ are update residuals of their linear stage equations in the sense of [[def-implicit-residual-and-algebraic-error-units]]. The coefficient $\alpha$ and the autonomous two-stage formula are the second-order Rosenbrock formula recorded for ode23s in WIAS Example 2.37. The first-stage $\alpha h\widetilde T_n$ term specifies the nonautonomous extension used here; its order is independently established under the stated boundedness hypotheses.

1. Form $W$ by exact outer arithmetic and set $W_s:=\operatorname{store}(W)$. If storage returns `unavailable`, return $(y_n,\texttt{representation-unavailable})$. Call `factor(W_s,u,evaluator)` of [[alg-rosenbrock-shifted-qr-solver-with-residual-certificate]]. If it returns a factorization failure status, return $(y_n,\texttt{factorization-failure})$; otherwise retain its factor object.
2. Call `evaluate_f(t_n,y_n)`. If it returns `evaluation-failure`, return $(y_n,\texttt{input-or-representation-failure})$. Otherwise denote its returned exact value by $f_0$, form $b_1=f_0+\alpha h\widetilde T_n$ by exact outer arithmetic, and set $b_{1,s}:=\operatorname{store}(b_1)$. If storage returns `unavailable`, return $(y_n,\texttt{input-or-representation-failure})$. Call the retained factor object's `solve(b_{1,s},\varepsilon_1)`. If it is not certified, return $(y_n,\text{stage-1 status})$. Otherwise set $k_1$ to its returned vector.
3. Check $(t_n+h/2,y_n+hk_1/2)\in D$. If not, return $(y_n,\texttt{invalid-stage-domain})$. Otherwise call `evaluate_f(t_n+h/2,y_n+hk_1/2)`. If it returns `evaluation-failure`, return $(y_n,\texttt{stage-2-input-or-representation-failure})$. Otherwise set $F_1$ to the returned exact value, form $b_2=F_1-k_1$ exactly, and set $b_{2,s}:=\operatorname{store}(b_2)$. If storage returns `unavailable`, return $(y_n,\texttt{stage-2-input-or-representation-failure})$. Call the same factor object's `solve(b_{2,s},\varepsilon_2)`. If this solve is not certified, return $(y_n,\text{stage-2 status})$.
4. Set $k_2=q_2+k_1$ and return $(y_n+h k_2,\texttt{success},\rho_1,\rho_2)$ with the two certified update-residual bounds.

The exact-J branch takes $\widetilde J_n=D_yf(t_n,y_n)$ and $\widetilde T_n=\partial_t f(t_n,y_n)$. The W-method branch permits any bounded matrix approximations satisfying the hypotheses of the local and global order results; it receives no scalar A/L-stability guarantee from the exact-J result. The factor matrix is the same in both stages, so the procedure performs one shifted-matrix factorization and two stage solves. For this mixed-arithmetic specification, field evaluations and outer affine combinations are exact real operations, and every matrix/RHS passed to factorization or solve must pass `store`; factorization, triangular solves, and residual dot products use the operationwise model, while residual-bound formation is delegated to the terminating certificate evaluator. A full hardware-rounding theorem for outer operations would need additional certified evaluation and update-error terms. A finite arithmetic residual is not a forward-error bound without an inverse estimate.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Use three scalar blocks, zero objectives, $\rho=1$, and the homogeneous
constraint $Ax=0$ with
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\1&1&2\\1&2&2\end{pmatrix}.$$
The sequential three-block recurrence of
[[alg-naive-sequential-three-block-admm]] has a rational initial state for
which its iterates are unbounded, although the unique primal-dual solution is
zero and every block subproblem is attained uniquely.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Three zero-objective scalar blocks have unique attained updates and unique zero primal/dual solution, yet one rational start has an unbounded recurrence.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Write the columns of $A$ as $a_1=(1,1,1)^T$, $a_2=(1,1,2)^T$, $a_3=(1,2,2)^T$. Their squared norms are $3,6,9$, so every scalar block subproblem has a strictly positive quadratic coefficient and a unique attained minimizer. Also $det A=-1$, so $Ax=0$ has only $x=0$. source_evidence.fullclaim:
For $0<h\le1$ and $\theta\in(-1,1)$, let the exact state be $u(\theta)=0$ and the approximate state be $u_h(\theta)=h^2\sin(\theta/h^3)$. The exact and approximate reduced objectives are these states themselves.

1.1 For every $\theta$ and $h$, $|u_h(\theta)-u(\theta)|=h^2|\sin(\theta/h^3)|\le h^2$. Thus the state error tends uniformly to zero as $h\downarrow0$. [given, algebra]

2.1 Differentiating gives $u_h'(\theta)=h^{-1}\cos(\theta/h^3)$ and $u'(\theta)=0$. At $\theta=0$, the gradient error is $|u_h'(0)-u'(0)|=h^{-1}$, which is unbounded as $h\downarrow0$. This refutes the stated implication; the example lacks a uniform derivative-data bound of the type required by [F1]. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Assume Countable Choice and the Galerkin and adjoint hypotheses of [[thm-elliptic-fe-gradient-error-in-energy-norms]]. Suppose the adjoint regularity and dual approximation assumptions of [[cor-aubin-nitsche-h-r-plus-s-rate-under-primal-and-dual-approximation]] hold separately for the state and adjoint equations, giving
$$\|u-u_h\|_{L^2}\le C_u h^{r+s},\qquad \|p-p_h\|_{L^2}\le C_p h^{r+s}$$
for $0<h\le1$, $r\ge1$, and $s\in(0,1]$. Assume the parameter derivative operators satisfy
$$|\ell_\theta'[\eta](v)|\le M_\ell^0\|\eta\|_2\|v\|_{L^2},\qquad |a_\theta'[\eta](v,w)|\le M_a^0\|\eta\|_2\|v\|_{L^2}\|w\|_{L^2}.$$
Assume the discrete derivative maps in [[thm-elliptic-fe-gradient-error-in-energy-norms]] have compatible $L^2$ extensions and constants $C_J,C_\ell,C_a$ independent of $h$ give, for every $\|\eta\|_2\le1$, a direct-objective derivative defect at most $C_Jh^{r+s}$, an $L^2$-dual load-derivative defect at most $C_\ell h^{r+s}$, and a bilinear derivative defect at most $C_ah^{r+s}\|v\|_{L^2}\|w\|_{L^2}$. Then the reduced-gradient error is $O(h^{r+s})$. This rate requires those extra $L^2$-bounded parameter derivative maps; the energy-norm result alone does not imply it.

actualproofparagraphs.3.1: Apply the exact gradient subtraction in [F2]. The direct-objective and derivative-data defects contribute their assumed $O(h^{r+s})$ bounds; step 2.1 bounds the state- and adjoint-dependent terms by constants times $h^{r+s}$. Taking the supremum over $\|\eta\|_2\le1$ proves the asserted rate. If the $L^2$ derivative bounds or either dual approximation hypothesis fails, this rate has not been proved. [A1, F2, step 2.1] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim:
For the finite-basis data on the model's open Hermitian domain in
[[def-finite-basis-projector-energy-model]], the Hermitian response
$$F(P)=h+G(P)+\nabla E_{xc}(P)$$
is $C^1$ on the model's open domain. At every $P_0$ with an occupied/unoccupied
gap, the occupied-projector map $\Phi(P)=\Pi_r(F(P))$ is $C^1$ on a sufficiently
small neighborhood of $P_0$ where that gap persists.

actualproofparagraphs.2.1: Continuity of $F$ gives a neighborhood $V$ of $P_0$ on which $\|F(P)-F(P_0)\|_F<g/4$, where $g$ is the gap at $P_0$. By [F5] this image lies in a common gap-preserving ball; [F3] makes its block projector $C^1$ there and [L1] identifies it with the defined occupied projector. By [F4], $\Phi=\Pi_r\circ F$ is $C^1$ on $V$. [step 1.1, F3, F4, F5, F6, L1, choose] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Assume Countable Choice. Put $V:=H^1_0(0,1)$ with its $H^1$ norm, and let $V_h\subseteq V$ be a finite-dimensional conforming piecewise-linear space on an interval partition with maximum cell width $h$. Let $u\in C^2([0,1])\cap V$ and assume its nodal interpolant $I_hu$ belongs to $V_h$. Let $A\in C^2([0,1])$ satisfy $0<\alpha\le A(x)\le M$, and write $C_A:=\|A''\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}$. Define $a(v,w)=\int_0^1A v'w'$ and let $a_h$ use one midpoint quadrature sample per cell. Let $F$ and $F_h$ be bounded exact and discrete loads, and put $\delta_{F,h}:=\sup_{w_h\ne0}|F(w_h)-F_h(w_h)|/\|w_h\|_{H^1}$. Then the exact and discrete solutions satisfy

$$\|u-u_h\|_{H^1}\le(1+2M/\alpha)\sqrt2h\|u''\|_\infty+\frac2\alpha\left(\frac{C_Ah^2}{24}(\|u'\|_2+h\|u''\|_\infty)+\delta_{F,h}\right).$$

The explicit $\delta_{F,h}$ is the data/source oscillation term; no rate or vanishing of it is asserted without an additional load approximation hypothesis. Here coercivity follows directly because every sampled coefficient satisfies $A(m_K)\ge\alpha$; this special argument does not infer stability from quadrature exactness.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Assume Countable Choice and the exact conforming Galerkin hypotheses of [[cor-symmetric-galerkin-best-approximation-in-energy-norm]], with Hermitian form $a$ bounded by $M$ in $\|\cdot\|_V$. Let $u_h^G$ be the exact Galerkin solution. Let $a_h$ be a bounded discrete form on the same $V_h$, coercive in $\|\cdot\|_V$ with constant $\alpha_h>0$, and let $F_h$ be a bounded discrete load with the matching test-linearity. Its unique perturbed solution $\widetilde u_h$ satisfies

$$\|u-\widetilde u_h\|_a\le\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_a+\frac{\sqrt M}{\alpha_h}\rho_h,$$

where $\rho_h:=\sup_{w_h\ne0}|F_h(w_h)-a_h(u_h^G,w_h)|/\|w_h\|_V$, defined as zero if $V_h=\{0\}$. This uses the exact Galerkin solution as a baseline; $\rho_h$ must be bounded from the actual form and load defects.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
For the autonomous split problem $y'=a(y)+b(y)$ of [[def-additive-ode-and-partition]], set
$$\gamma:=1-\frac1{\sqrt2},\qquad \delta:=-\frac1{\sqrt2}.$$
The explicit tableau and the lower-triangular implicit tableau, using the separate stage conventions of [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]] and [[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]], are
$$\widetilde A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\\gamma&0&0\\\delta&1-\delta&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \widetilde b=(\delta,1-\delta,0),\quad \widetilde c=(0,\gamma,1),$$
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\0&\gamma&0\\0&1-\gamma&\gamma\end{pmatrix},\quad b=(0,1-\gamma,\gamma),\quad c=(0,\gamma,1).$$
For a step $h>0$ from $y$, the method is defined by
$$Y_1=y,\qquad Y_2=y+\gamma h a(Y_1)+\gamma h b(Y_2),$$
$$Y_3=y+h\bigl[\delta a(Y_1)+(1-\delta)a(Y_2)\bigr]+h\bigl[(1-\gamma)b(Y_2)+\gamma b(Y_3)\bigr],\qquad y^+=Y_3.$$
Thus there are two implicit solves per step, one for each nonzero diagonal implicit stage. The unscaled stage-equation residual uses the update-residual convention of [[def-implicit-residual-and-algebraic-error-units]]. The tableaus and stages alone assert neither branch existence nor stability.

Exact current Definition anchor: Fix $T>0$, a globally Lipschitz kernel $K$ as in [[def-globally-lipschitz-mean-field-kernel]], and a Borel probability measure $\mu_0$ on $\mathbb R^d$ with finite first moment as in [[def-p-one-wasserstein-one]]. A characteristic solution on $[0,T]$ consists of a jointly Borel map $X:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$, defined up to a $\mu_0$-null set of labels, such that $t\mapsto X_t(x)$ is absolutely continuous for $\mu_0$-almost every $x$, $X_0(x)=x$, and
$$X_t(x)=x+\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb R^d}K(X_s(x),X_s(y))\,d\mu_0(y)\,ds$$
for $\mu_0$-almost every $x$. It transports $\mu_0$ to $\mu_t=(X_t)_\#\mu_0$, where $(X_t)_\#\mu_0(A):=\mu_0(X_t^{-1}(A))$. The weighted path integrability convention is $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t(x)|d\mu_0(x)<\infty$; in particular every time slice has finite first moment.

The kernel can be0, giving constant paths satisfying the equation. Exact current Definition anchor: Fix $T>0$, a globally Lipschitz kernel $K$ as in [[def-globally-lipschitz-mean-field-kernel]], and a Borel probability measure $\mu_0$ on $\mathbb R^d$ with finite first moment as in [[def-p-one-wasserstein-one]]. A characteristic solution on $[0,T]$ consists of a jointly Borel map $X:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$, defined up to a $\mu_0$-null set of labels, such that $t\mapsto X_t(x)$ is absolutely continuous for $\mu_0$-almost every $x$, $X_0(x)=x$, and
$$X_t(x)=x+\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb R^d}K(X_s(x),X_s(y))\,d\mu_0(y)\,ds$$
for $\mu_0$-almost every $x$. It transports $\mu_0$ to $\mu_t=(X_t)_\#\mu_0$, where $(X_t)_\#\mu_0(A):=\mu_0(X_t^{-1}(A))$. The weighted path integrability convention is $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t(x)|d\mu_0(x)<\infty$; in particular every time slice has finite first moment.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $M,d\ge1$, let $0\le c_1<\cdots<c_M\le1$ be distinct collocation nodes, and let $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_M$ be their cardinal polynomials from [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]. Define
$$Q_{ij}:=\int_0^{c_i}\ell_j(s)\,ds,\qquad b_j:=\int_0^1\ell_j(s)\,ds.$$
The matrix $Q\in\mathbb R^{M\times M}$ and vector $b\in\mathbb R^M$ are the collocation tableau coefficients. For an IVP $y'=f(t,y)$ on the open domain of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], write
$$F_j(U):=f(t+c_jh,U_j),\qquad QF(U):=\left(\sum_{j=1}^M Q_{ij}F_j(U)\right)_{i=1}^M.$$
All displayed integrals use the oriented Riemann convention of [[def-oriented-integral]]. In particular $Q_{ij}=0$ when $c_i=0$, and the integral in $u_h$ vanishes at $\tau=0$. The collocation stages and endpoint are the implicit Runge–Kutta equations of [[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]] with $A=Q$, nodes $c$, and weights $b$:
$$U=\mathbf1u+hQF(U),\qquad \Psi_h(t,u)=u+h\sum_{j=1}^M b_jF_j(U).$$
The associated collocation polynomial on normalized time $\tau\in[0,1]$ is
$$u_h(\tau):=u+h\int_0^\tau\sum_{j=1}^M\ell_j(s)F_j(U)\,ds.$$
Thus $u_h(c_i)=U_i$, $u_h'(c_i)=hF_i(U)$, and $u_h(1)=\Psi_h(t,u)$ whenever $U$ is an admissible solution. This definition alone asserts no branch existence or uniqueness.

For interpolation estimates define the **Lebesgue constant** of this fixed node set by
$$\Lambda_M:=\max_{0\le s\le1}\sum_{j=1}^M|\ell_j(s)|.$$
For a real matrix $A$, write $\|A\|_\infty:=\max_i\sum_j|a_{ij}|$. These constants depend on the nodes and on $M$; no uniform-in-$M$ bound is part of the definition.
source_evidence.case_anchor: Definition requires M>=1 distinct nodes, so its tableau, cardinal sum and Lebesgue-constant sum are nonempty. At c_i=0 or normalized time tau=0 the oriented integral is zero as explicitly stated; no node or polynomial is selected from an empty list, and branch existence is not asserted.

def-complex-grassmann-polar-retraction: At eta=0, I+eta*eta=I and the output is X. At r=n the horizontal equation X*eta=0 forces eta=0. For every admitted eta its Gram matrix has quadratic form ||v||^2+||eta v||^2>0, so rank degeneration never occurs. Exact current Definition anchor: For $X\in\operatorname{St}_{\mathbb C}(n,r)$ and horizontal $\eta\in T_{[X]}\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(r,n)$, so $X^*\eta=0$, define $R_X^{\rm pol}(\eta)=(X+\eta)\bigl((X+\eta)^*(X+\eta)\bigr)^{-1/2}$ and $R_{[X]}^{\rm pol}(\eta)=\operatorname{range}(R_X^{\rm pol}(\eta))$.
The inverse square root is the inverse of the unique positive-definite
Hermitian square root. The horizontal condition gives
$(X+\eta)^*(X+\eta)=I+\eta^*\eta\succ0$, so this map is defined for every
horizontal tangent vector, and its frame representative is unchanged as a
Grassmann point when $(X,\eta)$ is replaced by $(XQ,\eta Q)$ with unitary $Q$.

def-complex-stiefel-grassmann-optimization-conventions: For r=1 frames are complex unit vectors; r=n gives the unitary group and a one-point Grassmann quotient. Exact current Definition anchor: For $1\le r\le n$, set $\operatorname{St}_{\mathbb C}(n,r)=\{X\in\mathbb C^{n\times r}:X^*X=I_r\}$ and $\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(r,n)=\operatorname{St}_{\mathbb C}(n,r)/\operatorname U(r)$.
The class $[X]$ represents the complex column space of $X$; two orthonormal
frames represent the same space exactly when they differ by right multiplication
by a unitary $r\times r$ matrix. Regard each complex matrix space as a real
vector space and use the real Frobenius inner product
$$\langle U,V\rangle_{\mathbb R}:=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(U^*V).$$
Give the complex Stiefel manifold its induced metric. On the complex Grassmann
quotient, represent tangent vectors horizontally by matrices $Z$ with $X^*Z=0$
and pair these representatives by $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathbb R}$.
For $A=A_0+iA_1\in\mathbb C^{n\times r}$, write
$$\rho(A):=\begin{pmatrix}A_0&-A_1\\A_1&A_0\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{2n\times2r}$$
for its realification, the real matrix acting on real/imaginary coordinates as
$A$ acts on complex coordinates. Write $\operatorname{Herm}(A)=(A+A^*)/2$.

def-coordinatewise-product-moment-functional: d=1 is the one-coordinate functional. Zero coefficients give the zero polynomial and zero finite sum; zero exponents use the factor M0. Exact current Definition anchor: For $d\ge1$, let $(a_j,b_j,m_j,2m_j-1,\mu_j)$ be Gaussian moment data for
each coordinate $j=1,\ldots,d$, and write
$M^{(j)}_k:=\int x^k\,d\mu_j(x)$. A **coordinatewise tensor polynomial** is a
finite family $(c_\alpha)$, with $c_\alpha\in\mathbb R$ for every index, indexed by multi-indices
$\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)$ with
$0\le\alpha_j\le2m_j-1$, evaluated by
$$ P(x_1,\ldots,x_d)=\sum_{\alpha}c_\alpha\prod_{j=1}^{d}x_j^{\alpha_j}. $$
Define its **coordinatewise product-moment value** by
$$ I_\otimes(P):=\sum_{\alpha}c_\alpha\prod_{j=1}^{d}M^{(j)}_{\alpha_j}. $$
In both sums, list the finite multi-index box in increasing lexicographic
order (coordinate $1$ first, then coordinate $2$, and so on), and take the
ordinary finite-list sum in that order. The products use increasing coordinate
order $j=1,\ldots,d$. The real coefficient family is part of the formal
polynomial data, so these formulas specify finite real sums. This definition specifies the product-moment functional
used for coordinatewise exactness without requiring a measure-product
construction.

$M^{(j)}_k:=\int x^k\,d\mu_j(x)$. A **coordinatewise tensor polynomial** is a
finite family $(c_\alpha)$, with $c_\alpha\in\mathbb R$ for every index, indexed by multi-indices
$\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)$ with
$0\le\alpha_j\le2m_j-1$, evaluated by
$$ P(x_1,\ldots,x_d)=\sum_{\alpha}c_\alpha\prod_{j=1}^{d}x_j^{\alpha_j}. $$
Define its **coordinatewise product-moment value** by
$$ I_\otimes(P):=\sum_{\alpha}c_\alpha\prod_{j=1}^{d}M^{(j)}_{\alpha_j}. $$
In both sums, list the finite multi-index box in increasing lexicographic
order (coordinate $1$ first, then coordinate $2$, and so on), and take the
ordinary finite-list sum in that order. The products use increasing coordinate
order $j=1,\ldots,d$. The real coefficient family is part of the formal
polynomial data, so these formulas specify finite real sums. This definition specifies the product-moment functional
used for coordinatewise exactness without requiring a measure-product
construction.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $\mathcal H=\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, with square-summability as in [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Define the diagonal operator $A$ by
$$D(A)=\left\{u\in\mathcal H:\sum_{k\ge1} k^4|u_k|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad (Au)_k=-k^2u_k.$$
Let $g\in\mathcal H$ be the fixed sequence $g_k=1/k$ for odd $k$ and $g_k=0$ for even $k$; membership follows from [[thm-p-series-real-exponents]] with exponent $2$. The split evolution is $u'=Au+g$. For $t\ge0$, define the exact diagonal subflow $E_tu=(e^{-k^2t}u_k)_{k\ge1}$ and the exact translation subflow $B_tu=u+tg$. By [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]] and [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $0<e^{-k^2t}\le1$, so each $E_t$ maps $\mathcal H$ to itself; each $B_t$ does so because $g\in\mathcal H$. The associated Strang modal step is
$$S_h=E_{h/2}\circ B_h\circ E_{h/2},\qquad h>0,$$
where the rightmost map is applied first. Each coordinate of $E_t$ solves $u_k'=-k^2u_k$, and each coordinate of $B_t$ solves $u_k'=g_k$. This is a precisely defined sequence-space model; it records one Dirichlet sine-mode boundary mismatch and makes no general convergence assertion for unbounded PDE operators.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $\mathcal H=\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, with square-summability as in [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Define the diagonal operator $A$ by
$$D(A)=\left\{u\in\mathcal H:\sum_{k\ge1} k^4|u_k|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad (Au)_k=-k^2u_k.$$
Let $g\in\mathcal H$ be the fixed sequence $g_k=1/k$ for odd $k$ and $g_k=0$ for even $k$; membership follows from [[thm-p-series-real-exponents]] with exponent $2$. The split evolution is $u'=Au+g$. For $t\ge0$, define the exact diagonal subflow $E_tu=(e^{-k^2t}u_k)_{k\ge1}$ and the exact translation subflow $B_tu=u+tg$. By [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]] and [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $0<e^{-k^2t}\le1$, so each $E_t$ maps $\mathcal H$ to itself; each $B_t$ does so because $g\in\mathcal H$. The associated Strang modal step is
$$S_h=E_{h/2}\circ B_h\circ E_{h/2},\qquad h>0,$$
where the rightmost map is applied first. Each coordinate of $E_t$ solves $u_k'=-k^2u_k$, and each coordinate of $B_t$ solves $u_k'=g_k$. This is a precisely defined sequence-space model; it records one Dirichlet sine-mode boundary mismatch and makes no general convergence assertion for unbounded PDE operators.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $a,b:U\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^3$ fields on an open set, and restrict attention to points and time intervals for which the unique local solutions of $x'=a(x)$ and $x'=b(x)$ remain in $U$. Denote their exact solution maps by $\Phi_a^t$ and $\Phi_b^t$. The **Lie split map** applies $a$ and then $b$:
$$L_h:=\Phi_b^h\circ\Phi_a^h.$$
The **Strang split map** applies half of $a$, then $b$, then half of $a$:
$$S_h:=\Phi_a^{h/2}\circ\Phi_b^h\circ\Phi_a^{h/2}.$$
Define the vector-field Lie bracket convention
$$[a,b](y):=Db(y)a(y)-Da(y)b(y).$$
This definition is finite-dimensional. It asserts neither that an unbounded operator has a common invariant domain nor that its commutators are bounded.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$. Its **Fenchel conjugate** is the
extended-real function on the same Euclidean space
$$f^*(s):=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)\}.$$
When $f(x)=+\infty$, the corresponding term is $-\infty$ and does not increase
the supremum. Its effective domain is
$\operatorname{dom}f^*=\{s:f^*(s)<+\infty\}$.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $S=S^*\succ0$ be an $n\times n$ finite-basis overlap matrix and supply its
Cholesky factor $L$ with $S=LL^*$, $L$ invertible
([[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]],
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]).
If $h_0=h_0^*$ is the coefficient-basis one-body matrix, set
$h=L^{-1}h_0L^{-*}$, where $L^{-*}=(L^*)^{-1}$; this is the Cholesky
whitening whose generalized Ritz quotient is preserved by
[[prop-positive-definite-overlap-whitening-preserves-generalized-ritz-pencil]].
For coefficient vectors use $y=L^*c$; the interaction map and chosen
exchange-correlation functional below are supplied in these orthonormal
coordinates. Fix $1\le r<n$ and the
projector domain $\mathcal P_r$ of [[def-rank-r-orthogonal-projector-domain]].

Supply a Hermitian matrix $h$, a real-linear self-adjoint map
$G:\mathbb H_n\to\mathbb H_n$ for the Frobenius inner product, and a real-valued
$C^2$ functional $E_{xc}$ on an open neighborhood of $\mathcal P_r$. Define
$$E(P):=\operatorname{tr}(hP)+\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(P G(P))+E_{xc}(P),\qquad F(P):=h+G(P)+\nabla E_{xc}(P).$$
Here $F(P)$ is the Hermitian Frobenius-gradient formula justified by
[[prop-finite-projector-energy-reality-and-gradient]].

The finite-basis Hartree–Fock model is the special case $E_{xc}=0$ with a
supplied symmetry-compatible Coulomb/exchange tensor defining $G$. A
Kohn–Sham-like model supplies its density map and chosen differentiable
exchange-correlation functional. These are finite-dimensional mathematical
models; this definition makes no assertion that the selected functional is an
exact continuum physical energy.

def-gauss-moment-data: m=1 needs at least two support points; m=0 and zero measure are excluded. The k=0 moment is M0=mass and x^0=1 even at x=0. Exact current Definition anchor: Let $a<b$ be real numbers, let $m\ge1$ be an integer, and let
$r\in\{2m-1,2m\}$. A **Gaussian quadrature moment datum of order $r$** is a
finite positive measure $\mu$ on the relative Borel sigma-algebra
$\mathcal B([a,b])$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[def-measure-space]],
[[def-measure]], [[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) such that
$\mu([a,b])>0$, and whose **relative support**
$$ S_\mu:=\{x\in[a,b]:\mu(U)>0\text{ for every relatively open }U\subseteq[a,b]\text{ with }x\in U\} $$
contains at least $m+1$ distinct points. For every integer $0\le k\le r$,
require $x\mapsto |x|^k$ to be integrable with respect to $\mu$
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]) and put
$M_k:=\int_{[a,b]}x^k\,d\mu(x)$. Powers use the natural-exponent
recursion of [[def-integer-power]], with $x^0=1$ for every real $x$, including
$x=0$; thus $M_0$ is the integral of the constant function $1$.

The branch $r=2m-1$ supplies all moments used to construct the monic
degree-$m$ orthogonal polynomial and prove rule exactness. The stronger branch
$r=2m$ also defines its squared norm and is used for the remainder formula.
Because $[a,b]$ is bounded and $\mu$ is finite, these absolute-moment
integrability conditions follow from finiteness; they are stated to make the
two moment interfaces explicit.

after.evidence:
def-gauss-quadrature-rule: For m=1 the empty cardinal product is1, w1=M0, and Q1(f)=M0 f(x1). Zero nodal values give zero output; zero weights are not claimed by this definition. Exact current Definition anchor: Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]]. Let $p_m$ be its monic degree-$m$ orthogonal
polynomial and write its ordered roots as
$a<x_1<\cdots<x_m<b$, as established in
[[thm-gauss-orthogonal-polynomial-has-simple-interior-zeros]]. For
$i=1,\ldots,m$, define the Lagrange cardinal polynomial
$$ \ell_i(X):=\prod_{\substack{1\le j\le m\\j\ne i}}\frac{X-x_j}{x_i-x_j} $$
using the convention of [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]. Define
the **Gaussian quadrature weights** and the **m-node Gaussian rule** by
$$ w_i:=\int_{[a,b]}\ell_i(x)\,d\mu(x),\qquad Q_m(f):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i f(x_i) $$
for any real-valued function $f$ defined at the nodes. This definition
asserts no accuracy; well-definedness of the nodes, cardinal polynomials,
weights, and finite sum is proved in
[[lem-gauss-quadrature-rule-data-well-defined]].

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Assume AC. Fix a finite horizon $T>0$, finite dimensions $d,m\ge1$, and an
open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$. Use a complete usual filtered probability
space and an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments
after time $s$ are independent of $\mathcal F_s$, as in
[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] and
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. Let $b:[0,T]\times U\to\mathbb R^d$
and $\sigma:[0,T]\times U\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be Borel maps. Require
that they are bounded on every compact subset of $[0,T]\times U$ and locally
Lipschitz in the state uniformly in time: for every compact $K\subset U$ there
is $L_K<\infty$ such that, for every $t\in[0,T]$ and $x,y\in K$,
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L_K|x-y|.$$
Let $\xi$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, take values in $U$ almost surely, be
independent of the future Brownian increments, and satisfy $\mathbb E|\xi|^2<\infty$.

For $n\ge1$, set
$$K_n=\{x\in U: |x|\le n,\ \operatorname{dist}(x,U^c)\ge n^{-1}\}.$$
When $U=\mathbb R^d$, interpret $\operatorname{dist}(x,U^c)=+\infty$.
The compact sets $K_n$ are nested and their interiors exhaust $U$. A **local
strong solution up to exit** is the compatible family of stopped adapted
continuous processes $X^{(n)}$ and stopping times $\tau_n$ such that
$$\tau_n=\inf\{t\in[0,T]:X^{(n)}_t\notin\operatorname{int}K_n\}\wedge T, \qquad X^{(n)}_{t\wedge\tau_n}=\xi+\int_0^{t\wedge\tau_n}b(s,X^{(n)}_s)\,ds+ \int_0^{t\wedge\tau_n}\sigma(s,X^{(n)}_s)\,dW_s,$$
with the equation holding indistinguishably and with $X^{(n)}$ constant after
$\tau_n$. Empty early $K_n$ simply give $\tau_n=0$. Compatibility means that
for $m\ge n$, $X^{(m)}$ stopped at $\tau_n$ equals $X^{(n)}$ up to
indistinguishability. The maximal lifetime is $\zeta=\lim_n\tau_n$; for
$t<\zeta$, the common value of $X^{(n)}_t$ for sufficiently large $n$ defines
the maximal local solution $X_t$.

This definition records a local integral equation; it does not assert that a
solution exists or that $\zeta=T$. Those are separate theorem obligations.
The local coefficient conditions allow superlinear growth; global Lipschitz
hypotheses will be imposed only on the coefficient truncations used in the
existence proof.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Fix $n\in\mathbb N$ and the Euclidean space $E=\mathbb R^n$ with inner
product and norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. A **relation** $A$ on
$E$ is a subset of $E\times E$; write $a\in A(x)$ exactly when
$(x,a)\in A$. Its graph is this subset. The relation is **monotone** if
$$\langle x-x',a-a'\rangle\ge0\quad\text{for all }(x,a),(x',a')\in A.$$
It is **maximal monotone** if it is monotone and no strictly larger subset of
$E\times E$ is monotone. This definition is finite-dimensional and makes no
claim about infinite-dimensional spaces.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Fix $n\in\mathbb N$ and the Euclidean space $E=\mathbb R^n$ with inner
product and norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. A **relation** $A$ on
$E$ is a subset of $E\times E$; write $a\in A(x)$ exactly when
$(x,a)\in A$. Its graph is this subset. The relation is **monotone** if
$$\langle x-x',a-a'\rangle\ge0\quad\text{for all }(x,a),(x',a')\in A.$$
It is **maximal monotone** if it is monotone and no strictly larger subset of
$E\times E$ is monotone. This definition is finite-dimensional and makes no
claim about infinite-dimensional spaces.

before.reason: def-mean-field-and-weighted-vortex-particle-systems has no degenerate input parameter case affecting its stated claim.

after.evidence:
def-mean-field-and-weighted-vortex-particle-systems: N>=1 excludes an empty empirical probability sum and includes N=1. Real signed weights may be0; all zero weights give zero signed vorticity and zero weighted velocity. Exact current Definition anchor: For a globally Lipschitz interaction kernel $K$ and $N\ge1$, the equal-probability mean-field particle system is
$$\dot x_i(t)=\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N K(x_i(t),x_j(t)),\qquad i=1,\ldots,N.$$
Its empirical probability measure is $\mu_N(t)=N^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{x_i(t)}$.

For a mollified two-dimensional Biot-Savart kernel $K_\varepsilon$ from [[def-mollified-biot-savart-vortex-kernel]] and real weights $\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_N$, the weighted signed vortex particle system is
$$\dot x_i(t)=\sum_{j=1}^N\Gamma_jK_\varepsilon(x_i(t)-x_j(t)),\qquad i=1,\ldots,N,$$
with vorticity measure $\omega_N(t)=\sum_i\Gamma_i\delta_{x_i(t)}$. If $\Gamma_i=1/N$ and $K(x,y)=K_\varepsilon(x-y)$, the first system is the probability special case. The weighted signed system is a first-order Biot-Savart model.

def-mollified-biot-savart-vortex-kernel: The mollifier has unit mass, so an empty support/zero mollifier is excluded. The scaled family is for positive epsilon; epsilon=0 is not substituted into epsilon^-2 rho(z/epsilon). Exact current Definition anchor: In two dimensions let $z^\perp=(-z_2,z_1)$ and
$$G(z)=\frac1{2\pi}\log|z|,\qquad K(z)=\nabla^\perp G(z)=\frac{z^\perp}{2\pi|z|^2}\quad(z\ne0).$$
The locally integrable value assigned to $K(0)$ is immaterial. Fix a radial, nonnegative smooth bump $\rho$ supported in the unit ball with $\int\rho=1$; its scaled family is the mollifier family of [[def-mollifier-family-generated-by-a-unit-mass-smooth-bump]]. Put $\rho_\varepsilon(z)=\varepsilon^{-2}\rho(z/\varepsilon)$, $G_\varepsilon=G*\rho_\varepsilon$, and
$$K_\varepsilon=K*\rho_\varepsilon.$$
The kernel is a regularized interaction; its smoothness and global Lipschitz property are proved in a separate lemma. It does not define the singular physical interaction at a collision.

source_evidence.fullclaim: Let $V$ be a real Hilbert space, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and write $V^*$ for the continuous real dual. A parameter-dependent coercive elliptic variational problem is a family of bounded bilinear forms $a_\theta:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ and bounded linear functionals $\ell_\theta\in V^*$ such that, on each parameter neighborhood under discussion, $\|a_\theta\|\le M$ and $a_\theta(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2$ for fixed $M<\infty$ and $\alpha>0$. Operator-norm $C^1$ data means that the maps $\theta\mapsto A_\theta\in\mathcal L(V,V^*)$, $A_\theta u:=a_\theta(u,\cdot)$, and $\theta\mapsto\ell_\theta\in V^*$ are continuously Fréchet differentiable. A state at $\theta$ is a vector $u_\theta\in V$ satisfying $a_\theta(u_\theta,v)=\ell_\theta(v)$ for every $v\in V$. When a state is specified, a $C^1$ objective $J:V\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ defines the reduced objective $j(\theta)=J(u_\theta,\theta)$. This definition alone asserts neither state existence nor uniqueness of an optimizer.

Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $N\ge1$, and for $0\le n\le N$ let $U_n\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_n}$ be open. A finite parameterized state-step graph consists of a $C^1$ initial map $x_0:\Theta\to U_0$ and $C^1$ step maps $\Psi_n:U_n\times\Theta\to U_{n+1}$ for $0\le n<N$, such that the recursion $x_{n+1}(\theta)=\Psi_n(x_n(\theta),\theta)$ is defined for every $\theta$ in the chosen parameter neighborhood. A $C^1$ running objective consists of maps $\ell_n:U_n\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ and a terminal objective $\phi:U_N\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$, all $C^1$. Its reduced objective is
$$J(\theta)=\phi(x_N(\theta),\theta)+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\ell_n(x_n(\theta),\theta).$$
The maps and objective define one finite real-arithmetic graph. A gradient of this graph is the derivative of this finite composition; it is not the derivative of an exact implicit solution unless the step map itself is that solution map.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $(V,H,V^*)$ be the real evolution triple and let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open. A parameter-dependent parabolic variational problem specifies, for each $\theta\in\Theta$, a bilinear form $a_\theta(t;\cdot,\cdot)$ and data $f_\theta\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$, $u_{0,\theta}\in H$. A state is a function $u_\theta\in W(0,T;V)$ with continuous $H$ trace, $u_\theta(0)=u_{0,\theta}$, and
$$\langle u_\theta'(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}+a_\theta(t;u_\theta(t),v)=\langle f_\theta(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}$$
for every $v\in V$ and almost every $t$. When a state is specified, a differentiable terminal and running objective $\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)+\int_0^T L(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)\,dt$ defines its reduced objective. This definition does not assert existence, parameter differentiability, or optimality.

additional_source_clauses.text:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $c:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be smooth (that is, $C^\infty$) with $1\le m<d$, let $M$ be a constant symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix, and let $V:U\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. A **holonomic constraint** is the position condition $c(q)=0$. Write $J(q)=Dc(q)$, let $Q=\{q\in U:c(q)=0\}$, and define its regular part by $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}=\{q\in Q:\operatorname{rank}J(q)=m\}$. For $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A(q)=J(q)M^{-1}J(q)^T$ is positive definite. On a compact regular chart $K\subset Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A^{-1}$ is uniformly bounded: $\sup_{q\in K}\|A(q)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty$.

A position-momentum pair $(q,p)$ is **consistent** when $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$. The **regular constrained phase manifold** is
$$\mathcal M=\{(q,p)\in U\times\mathbb R^d:c(q)=0,\ J(q)M^{-1}p=0,\ q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}\}.$$
The ambient canonical two-form is $\omega_0=\sum_{i=1}^d dq_i\wedge dp_i$; its restriction to $\mathcal M$ is denoted $\omega_{\mathcal M}$.

For $v=M^{-1}p$, the constrained Hamilton equations are
$$\dot q=v,\qquad \dot p=-\nabla V(q)-J(q)^T\lambda,$$
with multiplier
$$\lambda=A(q)^{-1}\bigl(D^2c(q)[v,v]-J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)\bigr).$$
Here $D^2c(q)[v,v]\in\mathbb R^m$ has components $v^TD^2c_j(q)v$. This multiplier is the one that keeps both $c(q)=0$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$ satisfied.

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Fix a semi-explicit presentation $x'=f(t,x,z)$, $0=g(t,x,z)$ as in [[def-semi-explicit-index-one-dae-and-consistent-initial-data]] and a sufficiently differentiable consistent local solution. Differentiate the algebraic constraint along the differential equation, substituting $x'=f(t,x,z)$ and any previously obtained derivative relations at each stage. The **differentiation index in this convention** is the least positive integer $k$ for which the original constraint and its first $k$ differentiated equations locally determine $z$ and $z'$, with the equation for the highest derivative of $z$ having an invertible square Jacobian on a neighborhood of the solution. If no such finite $k$ exists, this local index is undefined. This convention counts through the first derivative of the algebraic variables and is local to the fixed presentation; it is not a universal index theory for arbitrary implicit systems.

If $g_z$ is invertible, one differentiation gives

$$
g_t+g_x f+g_z z'=0,
$$

which determines $z'$, so the index is one. If $g_z$ is singular, the index must be checked from the actual differentiated equations; no index-one conclusion follows from this definition alone.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $c:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be smooth (that is, $C^\infty$) with $1\le m<d$, let $M$ be a constant symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix, and let $V:U\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. A **holonomic constraint** is the position condition $c(q)=0$. Write $J(q)=Dc(q)$, let $Q=\{q\in U:c(q)=0\}$, and define its regular part by $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}=\{q\in Q:\operatorname{rank}J(q)=m\}$. For $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A(q)=J(q)M^{-1}J(q)^T$ is positive definite. On a compact regular chart $K\subset Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A^{-1}$ is uniformly bounded: $\sup_{q\in K}\|A(q)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty$.

A position-momentum pair $(q,p)$ is **consistent** when $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$. The **regular constrained phase manifold** is
$$\mathcal M=\{(q,p)\in U\times\mathbb R^d:c(q)=0,\ J(q)M^{-1}p=0,\ q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}\}.$$
The ambient canonical two-form is $\omega_0=\sum_{i=1}^d dq_i\wedge dp_i$; its restriction to $\mathcal M$ is denoted $\omega_{\mathcal M}$.

For $v=M^{-1}p$, the constrained Hamilton equations are
$$\dot q=v,\qquad \dot p=-\nabla V(q)-J(q)^T\lambda,$$
with multiplier
$$\lambda=A(q)^{-1}\bigl(D^2c(q)[v,v]-J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)\bigr).$$
Here $D^2c(q)[v,v]\in\mathbb R^m$ has components $v^TD^2c_j(q)v$. This multiplier is the one that keeps both $c(q)=0$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$ satisfied.

the inverse relation
$$J_{\rho A}:=(I+\rho A)^{-1},\qquad J_{\rho A}(y)=\{x\in E:y-x\in\rho A(x)\},$$
where $\rho A(x)=\{\rho a:a\in A(x)\}$. Its domain is the set of $y$ for
which this value set is nonempty. At this point it may be partial and
set-valued; full domain and single-valuedness are separate conclusions of
[[thm-maximal-monotone-resolvent-is-firmly-nonexpansive]].

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $d\ge1$, and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be a vector field ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]). For $(t,y)\in D$, a step size $h>0$, a parameter $\gamma>0$, and a matrix $\widetilde J\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$, put
$$A_{\gamma,h}(\widetilde J):=I_d-\gamma h\widetilde J.$$
When this matrix is invertible, the **one-stage Rosenbrock step** uses the stage slope $k$ and update
$$A_{\gamma,h}(\widetilde J)k=f(t,y),\qquad \Phi_{\gamma,h}^{\widetilde J}(t,y):=y+hk.$$
The **exact-Jacobian branch** sets $\widetilde J=D_yf(t,y)$, where $D_yf$ is the Jacobian in the state variables as in [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. An approximate-Jacobian branch may supply a different $\widetilde J$; the equation requires the chosen shifted matrix to be invertible. The name **Rosenbrock–Euler** here refers to the case $\gamma=1$. This definition specifies one linearized step and does not say that it solves the full backward-Euler nonlinear equation.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $X,Y$ be nonempty subsets of finite-dimensional real Euclidean spaces and
let $\Psi:X\times Y\to[-\infty,+\infty]$ be an extended-real function. A
pair $(x_*,y_*)$ is a
**saddle point** of $\Psi$ if $\Psi(x_*,y_*)$ is finite and
$$\Psi(x_*,y)\le \Psi(x_*,y_*)\le \Psi(x,y_*)\qquad(x\in X,\ y\in Y).$$
The inequalities must be defined at the arguments they display. For an
equality-constrained problem the primal set may be a product set of
finite-valued pairs $(x,z)$.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $X,Y$ be nonempty subsets of finite-dimensional real Euclidean spaces and
let $\Psi:X\times Y\to[-\infty,+\infty]$ be an extended-real function. A
pair $(x_*,y_*)$ is a
**saddle point** of $\Psi$ if $\Psi(x_*,y_*)$ is finite and
$$\Psi(x_*,y)\le \Psi(x_*,y_*)\le \Psi(x,y_*)\qquad(x\in X,\ y\in Y).$$
The inequalities must be defined at the arguments they display. For an
equality-constrained problem the primal set may be a product set of
finite-valued pairs $(x,z)$.

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let $d,m\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ and $g:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$. A **semi-explicit differential-algebraic equation (DAE)** on $\Omega$ is

$$
x'(t)=f(t,x(t),z(t)),\qquad 0=g(t,x(t),z(t)).
$$

The $x$-coordinates are the **differential variables** because their derivatives occur in the first equation. The $z$-coordinates are the **algebraic variables** because their derivatives do not occur. A solution on an interval $I$ is a pair of functions $x:I\to\mathbb R^d$, $z:I\to\mathbb R^m$ whose graph lies in $\Omega$, with $x$ differentiable, satisfying both displayed equations at every $t\in I$. An initial pair $(x_0,z_0)$ at $t_0$ is **algebraically consistent** when $g(t_0,x_0,z_0)=0$. On the regular index-one branch below this is the algebraic initial condition used for reduction. For higher-index systems, algebraic consistency is only necessary: differentiated constraints may impose additional initial conditions.

At a point with $g(t_*,x_*,z_*)=0$, the presentation is **regular index one** when $f,g$ are $C^1$ near the point and the square Jacobian $g_z(t_*,x_*,z_*)=D_zg(t_*,x_*,z_*)$ is invertible. The [[thm-index-one-dae-implicit-function-reduction]] then supplies a unique local branch $z=\psi(t,x)$ through that point. Only that selected branch is used in local numerical claims. Higher-index systems and points with singular $g_z$ are outside this index-one interface.

Let $d,m\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ and $g:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$. A **semi-explicit differential-algebraic equation (DAE)** on $\Omega$ is

$$
x'(t)=f(t,x(t),z(t)),\qquad 0=g(t,x(t),z(t)).
$$

The $x$-coordinates are the **differential variables** because their derivatives occur in the first equation. The $z$-coordinates are the **algebraic variables** because their derivatives do not occur. A solution on an interval $I$ is a pair of functions $x:I\to\mathbb R^d$, $z:I\to\mathbb R^m$ whose graph lies in $\Omega$, with $x$ differentiable, satisfying both displayed equations at every $t\in I$. An initial pair $(x_0,z_0)$ at $t_0$ is **algebraically consistent** when $g(t_0,x_0,z_0)=0$. On the regular index-one branch below this is the algebraic initial condition used for reduction. For higher-index systems, algebraic consistency is only necessary: differentiated constraints may impose additional initial conditions.

At a point with $g(t_*,x_*,z_*)=0$, the presentation is **regular index one** when $f,g$ are $C^1$ near the point and the square Jacobian $g_z(t_*,x_*,z_*)=D_zg(t_*,x_*,z_*)$ is invertible. The [[thm-index-one-dae-implicit-function-reduction]] then supplies a unique local branch $z=\psi(t,x)$ through that point. Only that selected branch is used in local numerical claims. Higher-index systems and points with singular $g_z$ are outside this index-one interface.

The Jordan total-variation formula gives $M=\omega_0^+(\mathbb R^2)+\omega_0^-(\mathbb R^2)$. If $M=0$, its characteristic solution is the constant zero measure curve. If $M>0$, set $E=\mathbb R^2\times\{+1,-1\}$ with sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2)\otimes 2^{\{+1,-1\}}$, and define the probability measure $\lambda_0$ by $\lambda_0(A\times\{s\})=\omega_0^s(A)/M$ for Borel $A$ and $s\in\{+1,-1\}$; its total mass is one by the displayed formula. such that its time-supremum function is measurable and $\int_E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|Z_t(x,s)|\,d\lambda_0(x,s)<\infty$. It represents the signed measure curve

Only when M>0 is the signed-label probability lambda0 formed. Exact current Definition anchor: Assume AC. Let $\omega_0$ be a finite signed Borel measure on $\mathbb R^2$, set $M=|\omega_0|(\mathbb R^2)$, and let $\omega_0=\omega_0^+-\omega_0^-$ be its Jordan decomposition. The Jordan total-variation formula gives $M=\omega_0^+(\mathbb R^2)+\omega_0^-(\mathbb R^2)$. If $M=0$, its characteristic solution is the constant zero measure curve. If $M>0$, set $E=\mathbb R^2\times\{+1,-1\}$ with sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2)\otimes 2^{\{+1,-1\}}$, and define the probability measure $\lambda_0$ by $\lambda_0(A\times\{s\})=\omega_0^s(A)/M$ for Borel $A$ and $s\in\{+1,-1\}$; its total mass is one by the displayed formula. A signed characteristic solution for the regularized kernel $K_\varepsilon$ on $[0,T]$ is a jointly measurable path map $Z:[0,T]\times E\to\mathbb R^2$, modulo $\lambda_0$-almost everywhere equality, with absolutely continuous paths for almost every label, $Z_0(x,s)=x$, and

$$Z_t(x,s)=x+M\int_0^t\int_E rK_\varepsilon(Z_u(x,s)-Z_u(y,r))\,d\lambda_0(y,r)\,du,$$

such that its time-supremum function is measurable and $\int_E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|Z_t(x,s)|\,d\lambda_0(x,s)<\infty$. It represents the signed measure curve

$$\omega_t=M\int_E s\,\delta_{Z_t(x,s)}\,d\lambda_0(x,s).$$

Here $\omega_0^s$ denotes $\omega_0^+$ when $s=+1$ and $\omega_0^-$ when $s=-1$. The total variation mass is $M$ at time zero, and the sign coordinate records each Jordan part separately.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Fix a dimension $d\ge1$. A finite set $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d$ is
**downward closed** if, whenever $\ell\in\Lambda$ and $\ell_j>0$, the index
$\ell-e_j$ also belongs to $\Lambda$; here $e_j$ is the $j$th coordinate unit
vector. In this pair an admissible Smolyak set is a nonempty finite downward-
closed $\Lambda$ that contains $0$.

For a level hierarchy from [[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]], define
the **Smolyak cubature functional**
$$Q_\Lambda(f):=\sum_{\ell\in\Lambda}(\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)})(f).$$
Each summand is a finite signed weighted sum. Expanding all differences and
adding coefficients at equal points gives one finite signed weight for each
distinct node in
$$\mathcal N_\Lambda:=\bigcup_{\ell\in\Lambda}X_{\ell_1}\times\cdots\times X_{\ell_d}.$$
The **node-union work count** for this direct evaluation convention is
$W(\Lambda):=|\mathcal N_\Lambda|$, so shared nodes are counted once. A
combined weight may be negative or zero; no positivity claim follows from the
definition.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $Q:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be a finite quadrature functional of the form
$$Q(g)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i g(x_i),$$
where $m\ge1$, the nodes $x_i\in[0,1]$ are distinct, and $w_i\in\mathbb R$.
A one-dimensional **nested level hierarchy** is a sequence
$(Q_\ell)_{\ell\in\mathbb N_0}$ of such functionals, with node sets
$X_\ell=\{x_{\ell,i}:1\le i\le m_\ell\}$ satisfying
$X_{\ell-1}\subseteq X_\ell$ for every $\ell\ge1$.
Set $Q_{-1}:=0$, the zero functional, and define the **detail functional**
$$\Delta_0:=Q_0,\qquad \Delta_\ell:=Q_\ell-Q_{\ell-1}\quad(\ell\ge1).$$
Finite sums are as in [[def-finite-sum]]. For each $d\ge1$, the integration
functional used below is $I_d(f):=\int_{[0,1]^d}f$, with the multiple Riemann
integral convention of [[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]].

The convergence and rate results in this pair use the **dyadic composite-
Simpson hierarchy**
$$Q_\ell(g):=Q_S(g;0,1,2^{\ell+1}),\qquad X_\ell=\{k/2^{\ell+1}:0\le k\le2^{\ell+1}\},$$
where $Q_S$ is the even-panel rule of [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]]. The
number of panels is even and at least two. The sets are nested because
$k/2^{\ell}=2k/2^{\ell+1}$, and their weights are nonnegative with total

Use the nonlinear program and SQP subproblem conventions of
[[def-sqp-linearized-quadratic-subproblem]]. For $\rho>0$, define the
nondifferentiable L1 merit function
$$\psi_\rho(x)=f(x)+\rho\left(\|h(x)\|_1+\|[g(x)]_+\|_1\right).$$
For a subproblem step $p$ at $x$, its linearized predicted decrease is
$$D_\rho(x,p)=-\left[\nabla f(x)^Tp+\rho\left(\|h(x)+Dh(x)p\|_1-\|h(x)\|_1+ \|[g(x)+Dg(x)p]_+\|_1-\|[g(x)]_+\|_1\right)\right].$$
A trial fraction $t\in(0,1]$ satisfies the Armijo test with coefficient
$\sigma\in(0,1)$ when
$$\psi_\rho(x+tp)\le\psi_\rho(x)-\sigma tD_\rho(x,p).$$
The definition alone does not assert $D_\rho(x,p)>0$, existence of an
accepted fraction, or convergence of a sequence of accepted SQP steps.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Use the smooth nonlinear program convention of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]]: minimize a $C^2$
objective $f:U\to\mathbb R$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, subject to
$h(x)=0$ and componentwise $g(x)\le0$. Fix a current point $x\in U$ and a
symmetric positive-definite matrix $B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$. The
**SQP quadratic subproblem** is
$$\min_{p\in\mathbb R^n}\quad \nabla f(x)^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp \quad\text{subject to}\quad h(x)+Dh(x)p=0,\quad g(x)+Dg(x)p\le0.$$
The variable $p$ is the proposed displacement. Its feasible set is the
polyhedron defined by the displayed affine constraints. A constraint index
$i$ is **active at $p$** when $g_i(x)+Dg_i(x)p=0$. For equality multiplier
$\nu$ and inequality multipliers $\lambda\ge0$, a **KKT tuple** for the
subproblem satisfies primal feasibility,
$$Bp+\nabla f(x)+Dh(x)^T\nu+Dg(x)^T\lambda=0, \qquad \lambda_i\bigl(g_i(x)+Dg_i(x)p\bigr)=0\quad(1\le i\le m).$$
Rows of $Dh(x)$ and active rows of $Dg(x)$ are stacked in that order in the
subproblem KKT matrix $\begin{bmatrix}B&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}$.

All inequality signs and multiplier signs here agree with the source program:
$g_i\le0$ and $\lambda_i\ge0$.

after.evidence:
def-stiefel-grassmann-optimization-conventions: For r=1 frames are unit vectors; r=n gives the full orthogonal group and the one-point full-dimensional Grassmann quotient. The matrix X=0 is excluded by X^T X=I, while zero tangent vectors are included in the horizontal subspace. Exact current Definition anchor: For integers $1\le r\le n$, the **real Stiefel manifold** is
$$\operatorname{St}(n,r):=\{X\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}:X^{\mathsf T}X=I_r\}.$$
The **real Grassmannian** $\operatorname{Gr}(r,n)$ is the set of $r$-dimensional
linear subspaces of $\mathbb R^n$, identified with the quotient of
$\operatorname{St}(n,r)$ by the right action $X\mapsto XQ$ of
$\operatorname O(r)$. A frame $X$ represents the subspace
$[X]=\operatorname{range}(X)$.

On matrix spaces use the Frobenius inner product
$\langle U,V\rangle_F=\operatorname{tr}(U^{\mathsf T}V)$. Give Stiefel its
induced metric. On the Grassmann quotient use the quotient metric: identify a
tangent vector at $[X]$ with its unique horizontal representative $Z$ satisfying
$X^{\mathsf T}Z=0$, and pair horizontal representatives by the Frobenius inner
product. A Grassmann formula written with a frame representative must be
unchanged under $(X,Z)\mapsto(XQ,ZQ)$ for $Q\in\operatorname O(r)$.

For a matrix $M$, set $\operatorname{sym}(M)=(M+M^{\mathsf T})/2$.

The matrix X=0 is excluded by X^T X=I, while zero tangent vectors are included in the horizontal subspace. Exact current Definition anchor: For integers $1\le r\le n$, the **real Stiefel manifold** is
$$\operatorname{St}(n,r):=\{X\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}:X^{\mathsf T}X=I_r\}.$$
The **real Grassmannian** $\operatorname{Gr}(r,n)$ is the set of $r$-dimensional
linear subspaces of $\mathbb R^n$, identified with the quotient of
$\operatorname{St}(n,r)$ by the right action $X\mapsto XQ$ of
$\operatorname O(r)$. A frame $X$ represents the subspace
$[X]=\operatorname{range}(X)$.

On matrix spaces use the Frobenius inner product
$\langle U,V\rangle_F=\operatorname{tr}(U^{\mathsf T}V)$. Give Stiefel its
induced metric. On the Grassmann quotient use the quotient metric: identify a
tangent vector at $[X]$ with its unique horizontal representative $Z$ satisfying
$X^{\mathsf T}Z=0$, and pair horizontal representatives by the Frobenius inner
product. A Grassmann formula written with a frame representative must be
unchanged under $(X,Z)\mapsto(XQ,ZQ)$ for $Q\in\operatorname O(r)$.

For a matrix $M$, set $\operatorname{sym}(M)=(M+M^{\mathsf T})/2$.

after.evidence:
def-stiefel-qr-polar-retractions: At eta=0 the positive-diagonal QR is X I and the polar Gram factor is I. For every tangent eta, ||(X+eta)v||^2=||v||^2+||eta v||^2 proves full rank even at r=n; the positive norms in the finite Gram-Schmidt recursion never vanish. Exact current Definition anchor: For $X\in\operatorname{St}(n,r)$ and $\eta\in T_X\operatorname{St}(n,r)$,
put $Y=X+\eta$. On the domain where $Y$ has full column rank, let
$\operatorname{qf}(Y)$ be the $Q$ factor in the unique reduced QR factorization
$Y=QR$ with $R$ upper triangular and positive diagonal. Define the **QR map**
by $R_X^{\rm QR}(\eta)=\operatorname{qf}(X+\eta)$. Define the **polar map**
by
$$R_X^{\rm pol}(\eta)=(X+\eta)\bigl((X+\eta)^{\mathsf T}(X+\eta)\bigr)^{-1/2},$$
where the exponent denotes the inverse of the unique positive-definite square
root. Both Stiefel maps induce Grassmann maps by taking the output column space.
The polar formula is right-equivariant:
$R_{XQ}^{\rm pol}(\eta Q)=R_X^{\rm pol}(\eta)Q$ for every $Q\in\operatorname O(r)$.

These are defined only where the displayed input is full rank. In fact, for a
Stiefel tangent $\eta$, $X+\eta$ always has full column rank, since
$\|(X+\eta)v\|_2^2=\|v\|_2^2+\|\eta v\|_2^2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^r$.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $V$ and $U$ be as in [[def-regular-minimum-energy-path-in-a-collision-free-tube]], let $x\in U$, and let $H=\nabla^2V(x)$ use the convention of [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]. Since $V\in C^4(U)$, it is $C^2$; [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]] gives $H^T=H$. In the standard Euclidean inner product this makes the endomorphism represented by $H$ self-adjoint. Therefore the real spectral theorem [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]] applies, and $H$ has ordered eigenvalues $\lambda_1(H)\le\cdots\le\lambda_d(H)$.

A **validated ordered eigenvalue enclosure** is a list of intervals $I_j=[\ell_j,u_j]$ together with an independently checked certificate proving $\lambda_j(H)\in I_j$ for every $j$ and preserving the stated ordering. The exact Hessian $H$, interval arithmetic or another validated spectral method, and all rounding assumptions used by the certificate are part of that external certificate; a Ritz value or residual alone is not, by definition, such a certificate.

For $d\ge2$ and $\gamma>0$, the enclosure certifies **index one with gap $\gamma$** when $u_1\le-\gamma$ and $\ell_j\ge\gamma$ for every $j\ge2$. For $d=1$, the condition is $u_1\le-\gamma$, with no positive-eigenvalue clauses. A validated enclosure records the input evidence; this definition does not assert that any particular eigensolver produces it.

## Definition

Let $V$ and $U$ be as in [[def-regular-minimum-energy-path-in-a-collision-free-tube]], let $x\in U$, and let $H=\nabla^2V(x)$ use the convention of [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]. Since $V\in C^4(U)$, it is $C^2$; [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]] gives $H^T=H$. In the standard Euclidean inner product this makes the endomorphism represented by $H$ self-adjoint. Therefore the real spectral theorem [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]] applies, and $H$ has ordered eigenvalues $\lambda_1(H)\le\cdots\le\lambda_d(H)$.

A **validated ordered eigenvalue enclosure** is a list of intervals $I_j=[\ell_j,u_j]$ together with an independently checked certificate proving $\lambda_j(H)\in I_j$ for every $j$ and preserving the stated ordering. The exact Hessian $H$, interval arithmetic or another validated spectral method, and all rounding assumptions used by the certificate are part of that external certificate; a Ritz value or residual alone is not, by definition, such a certificate.

For $d\ge2$ and $\gamma>0$, the enclosure certifies **index one with gap $\gamma$** when $u_1\le-\gamma$ and $\ell_j\ge\gamma$ for every $j\ge2$. For $d=1$, the condition is $u_1\le-\gamma$, with no positive-eigenvalue clauses. A validated enclosure records the input evidence; this definition does not assert that any particular eigensolver produces it.

Instantiate the strong-constraint objective of [[alg-four-dimensional-variational-assimilation]] with $T=2$, $d_0=d_1=d_2=p_1=p_2=1$, $U_0=U_1=U_2=\mathbb R$, model maps $\Psi_0(x)=2x$ and $\Psi_1(x)=3x$, and observation maps $G_1=G_2=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb R}$. Choose $m_b=y_1=y_2=0$ and the scalar positive-definite covariance matrices $B=\Gamma_1=\Gamma_2=[1]$. The decision variable is the initial state $x_0=\theta$; there are no weak-constraint model-error penalties. The objective is exactly
$$J(\theta)=\tfrac12x_0^2+\tfrac12x_1^2+\tfrac12x_2^2.$$

actualproofparagraphs.2.1: The terminal adjoint seed is $p_2=x_2=6\theta$. The reverse recursion [F1] gives $p_1=x_1+3p_2=20\theta$ and $p_0=x_0+2p_1=41\theta$. Since $Dx_0/D\theta=1$, the adjoint gradient is $p_0=41\theta$, agreeing with the direct derivative. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Take the scalar discrete model $x_0(\theta)=\theta$, $x_1=2x_0$, and $x_2=3x_1$. Instantiate the strong-constraint objective of [[alg-four-dimensional-variational-assimilation]] with $T=2$, $d_0=d_1=d_2=p_1=p_2=1$, $U_0=U_1=U_2=\mathbb R$, model maps $\Psi_0(x)=2x$ and $\Psi_1(x)=3x$, and observation maps $G_1=G_2=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb R}$. Choose $m_b=y_1=y_2=0$ and the scalar positive-definite covariance matrices $B=\Gamma_1=\Gamma_2=[1]$. The decision variable is the initial state $x_0=\theta$; there are no weak-constraint model-error penalties. The objective is exactly
$$J(\theta)=\tfrac12x_0^2+\tfrac12x_1^2+\tfrac12x_2^2.$$

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: Direct substitution gives $x_1=2\theta$ and $x_2=6\theta$, so $J(\theta)=\frac12(1+4+36)\theta^2=\frac{41}{2}\theta^2$ and $J'(\theta)=41\theta$. [given, F2, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.2.1: The terminal adjoint seed is $p_2=x_2=6\theta$. The reverse recursion [F1] gives $p_1=x_1+3p_2=20\theta$ and $p_0=x_0+2p_1=41\theta$. Since $Dx_0/D\theta=1$, the adjoint gradient is $p_0=41\theta$, agreeing with the direct derivative. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

For a continuous $f$ on $[-1,1]$, define its Chebyshev coefficients by
$$a_0(f)=\frac1\pi\int_0^\pi f(\cos\theta)\,d\theta,\qquad a_n(f)=\frac2\pi\int_0^\pi f(\cos\theta)\cos(n\theta)\,d\theta\quad(n\ge1).$$
For the analytic function $f_a(x)=1/(2-x)$, these coefficients are $a_0=1/\sqrt3$ and $a_n=2(2-\sqrt3)^n/\sqrt3$ for $n\ge1$, a geometric decay. For the nonsmooth function $f_s(x)=|x|$, they are $a_0=2/\pi$, $a_{2m}=4(-1)^{m-1}/(\pi(4m^2-1))$ for $m\ge1$, and $a_{2m+1}=0$; the nonzero coefficients decay algebraically like $m^{-2}$.

proofparagraphs.text: Put $q=2-\sqrt3$. Then $0<q<1$, $q^{-1}=2+\sqrt3$, $q+q^{-1}=4$, and $1-q^2=2\sqrt3q$. By [F8], $z=qe^{i\theta}$ has modulus $q$. For $m\ge1$, put $S_m(z)=\sum_{n=1}^m z^n$. Multiplying the finite sum by $1-z$ cancels consecutive terms and gives $(1-z)S_m=z-z^{m+1}$. The triangle inequality in [F3] gives $|1-z|\ge1-q>0$, so $$\left|S_m(z)-\frac z{1-z}\right|=\frac{|z|^{m+1}}{|1-z|}\le\frac{q^{m+1}}{1-q}.$$ Induction using the addition formulas in [F5] and Euler's identity in [F8] gives $z^n=q^n(\cos(n\theta)+i\sin(n\theta))$. Thus $C_m(\theta):=1+2\sum_{n=1}^m q^n\cos(n\theta)$ differs from $1+2\operatorname{Re}(z/(1-z))$ by at most $2q^{m+1}/(1-q)$, uniformly for $\theta\in[0,\pi]$. [F3, F4, F5, F8, algebra, induction]

Multiplying numerator and denominator by $1-q\cos\theta+iq\sin\theta$ and using [F10] gives $$\operatorname{Re}\frac z{1-z}=\frac{q\cos\theta-q^2}{1-2q\cos\theta+q^2}.$$ Hence $$1+2\operatorname{Re}\frac z{1-z}=\frac{1-q^2}{1-2q\cos\theta+q^2}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2-\cos\theta},$$ because the denominator equals $2q(2-\cos\theta)$. By step 1.3, the continuous functions $C_m/\sqrt3$ satisfy $$\sup_{0\le\theta\le\pi}\left|\frac{C_m(\theta)}{\sqrt3}-f_a(\cos\theta)\right|\le\eta_m:=\frac{2q^{m+1}}{\sqrt3(1-q)}\longrightarrow0$$ by [F3]. This also establishes the claimed convergent Chebyshev expansion through [F1]. [F1, F3, F4, F8, F10, step 1.3, algebra]

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
For $\omega=2\pi/3$, consider the annular oscillator
$$ \dot x=(1-r)x-\omega y,\qquad \dot y=(1-r)y+\omega x, \quad r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. $$
The unit circle has period $T=3$ and exact transverse variational equation $\dot\eta=-\eta$, whose multiplier is $e^{-3}<1$. Define one forward-Euler step of length $h$ on that transverse equation by $\eta_1=\eta_0+h(-\eta_0)$. With $h=3$ it multiplies the perturbation by $1-h=-2$, whose modulus exceeds one. This approximate number is not a validated Floquet enclosure.

$$ \dot x=(1-r)x-\omega y,\qquad \dot y=(1-r)y+\omega x, \quad r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. $$
The unit circle has period $T=3$ and exact transverse variational equation $\dot\eta=-\eta$, whose multiplier is $e^{-3}<1$. Define one forward-Euler step of length $h$ on that transverse equation by $\eta_1=\eta_0+h(-\eta_0)$. With $h=3$ it multiplies the perturbation by $1-h=-2$, whose modulus exceeds one. This approximate number is not a validated Floquet enclosure.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: A unit-cycle annular oscillator has a genuinely decaying transverse multiplier while a single length-three Euler variational step gives a spurious factor minus two.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 The identities $\dot r=(xx'+yy')/r$ and $\dot\vartheta=(xy'-yx')/r^2$ give $\dot r=r(1-r)$ and $\dot\vartheta=\omega$. Hence $r=1$ is a periodic orbit with least period $2\pi/\omega=3$. Differentiating $r(1-r)$ at $r=1$ gives $\dot\eta=-\eta$, whose exact solution is $\eta(3)=e^{-3}\eta(0)$; this transverse multiplier lies strictly between zero and one. [given, algebra]

2.1 By the forward-Euler update specified in the Statement, with $a=-1$ and $h=3$ we have $\eta_1=(1-3)\eta_0=-2\eta_0$. Thus its one-step amplification has modulus $2>1$, despite the exact transverse multiplier being stable. Since this calculation provides no enclosure of the truncation defect or exact variational flow, it cannot serve as a certified multiplier claim under [F1]. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Take $f(x)=\tfrac12(x-1)^2$, $g(z)=\tfrac12(z+1)^2$, constraint $x-z=0$,
$\rho=1$, and scaled initial values $z^0=u^0=0$. The primal optimizer is
$x_*=z_*=0$ with value $p_*=1$; $y_*=1$ is a saddle and dual optimizer. The
first two exact scaled ADMM sweeps are
$$(x^1,z^1,u^1)=\left(\tfrac12,-\tfrac14,\tfrac34\right),\qquad (x^2,z^2,u^2)=\left(0,-\tfrac18,\tfrac78\right).$$
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: The fixed two scalar quadratics with unit penalty have zero consensus optimizer and the displayed two exact rational sweeps.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.2 Differentiating the first strictly convex quadratic in [F1] gives $2x^{k+1}=1+z^k-u^k$. At $k=0$ this yields $x^1=1/2$. Differentiating the second gives $2z^{k+1}=x^{k+1}+u^k-1$, hence $z^1=-1/4$ and then $u^1=u^0+x^1-z^1=3/4$. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

3.1 The same two equations give $x^2=(1-1/4-3/4)/2=0$, $z^2=(0+3/4-1)/2=-1/8$, and $u^2=3/4+0-(-1/8)=7/8$. Each subproblem is a strictly convex quadratic, so both minimizers in each of these sweeps are attained and unique. The recurrence values are exact rationals. [A1, F1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 On the feasible set $z=x$, the objective is $$f(x)+g(x)=\tfrac12(x-1)^2+\tfrac12(x+1)^2=x^2+1,$$ which is uniquely minimized at $x=z=0$ with value $1$. For $y_*=1$, $$\mathcal L((x,z),1)=f(x)+g(z)+x-z=1+\tfrac12x^2+\tfrac12z^2\ge1,$$ with equality at $(0,0)$; feasibility makes $\mathcal L((0,0),y)=1$ for every $y$. These are exactly the saddle inequalities [F2]. [A1, given, F2, algebra]

3.1 The same two equations give $x^2=(1-1/4-3/4)/2=0$, $z^2=(0+3/4-1)/2=-1/8$, and $u^2=3/4+0-(-1/8)=7/8$. Each subproblem is a strictly convex quadratic, so both minimizers in each of these sweeps are attained and unique. The recurrence values are exact rationals. [A1, F1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

additional_source_clauses.text:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $c:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be smooth (that is, $C^\infty$) with $1\le m<d$, let $M$ be a constant symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix, and let $V:U\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. A **holonomic constraint** is the position condition $c(q)=0$. Write $J(q)=Dc(q)$, let $Q=\{q\in U:c(q)=0\}$, and define its regular part by $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}=\{q\in Q:\operatorname{rank}J(q)=m\}$. For $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A(q)=J(q)M^{-1}J(q)^T$ is positive definite. On a compact regular chart $K\subset Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A^{-1}$ is uniformly bounded: $\sup_{q\in K}\|A(q)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty$.

A position-momentum pair $(q,p)$ is **consistent** when $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$. The **regular constrained phase manifold** is
$$\mathcal M=\{(q,p)\in U\times\mathbb R^d:c(q)=0,\ J(q)M^{-1}p=0,\ q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}\}.$$
The ambient canonical two-form is $\omega_0=\sum_{i=1}^d dq_i\wedge dp_i$; its restriction to $\mathcal M$ is denoted $\omega_{\mathcal M}$.

For $v=M^{-1}p$, the constrained Hamilton equations are
$$\dot q=v,\qquad \dot p=-\nabla V(q)-J(q)^T\lambda,$$
with multiplier
$$\lambda=A(q)^{-1}\bigl(D^2c(q)[v,v]-J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)\bigr).$$
Here $D^2c(q)[v,v]\in\mathbb R^m$ has components $v^TD^2c_j(q)v$. This multiplier is the one that keeps both $c(q)=0$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$ satisfied.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $D=(-\pi/4,\pi/4)\times(-1/4,1/4)$ and define

$$X(s,n)=(1+n)(\cos s,\sin s),\qquad U:=X(D).$$

This is an open annular sector: its points have radius $3/4<\|x\|_2<5/4$, positive first coordinate, and angular coordinate in $(-\pi/4,\pi/4)$. The displayed polar map is one-to-one on $D$ with smooth inverse $s=\arctan(y/x)$ and $n=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}-1$. Let $a=\pi/6$, $W(s)=(s^2-a^2)^2$, and define $V(X(s,n))=W(s)+n^2/2$ on $U$. The curve $R(t)=X(-a+2at,0)$, $0\le t\le1$, is a regular MEP joining the two minima $X(-a,0)$ and $X(a,0)$. Its image is the circular arc of radius one. The point $X(0,0)$ is an index-one saddle.
