source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $P_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$, $P_1=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$, and
$X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. In the finite-basis model choose
$S=L=I_2$, $h=0$, $E_{xc}=0$, and the real-linear map
$$G(P)=\bigl(\langle P,P_0\rangle_F-\langle P,P_1\rangle_F\bigr)X+\langle P,X\rangle_F(P_0-P_1).$$
At $P_0$ and $P_1$ the commutator residuals are equal and nonzero, making the
two-vector Gram matrix singular. A solver that reports this singular system
uses the specified baseline fallback, even though the exact capped minimizer
exists.

actualproofparagraphs.2.1: Substitution gives $G(P_0)=X$ and $G(P_1)=-X$. The matrices $X$ and $-X$ have eigenvalues $-1,1$, so both iterates have gap $2$. Direct multiplication gives $[G(P_0),P_0]=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}=[G(P_1),P_1]\ne0.$ [step 1.1, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.3.1: Writing the common residual as $J$, the Gram matrix is $B_{ij}=\langle J,J\rangle_F=2,\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix},$ which is singular. The equality-constrained bordered system has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&2&1\\2&2&1\\1&1&0\end{pmatrix}$, whose first two rows coincide, so a solver that reports singularity takes the prescribed fallback. With $C=2$, $c=(1/2,1/2)$ is feasible and minimizes the objective; the objective is constant on $c_1+c_2=1$, so [F2] selects this unique minimum-norm minimizer. If a rank-revealing solver returns it instead of reporting singularity, then $F_{mix}=\tfrac12X-\tfrac12X=0$ has no strict gap, and the proposal algorithm again falls back by its candidate-gap branch. Thus either outcome of this configured solve uses the baseline. [step 2.1, F2, F3, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $P_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$, $P_1=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$, and
$X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. In the finite-basis model choose
$S=L=I_2$, $h=0$, $E_{xc}=0$, and the real-linear map
$$G(P)=\bigl(\langle P,P_0\rangle_F-\langle P,P_1\rangle_F\bigr)X+\langle P,X\rangle_F(P_0-P_1).$$
At $P_0$ and $P_1$ the commutator residuals are equal and nonzero, making the
two-vector Gram matrix singular. A solver that reports this singular system
uses the specified baseline fallback, even though the exact capped minimizer
exists.

With exact gradients, the central dimer estimate is $D_\epsilon=(\epsilon^2/6)e_1$. source_evidence.fullclaim:
Use the sequence-space Dirichlet heat model in [[def-dirichlet-sine-mode-heat-splitting-model]] with zero initial state and forcing coefficients $g_k=1/k$ for odd $k$, zero for even $k$. The generator-domain and boundary mismatch are certified by [[lem-diagonal-heat-semigroup-generator-domain]] and [[lem-dirichlet-forcing-coefficients-exceed-the-generator-domain]]. At a fixed time $T>0$, the exact coordinatewise solution and the Strang approximation with $N=T/h$ steps satisfy
$$c_T h^{5/4}\le\|\widetilde u_N-u(T)\|_{\ell^2}\le C_T h^{5/4}$$
for all sufficiently small $h=T/N$, with constants $c_T,C_T>0$. This is a rigorously specified modal example of boundary-induced order reduction. It is not a convergence theorem for general unbounded PDE operators.

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: For each mode, solving $u_k'=-k^2u_k+g_k$, $u_k(0)=0$, gives $u_k(t)=\frac{g_k}{k^2}(1-e^{-k^2t}).$ Differentiating verifies the equation and initial value. Also $|u_k(t)|\le |g_k|/k^2\le k^{-3}$, so [F4] shows the reference state belongs to $\ell^2$ for every $t\ge0$. [F1, F4, F5, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.1.2: Put $x=k^2h$. By [F1], each Strang coordinate obeys $\widetilde u_{n+1,k}=e^{-x}\widetilde u_{n,k}+h e^{-x/2}g_k.$ Starting from zero and summing this scalar recurrence gives $\widetilde u_{N,k}=h e^{-x/2}\frac{1-e^{-Nx}}{1-e^{-x}}g_k,$ where the finite geometric identity follows by multiplying the sum by $1-e^{-x}$; the denominator is positive because $x>0$ and the exponential is strictly increasing. [F1, F5, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.2.2: Since $Nx=k^2T$, the identity $\frac{h e^{-x/2}}{1-e^{-x}}=\frac{1}{k^2}\frac{x}{e^{x/2}-e^{-x/2}}$ turns the numerical value into the exact modal value times $x/\sigma(x)$, where $\sigma(x):=e^{x/2}-e^{-x/2}$. Therefore for odd $k$, $|\widetilde u_{N,k}-u_k(T)|=k^{-3}(1-e^{-k^2T})q(k^2h),\qquad q(x):=1-\frac{x}{\sigma(x)},$ and the error is zero for even $k$. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.4.1: For sufficiently small $h$, $H\ge8$ and $h\le T$. The interval $[H,2H]$ contains at least $H-1$ integers, and among any $m$ consecutive integers at least $(m-1)/2$ are odd; hence it contains at least $H/4$ odd integers. For each such $k$, $1\le k^2h\le4$, $k^{-6}\ge(2H)^{-6}$, $q(k^2h)\ge q(1)$ by step 2.3, and $1-e^{-k^2T}\ge1-e^{-T/h}>1/2$ since $T/h\ge1$ and $e=1+1+\sum_{n\ge2}1/n!>2$. Therefore the sum of squared errors over these modes is at least $\frac H4\,(2H)^{-6}\,\frac{q(1)^2}{4}=cH^{-5}=c h^{5/2}$ for a constant $c>0$. Taking square roots of the upper bound in step 3.1 and this lower bound proves the claimed two-sided $h^{5/4}$ error rate. [F5, step 2.3, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim: Let $V=H_0^1(0,1)$ with its standard $H^1$ norm, let $\Theta=(-1,\infty)$, and define $a_\theta(u,v)=(1+\theta)\int_0^1u'v'\,dx$ and $\ell(v)=\int_0^1v\,dx$. Take $J(u)=\int_0^1u\,dx$. On a neighborhood of each fixed $\theta>-1$, the form is uniformly coercive in the $H^1$ norm, so this is a parameterized coercive elliptic problem in the sense of [[def-parameterized-elliptic-variational-problem]].

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: Put $w(x)=x(1-x)/2$. Direct differentiation gives $w''=-1$, $w(0)=w(1)=0$, and [F3] gives $w\in V$. For each $v\in V$ and $\varepsilon>0$, [F5] supplies $v_\varepsilon\in C_c^\infty(0,1)$ with $\|v-v_\varepsilon\|_{H^1}<\varepsilon$. By the product rule [F7], $(w'v_\varepsilon)'=w''v_\varepsilon+w'v_\varepsilon'$; since $v_\varepsilon$ vanishes at both endpoints, [F6] gives $\int_0^1w'v_\varepsilon'=\int_0^1v_\varepsilon$. By [F8], the difference between the two sides with $v$ in place of $v_\varepsilon$ is at most $(\|w'\|_{L^2}+1)\varepsilon$, so the weak identity $\int_0^1w'v'=\int_0^1v$ follows as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Also, [F4] gives $a_\theta(v,v)\ge(1+\theta)\|v\|_{H^1}^2/2$; on a neighborhood of each $\theta>-1$ this is a uniform coercivity bound. Hence $u_\theta=w/(1+\theta)$ solves the state equation and is unique. Finally $\int_0^1w=1/12$, so $j(\theta)=1/(12(1+\theta))$. [A1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, given, algebra]

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Realify $\mathbb C^2$ as $\mathbb R^4$ and let
$$H_K=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad V=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad A=-iH_K,\quad B=-iV.$$
Here $H_K$ is a two-level kinetic matrix and $V$ is a Hermitian potential coupling. The finite-dimensional Schrödinger equation is $\psi'=(A+B)\psi=-i(H_K+V)\psi$. Each exact kinetic or potential subflow preserves the Euclidean norm, so every exact Lie or Strang composition does as well. The local errors are nonzero for suitable initial data because the two generators do not commute; no spatial PDE or unbounded-operator conclusion is claimed.

Realify $\mathbb C^2$ as $\mathbb R^4$ and let
$$H_K=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad V=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad A=-iH_K,\quad B=-iV.$$
Here $H_K$ is a two-level kinetic matrix and $V$ is a Hermitian potential coupling. The finite-dimensional Schrödinger equation is $\psi'=(A+B)\psi=-i(H_K+V)\psi$. actualproofparagraphs.1.1: Let $H$ be any of $H_K$, $V$, or $H_K+V$. Its exact flow exists for all real time by [F7], and every solution obeys $\psi'=-iH\psi$. By [F3]–[F6], differentiating the real function $\psi^*\psi$ gives $\frac{d}{dt}(\psi^*\psi)=(\psi')^*\psi+\psi^*\psi'=i\psi^*H^*\psi-i\psi^*H\psi=0,$ where [A1] supplies $H^*=H$. Therefore [F6] makes $\|\psi(t)\|_2^2$ constant on every admitted interval, and each exact subflow and the total flow preserve norm. [A1, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.3.1: For $\psi=e_1$, the Lie coefficient $\frac12C\psi$ is nonzero. The Strang coefficient $-\frac1{24}(CA-AC)\psi-\frac1{12}(CB-BC)\psi$ is also nonzero, since its first coordinate is $-i/6$. Applying [F2] shows the exact subflows retain norm while the Lie and Strang maps have their respective nonzero local splitting defects. [F2, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

The observation is zero and the terminal loss is $J(k)=\frac12Y(k)^2$.

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: Solving the scalar residual gives $(1+hk)Y=u_0$, hence $Y=u_0/(1+hk)$. Since $1+hk>0$, this is the unique root in the stated interval and agrees with the branch in [F1]. [F1, F3, given, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.2.1: Differentiate the residual $(1+hk)Y-u_0=0$: $(1+hk)Y_k+hY=0$, so [F2] gives $Y_k=-hu_0/(1+hk)^2$. Therefore $J_k=YY_k=-hu_0^2/(1+hk)^3$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let $v(t)$ be the capacitor voltage and $i(t)$ the series current in a circuit with capacitance $C>0$, resistance $R>0$, and source voltage $u(t)$. Kirchhoff's current law and voltage law give the semi-explicit system

$$
C v'=i,\qquad 0=R i+v-u(t).
$$

The algebraic equation determines $i=(u(t)-v)/R$. With $C=R=1$, $u(t)=1$, and $v(0)=0$, the consistent initial current is $i(0)=1$, and the reduced ODE is $v'=1-v$. One backward-Euler step of size $h$ gives

$$
v_1=\frac{h}{1+h},\qquad i_1=\frac1{1+h}.
$$

For $h=1$, this is $(v_1,i_1)=(1/2,1/2)$. The pair $v(0)=0,i(0)=0$ is inconsistent for this same source.

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let $v(t)$ be the capacitor voltage and $i(t)$ the series current in a circuit with capacitance $C>0$, resistance $R>0$, and source voltage $u(t)$. Kirchhoff's current law and voltage law give the semi-explicit system

$$
C v'=i,\qquad 0=R i+v-u(t).
$$

The algebraic equation determines $i=(u(t)-v)/R$. With $C=R=1$, $u(t)=1$, and $v(0)=0$, the consistent initial current is $i(0)=1$, and the reduced ODE is $v'=1-v$. One backward-Euler step of size $h$ gives

$$
v_1=\frac{h}{1+h},\qquad i_1=\frac1{1+h}.
$$

For $h=1$, this is $(v_1,i_1)=(1/2,1/2)$. The pair $v(0)=0,i(0)=0$ is inconsistent for this same source.

For $q,v\in\mathbb R^2$, multiplier $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, length $\ell>0$, and gravitational acceleration $g_0>0$, consider

$$
q'=v,\qquad v'=-g_0 e_2-\lambda q,\qquad 0=\frac12(q^\mathsf Tq-\ell^2),
$$

where $e_2=(0,1)^\mathsf T$. The position constraint, tangency condition, and acceleration constraint determine the allowed initial position, velocity, and multiplier. On the constraint manifold the multiplier is

$$
\lambda=\frac{\|v\|_2^2-g_0q_2}{\ell^2}.
$$

This is a regular index-three DAE in the convention of [[def-regular-differentiation-index]].

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Consider the scalar semi-explicit system

$$
x'=z,\qquad 0=g(x,z):=x.
$$

Its algebraic Jacobian is $g_z=0$, so it is not regular index one. In the convention of [[def-regular-differentiation-index]], differentiating $x=0$ once gives $z=0$, and differentiating again gives $z'=0$; the system has differentiation index two. The algebraic residual is $g(x,z)=x$: at every candidate $(0,M)$, it is zero for any $M$, although the algebraic variable of a solution must be $z=0$. Thus no residual-to-$z$-error bound holds near $(0,0)$. The initial pair $(0,1)$ satisfies the algebraic equation but is not consistent with a solution, while $(1,0)$ violates the algebraic equation and cannot be an initial value.

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Consider the scalar semi-explicit system

$$
x'=z,\qquad 0=g(x,z):=x.
$$

Its algebraic Jacobian is $g_z=0$, so it is not regular index one. In the convention of [[def-regular-differentiation-index]], differentiating $x=0$ once gives $z=0$, and differentiating again gives $z'=0$; the system has differentiation index two. The algebraic residual is $g(x,z)=x$: at every candidate $(0,M)$, it is zero for any $M$, although the algebraic variable of a solution must be $z=0$. Thus no residual-to-$z$-error bound holds near $(0,0)$. The initial pair $(0,1)$ satisfies the algebraic equation but is not consistent with a solution, while $(1,0)$ violates the algebraic equation and cannot be an initial value.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $K=\operatorname{diag}(1,2)$ and start exact symmetric Lanczos at the unit
vector $b=e_1=(1,0)^T$. At $m=0$, $K_0(K,b)=\{0\}$ and there is no Ritz value. For every $m\ge1$, $K_m(K,b)=\operatorname{span}\{e_1\}$,
so its only Ritz value is $1$, while the induced Euclidean operator norm is
$\|K\|_2=2$. The Ritz value from this start does not certify the PDHG upper
step-size bound.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: The chosen diagonal matrix and first-coordinate start keep every positive-dimensional Krylov subspace one-dimensional, so the only Ritz value misses the larger matrix norm.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Since $Kb=e_1=b$, every power $K^j b=b$. For $m=0$, the spanning list is empty and its span is $\{0\}$, with no nonzero vector on which to evaluate a Rayleigh quotient. For every $m\ge1$, the spanning set in [F1] consists of repetitions of the single nonzero vector $e_1$, and the Rayleigh quotient on this one-dimensional subspace is $e_1^TKe_1/(e_1^Te_1)=1$. Exact Lanczos terminates after one vector with Ritz value $1$. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 For $x=(x_1,x_2)$, $\|Kx\|_2^2=x_1^2+4x_2^2\le4(x_1^2+x_2^2)$, with equality at $e_2$, so [F4] gives $\|K\|_2=2$. The top eigenspace is $\operatorname{span}\{e_2\}$ and $Pb=0$; [F2] identifies exactly this degenerate branch and supplies no top-eigenvalue convergence bound. Therefore the Ritz value $1$ is not the norm upper bound $2$ required by [F3]. [A1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

Let $K=\operatorname{diag}(1,2)$ and start exact symmetric Lanczos at the unit
vector $b=e_1=(1,0)^T$. At $m=0$, $K_0(K,b)=\{0\}$ and there is no Ritz value. For every $m\ge1$, $K_m(K,b)=\operatorname{span}\{e_1\}$,
so its only Ritz value is $1$, while the induced Euclidean operator norm is
$\|K\|_2=2$. The Ritz value from this start does not certify the PDHG upper
step-size bound.

selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Since $Kb=e_1=b$, every power $K^j b=b$. For $m=0$, the spanning list is empty and its span is $\{0\}$, with no nonzero vector on which to evaluate a Rayleigh quotient. For every $m\ge1$, the spanning set in [F1] consists of repetitions of the single nonzero vector $e_1$, and the Rayleigh quotient on this one-dimensional subspace is $e_1^TKe_1/(e_1^Te_1)=1$. Exact Lanczos terminates after one vector with Ritz value $1$. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 For $x=(x_1,x_2)$, $\|Kx\|_2^2=x_1^2+4x_2^2\le4(x_1^2+x_2^2)$, with equality at $e_2$, so [F4] gives $\|K\|_2=2$. The top eigenspace is $\operatorname{span}\{e_2\}$ and $Pb=0$; [F2] identifies exactly this degenerate branch and supplies no top-eigenvalue convergence bound. Therefore the Ritz value $1$ is not the norm upper bound $2$ required by [F3]. [A1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim: For $u'=\theta u$ on two intervals of length $\tau>0$, define shooting nodes $z_0,z_1,z_2$ and residuals $R_0=z_0-a$, $R_1=z_1-e^{\tau\theta}z_0$, and $R_2=z_2-e^{\tau\theta}z_1$. This uses the exact parameterized ODE flow covered locally by [[lem-parameter-ode-flow-tangent-on-common-tube]]. On the shooting solution set, take terminal objective $J=z_2$.

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: The function $u(t)=e^{\theta t}s$ satisfies $u'=\theta u$ and $u(0)=s$. Conversely, for any solution $v$ with this initial value, the product and chain rules give $(e^{-\theta t}v(t))'=0$. By [F4] this product is constantly $s$ on its solution interval, and positivity and the reciprocal identity in [F3] imply $v(t)=e^{\theta t}s$. Thus the displayed solution exists globally and is unique. [F3, F4]
actualproofparagraphs.2.1: Verify the actual common-tube hypotheses locally at any $(s_*,\theta_*)$. Fix $\varepsilon,\delta,\eta>0$ and restrict the parameters to $|s-s_*|<\varepsilon$, $|\theta-\theta_*|<\delta$. For $-\eta\le t\le\tau+\eta$, $$|e^{\theta t}s|\le B:=(|s_*|+\varepsilon)\exp((|\theta_*|+\delta)(\tau+\eta)).$$ Treat $(s,\theta)$ as the flow parameter, with initial map $(s,\theta)\mapsto s$ and field $(t,u,s,\theta)\mapsto\theta u$ on $\mathbb R^4$. The bounded convex open set $$(-\eta,\tau+\eta)\times(-B-1,B+1)\times(s_*-2\varepsilon,s_*+2\varepsilon)\times(\theta_*-2\delta,\theta_*+2\delta)$$ has compact closure inside that field's domain and contains all these trajectories for $0\le t\le\tau$ and the restricted parameters. The field and initial map are $C^1$. Step 1.1 supplies existence and uniqueness, so [F1] applies. Each shooting interval uses this same argument with its own initial node; since there are two intervals, a common finite bound may also be taken. [F1, F3, step 1.1]

actualproofparagraphs.4.1: Solving $R=0$ gives $z_0=a$, $z_1=Ea$, and $z_2=E^2a$. Direct differentiation yields $D_\theta z_2=2\tau E^2a$. The discrete adjoint for the two flow steps seeds $p_2=1$, then gives $p_1=E$ and $p_0=E^2$; its parameter sum is $\tau E z_0p_1+\tau E z_1p_2=2\tau E^2a$. Thus the reverse gradient agrees with the differentiated shooting solution. [F2, F3, F4, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim:
For each $\delta>0$, let

$$H_\delta=\begin{pmatrix}-\delta&0\\0&\delta\end{pmatrix},\qquad E_\delta=\begin{pmatrix}0&\delta\\\delta&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \widehat H_\delta=H_\delta+E_\delta.$$

The exact lowest eigenvector is $e_1$. The perturbation has Euclidean operator norm $\delta$, which tends to zero with the gap, but the lowest eigenvector of $\widehat H_\delta$ remains at angle $\arctan(\sqrt2-1)>0$ from $e_1$. Thus an absolute perturbation tolerance alone cannot guarantee a mode error tending to zero as the spectral gap collapses.

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Consider the mean-square stable scalar SDE
$$dX_t=-2X_tdt+\sqrt3X_t\,dW_t,\qquad X_0=1.$$
Its exact second moment is $\mathbb E|X_t|^2=e^{-t}$. On a grid with
$h=1/2$, explicit Euler–Maruyama has one-step mean-square amplification
$3/2>1$, even though the deterministic Euler multiplier is zero. The
drift-implicit Euler–Maruyama update has one-step mean-square factor
$5/8<1$.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
On $\mathbb R^2$, let $a(x)=Ax$ and $b(x)=Bx$, where
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
The fields are smooth and their exact flows exist globally. With the bracket convention in [[def-exact-split-flows-lie-strang-and-bracket]], the Lie split has a nonzero $h^2$ local defect and the symmetric Strang split has a nonzero $h^3$ local defect at $x=e_1=(1,0)^T$.

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: By [F4], the linear fields have global exact flows. Direct multiplication gives $BA=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad AB=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad C:=BA-AB=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.$ By [F1], $[a,b](x)=Cx$. [F1, F3, F4, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.2.1: Multiplying once more gives $CA-AC=\begin{pmatrix}0&-2\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad CB-BC=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\2&0\end{pmatrix}.$ These are the matrices of $[a,[a,b]]$ and $[b,[a,b]]$ under the same convention. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.2.2: At $e_1$, $Ce_1=-e_1\ne0$, so [F2] gives Lie local defect $-\frac12h^2e_1+O(h^3)$, whose leading coefficient is nonzero. Thus its local error has exact order two. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.3.1: The Strang leading matrix from step 2.1 is $-\frac1{24}(CA-AC)-\frac1{12}(CB-BC)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1/12\\-1/6&0\end{pmatrix}.$ It sends $e_1$ to $(0,-1/6)^T\ne0$, so [F2] gives a nonzero cubic leading local defect and exact local order three. [F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

For the nonconforming discrete space, take broken piecewise-affine functions on $[0,1/2]\cup[1/2,1]$ that vanish at $0$ and $1$, with no continuity imposed at $1/2$. Identify each such function with its two cellwise slopes, a two-dimensional space $V_h$ of piecewise-constant fields. For $\omega_h=s_L\mathbf1_{[0,1/2]}+s_R\mathbf1_{(1/2,1]}$, define its associated broken function by $U_{\omega_h}(x)=s_Lx$ on the left cell and $U_{\omega_h}(x)=s_R(x-1)$ on the right cell. Use $\widetilde a_h(g,\omega_h):=\int_0^1g\omega_h$ and $F_h(\omega_h):=\int_0^16xU_{\omega_h}(x)\,dx$. The left basis function $\phi_L(x)=2x$ on the first cell and $0$ on the second corresponds to slope field $\omega_L=2\mathbf1_{[0,1/2]}$; it has residual $F_h(\omega_L)-\widetilde a_h(g_u,\omega_L)=-1/4$. Thus the exact solution does not satisfy the broken discrete equation on $V_h$: its consistency residual is nonzero. This is the term retained by the second Strang estimate in place of an exact Galerkin identity. The conforming Céa hypothesis $V_h\subseteq V$ is also false.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
On the annulus $U=\{(x,y):1/2<\sqrt{x^2+y^2}<3/2\}$ consider
$$
\dot x=(1-r)x-y,\qquad \dot y=(1-r)y+x,\qquad r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}.
$$
The unit circle is an orbitally asymptotically stable periodic orbit of period $2\pi$. At $x_*=(1,0)$ the affine phase $\psi_b(x,y)=x-1$ has a singular phase-bordered shooting Jacobian, while $\psi_g(x,y)=y$ is transverse and gives an invertible phase-bordered shooting Jacobian.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: The same stable unit-circle orbit has a singular radial phase border and an invertible transverse phase border; phase conditioning is separate from orbital stability.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 The identities $\dot r=(xx'+yy')/r$ and $\dot\vartheta=(xy'-yx')/r^2$ give $\dot r=r(1-r)$ and $\dot\vartheta=1$. Thus $r=1$ is invariant and $\vartheta(t)=\vartheta(0)+t$, so the least period is $2\pi$. Differentiating $r(1-r)$ at $r=1$ gives the radial variational equation $\dot\rho=-\rho$, whose multiplier is $e^{-2\pi}<1$; the angular variational equation is $\dot\alpha=0$, whose multiplier is $1$. Because the polar-coordinate Jacobian at times $0$ and $2\pi$ is the same invertible matrix, the Cartesian monodromy is conjugate to $\operatorname{diag}(e^{-2\pi},1)$. For $r<1$ the radial derivative is positive, and for $r>1$ it is negative, so nearby radii move monotonically toward $1$ and cannot leave their initial radial interval. Their distance to the unit circle therefore tends to zero while remaining small. This proves orbital asymptotic stability and shows the neutral multiplier is simple. [given, algebra]

2.1 At $(1,0)$ the vector field is $(0,1)$. For $\psi_b=x-1$, $c_b=(1,0)$ and $c_b^\top f(x_*)=0$, so [F2] gives a singular shooting Jacobian. For $\psi_g=y$, $c_g=(0,1)$ and $c_g^\top f(x_*)=1$; the phase multiplier is simple by step 1.1, so [F2] gives an invertible Jacobian. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

additional_source_clauses.text:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $c:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be smooth (that is, $C^\infty$) with $1\le m<d$, let $M$ be a constant symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix, and let $V:U\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. A **holonomic constraint** is the position condition $c(q)=0$. Write $J(q)=Dc(q)$, let $Q=\{q\in U:c(q)=0\}$, and define its regular part by $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}=\{q\in Q:\operatorname{rank}J(q)=m\}$. For $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A(q)=J(q)M^{-1}J(q)^T$ is positive definite. On a compact regular chart $K\subset Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A^{-1}$ is uniformly bounded: $\sup_{q\in K}\|A(q)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty$.

A position-momentum pair $(q,p)$ is **consistent** when $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$. The **regular constrained phase manifold** is
$$\mathcal M=\{(q,p)\in U\times\mathbb R^d:c(q)=0,\ J(q)M^{-1}p=0,\ q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}\}.$$
The ambient canonical two-form is $\omega_0=\sum_{i=1}^d dq_i\wedge dp_i$; its restriction to $\mathcal M$ is denoted $\omega_{\mathcal M}$.

For $v=M^{-1}p$, the constrained Hamilton equations are
$$\dot q=v,\qquad \dot p=-\nabla V(q)-J(q)^T\lambda,$$
with multiplier
$$\lambda=A(q)^{-1}\bigl(D^2c(q)[v,v]-J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)\bigr).$$
Here $D^2c(q)[v,v]\in\mathbb R^m$ has components $v^TD^2c_j(q)v$. This multiplier is the one that keeps both $c(q)=0$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$ satisfied.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Consider the two-cell no-flux graph diffusion matrix
$$L=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$$
and the linear reaction-diffusion semidiscretization $y'=\rho y+D Ly$ with reaction rate $\rho=1$, diffusion coefficient $D=10$. Treat reaction explicitly and diffusion implicitly in [[def-ars222-additive-tableau-and-stages]]. The constant mode has amplification $221/200>1$, matching its reaction growth. With step $h=1/10$, the nonconstant mode has amplification
$$R(1/10,-2)=\frac{661/200-(11/5)\sqrt2}{11-6\sqrt2},$$
which lies strictly between $0$ and $9/80$. This is a two-mode scalar calculation for a finite grid; it makes no nonnormal-matrix or PDE stability assertion.

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: Direct multiplication gives $Lv_0=0$ for $v_0=(1,1)^T$ and $Lv_1=-2v_1$ for $v_1=(1,-1)^T$. These vectors are linearly independent, so they form a basis of $\mathbb R^2$ and diagonalize both $a(y)=y$ and $b(y)=10Ly$. [F4, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.2.1: On each span $\mathbb Rv_j$, every stage equation in [F1] remains in that span. The implicit denominators are $1$ on $v_0$ and $1+20\gamma h>0$ on $v_1$, so the stage solves are unique there. Hence [F2] applies with $z_a=h$ and $z_b=0$ or $z_b=-20h$, respectively. Proof1.1 gives zero projected gradient at e2; Proof2.1 uses sufficiently small nonzero t to get both lower and higher values, while t=0 is the common base point with value1. Criticality is not claimed equivalent to minimality. Exact current Example anchor: For $A=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,2)$, minimize $f(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Ax$ on
$\operatorname{St}(3,1)=S^2$. The point $e_2$ is critical, but one unit-speed
tangent curve decreases $f$ and another increases it. Thus it is a strict
saddle, not a local minimum.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $M=mI_2$, $m,\ell,\omega>0$, $V=0$, and $c(q)=(\|q\|_2^2-\ell^2)/2$. Start from $q_0=(\ell,0)$ and $p_0=(0,m\omega\ell)$, and take $0<h\omega\le\frac12$. The selected exact RATTLE step has
$$q_1=\ell\bigl(\sqrt{1-h^2\omega^2},h\omega\bigr),\qquad p_1=m\omega\ell\bigl(-h\omega,\sqrt{1-h^2\omega^2}\bigr).$$
Its position constraint and momentum tangency are exact. The exact constrained flow rotates by angle $h\omega$, whereas RATTLE rotates by $\arcsin(h\omega)$, so the one-step phase defect is $O(h^3)$ as $h\omega\to0$.

Exact current Example anchor: Assume Countable Choice. Let $\omega_0\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ be nonnegative with mass one, and suppose the smooth Euler flow satisfies $\omega_t=(X_t)_\#\omega_0$, $\dot X_t=(K*\omega_t)(X_t)$, and $\sup_{t\le T}\|\omega_t\|_\infty\le W$, with $\int\sup_{t\le T}|X_t(x)|d\omega_0(x)<\infty$. Approximate it by $N\ge1$ distinct initial positions $x_1^0,\ldots,x_N^0$ with equal weights $1/N$, define $\mu_N^0=N^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{x_i^0}$, and let $E_0=W_1(\omega_0,\mu_N^0)$. Let $r_q(t,x)$ be a common smooth force correction whose tensor Simpson residual is bounded by $\eta_q$, and let the exact particles solve $\dot x_i=\frac1N\sum_jK_\varepsilon(x_i-x_j)+r_q(t,x_i)$. Assume the resulting finite-particle field is jointly $C^4$ in time and state with derivatives through order four bounded on a compact tube containing the exact paths and RK4 stages. For an integer $n\ge1$ with $h=T/n\le h_0$, let $x_i^h(T)$ be their RK4 approximations from the same initial nodes, with all paths and stages in that tube. Define $\omega_{N,h}^{\varepsilon,q}(T)=N^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{x_i^h(T)}$. If $C_{RK}$ is the coefficient from [[thm-rk4-global-error-for-regularized-vortex-particles]] for this $h_0$, then

$$W_1(\omega_T,\omega_{N,h}^{\varepsilon,q}(T))\le e^{2L_\varepsilon T}\left(E_0+T(C_\rho\varepsilon W+\eta_q)\right)+C_{RK}h^4.$$

The RK4 tube hypothesis includes all numerical grid states and every stage generated at each grid step from both the exact start and the numerical start, and both one-step maps are defined, as required by [[thm-rk4-global-error-for-regularized-vortex-particles]].

The initial density has mass1, excluding the zero density; N>=1 includes one particle but the specified initial nodes are distinct. Zero quadrature residual is allowed. Exact current Example anchor: Assume Countable Choice. Let $\omega_0\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ be nonnegative with mass one, and suppose the smooth Euler flow satisfies $\omega_t=(X_t)_\#\omega_0$, $\dot X_t=(K*\omega_t)(X_t)$, and $\sup_{t\le T}\|\omega_t\|_\infty\le W$, with $\int\sup_{t\le T}|X_t(x)|d\omega_0(x)<\infty$. Approximate it by $N\ge1$ distinct initial positions $x_1^0,\ldots,x_N^0$ with equal weights $1/N$, define $\mu_N^0=N^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{x_i^0}$, and let $E_0=W_1(\omega_0,\mu_N^0)$. Let $r_q(t,x)$ be a common smooth force correction whose tensor Simpson residual is bounded by $\eta_q$, and let the exact particles solve $\dot x_i=\frac1N\sum_jK_\varepsilon(x_i-x_j)+r_q(t,x_i)$. Assume the resulting finite-particle field is jointly $C^4$ in time and state with derivatives through order four bounded on a compact tube containing the exact paths and RK4 stages. For an integer $n\ge1$ with $h=T/n\le h_0$, let $x_i^h(T)$ be their RK4 approximations from the same initial nodes, with all paths and stages in that tube. Define $\omega_{N,h}^{\varepsilon,q}(T)=N^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{x_i^h(T)}$. If $C_{RK}$ is the coefficient from [[thm-rk4-global-error-for-regularized-vortex-particles]] for this $h_0$, then

$$W_1(\omega_T,\omega_{N,h}^{\varepsilon,q}(T))\le e^{2L_\varepsilon T}\left(E_0+T(C_\rho\varepsilon W+\eta_q)\right)+C_{RK}h^4.$$

The RK4 tube hypothesis includes all numerical grid states and every stage generated at each grid step from both the exact start and the numerical start, and both one-step maps are defined, as required by [[thm-rk4-global-error-for-regularized-vortex-particles]].

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Take $n=2$, $r=1$, overlap $S=I_2$, Cholesky factor $L=I_2$, $h=0$, and
$E_{xc}=0$ in [[def-finite-basis-projector-energy-model]]. Define
$G:\mathbb H_2\to\mathbb H_2$ by $G(X)=\operatorname{diag}(X_{11},X_{22})$.
Here matrix-entry labels $1,2$ mean the first and second rows/columns, corresponding to canonical indices $0,1$.
The associated response map is $F(P)=G(P)$. Let
$$P_0=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad P_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$
For the undamped occupied-projector iteration, $P_0$ and $P_1$ form a strict
two-cycle even though the occupied/unoccupied eigenvalue gap equals $1$ at both
iterates.

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: For Hermitian $X,Y$, the diagonal entries are real and $\langle G(X),Y\rangle_F=X_{11}Y_{11}+X_{22}Y_{22}=\langle X,G(Y)\rangle_F.$ Thus $G$ is real-linear, Hermitian-valued, and self-adjoint for the Frobenius inner product, so the stated data satisfy [F1]. Each $P_i$ is Hermitian, idempotent, and has trace $1$, hence lies in $\mathcal P_1$. [given, F1, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.1.2: Direct substitution gives $F(P_0)=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ and $F(P_1)=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$. Each matrix has eigenvalues $0<1$, so the strict occupied gap is $1$. By [F2], the lowest eigenspace of $F(P_0)$ is $\operatorname{span}\{(0,1)^T\}$ and that of $F(P_1)$ is $\operatorname{span}\{(1,0)^T\}$; [F4] guarantees these give the unique projectors $\Phi(P_0)=P_1$ and $\Phi(P_1)=P_0$. [given, F2, F4, algebra]

$$\min_{x\in\mathbb R^2}\frac12(x_1^2+x_2^2) \quad\text{subject to }1-x_1-x_2\le0.$$
At $x_0=(0,0)$, use $B=I$ in the SQP quadratic subproblem. The exact
active-set solve returns $p=(1/2,1/2)$, and $x_0+p$ is the unique global
minimizer of the nonlinear problem, with active demand constraint and
multiplier $1/2$.

$f(x)=2(x_1^2+x_2^2-1)-x_1$. At a feasible point
$x=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)=(c,s)$, use multiplier estimate $\nu=-3/2$
and SQP Hessian model $B=I$. For nonzero sufficiently small $\theta$, the
SQP step $p=(s^2,-sc)$ has predicted decrease $D_\rho=s^2>0$, but its full
step increases the L1 merit for every $\rho>0$. The minimum-norm SOC
correction makes the full corrected step pass the Armijo test with
$\sigma=1/4$ for every fixed $\rho>0$ and all sufficiently small nonzero
$\theta$. The existing argument records step 2.1: Since $x^Tp=0$ and $\|p\|_2^2=s^2$, $h(x+p)=s^2$. Also $\nabla f(x)^Tp=-s^2$, so [F2] gives $D_\rho=s^2$. The objective changes by $s^2$, while the equality violation changes from zero to $s^2$; hence the full-step merit change is $(1+\rho)s^2>0$, which fails the Armijo right side $-\sigma s^2<0$. [A1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]; step 3.1: Divide the corrected merit change plus $\sigma D_\rho$ by $s^2$. With $\sigma=1/4$, the result is $-1+c/2+s^2(1/2+\rho/4)+1/4$, which tends to $-1/4$ as $\theta\to0$. It is therefore negative for all sufficiently small nonzero $\theta$, proving the SOC Armijo test passes. The explicit correction also has the $O(s^2)$ norm and $O(s^4)$ residual predicted by [F4]. [A1, F4, F5, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim: Take the scalar decay equation $y'=-\kappa y$ with $\kappa>0$ and $y_0=1$. Treat the whole stiff term explicitly, so $a(y)=-\kappa y$ and $b(y)=0$. IMEX Euler gives amplification $1-h\kappa$; for $h\kappa>2$ its magnitude exceeds one although the exact solution $e^{-\kappa t}$ decays. If instead this same term is implicit, the amplification is $(1+h\kappa)^{-1}$, which lies in $(0,1)$ for every $h\kappa>0$. This scalar comparison does not imply matrix stability for nonnormal operators.

review_basis.full_actual_interface: Let a finite sum have $n,d\ge1$ components and dimension, and let an SVRG epoch and SAGA block each have $m\ge1$ inner updates. Count component-gradient evaluations separately from scalar coordinate arithmetic, and do not cache SVRG snapshot gradients. SVRG uses $n+2m$ component-gradient evaluations per epoch, $O(nd)$ arithmetic to assemble its full gradient, $O(d)$ arithmetic per inner update, and $O(d)$ working storage. SAGA uses $n+m$ component-gradient evaluations during its initialized block and $m$ new evaluations in each later equally long block; initializing its mean takes $O(nd)$ arithmetic, each later update takes $O(d)$ arithmetic, and its table plus auxiliary vectors use $O(nd)$ storage. The cost of evaluating a component gradient is not bounded here. For $n=1000$, $d=20$, and $m=2n=2000$, the gradient counts are 5000 SVRG evaluations per epoch, 3000 SAGA evaluations in the initial block, and 2000 in a later block; the SAGA table has 20,000 scalar coordinates.

review_basis.full_actual_interface: Let a finite sum have $n,d\ge1$ components and dimension, and let an SVRG epoch and SAGA block each have $m\ge1$ inner updates. Count component-gradient evaluations separately from scalar coordinate arithmetic, and do not cache SVRG snapshot gradients. SVRG uses $n+2m$ component-gradient evaluations per epoch, $O(nd)$ arithmetic to assemble its full gradient, $O(d)$ arithmetic per inner update, and $O(d)$ working storage. SAGA uses $n+m$ component-gradient evaluations during its initialized block and $m$ new evaluations in each later equally long block; initializing its mean takes $O(nd)$ arithmetic, each later update takes $O(d)$ arithmetic, and its table plus auxiliary vectors use $O(nd)$ storage. The cost of evaluating a component gradient is not bounded here. For $n=1000$, $d=20$, and $m=2n=2000$, the gradient counts are 5000 SVRG evaluations per epoch, 3000 SAGA evaluations in the initial block, and 2000 in a later block; the SAGA table has 20,000 scalar coordinates.

No infinite-time exponent or orbit-shadowing claim is involved. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

search accepts its full step. The Cauchy and first truncated-CG boundary
steps coincide and have smaller predicted reduction.

$\eta_k=\bar\eta=0$, $\sigma=1/2$, $J=0$, $E,Z\ge1$,

two-dimensional projected solver specified in step 1.1 with iteration count
$m=2$, returning `no-candidate` if its two-dimensional basis or projected matrix is singular
or if $M<2$.

Exact current Example anchor: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and take Lebesgue measure restricted to
the relative Borel sets of $[-1,1]$. Its relative support is all of $[-1,1]$,
so it gives order-three moment data for $m=2$. The moments are
$\mu_0=2$, $\mu_1=0$, $\mu_2=2/3$, and $\mu_3=0$. The monic orthogonal
polynomials through degree two are $p_0=1$, $p_1=X$, and
$p_2=X^2-1/3$. Thus the Gaussian nodes are
$x_1=-1/\sqrt3$ and $x_2=1/\sqrt3$.

The Jacobi matrix is
$$ J_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1/\sqrt3\\1/\sqrt3&0\end{pmatrix}. $$
Its unit eigenvectors $(1,-1)/\sqrt2$ and $(1,1)/\sqrt2$ give weights
$w_1=w_2=\mu_0/2=1$. Therefore
$$ Q_2(f)=f(-1/\sqrt3)+f(1/\sqrt3) $$
is exact for every real polynomial of degree at most three.

where $\mu_j=\int x^j\,d\mu$ for $j=0,1,2$.

## Example

Let $U=\mathbb R^2$ and $V\equiv0$. Every regular path from $A=(0,0)$ to $B=(1,0)$ satisfies the MEP equation, so there are infinitely many distinct continuum MEPs. For a finite string with $M=2$, both chains

$$R_1^{(0)}=(1/2,0),\qquad R_1^{(1)}=(1/2,1)$$

have equal adjacent segment lengths and zero projected force. The improved-tangent NEB ordinary force also vanishes for both. Thus their discrete residuals are exactly zero, although their interior images differ.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The zero potential, fixed endpoints $A,B$, two finite chains, and the definitions of the string, NEB, and stable path comparison.

[F1] [[def-regular-minimum-energy-path-in-a-collision-free-tube]]: a regular path is an MEP when the normal gradient vanishes; fixed endpoints are part of the path data.

[F2] [[alg-finite-image-string-method]]: the string stops when the projected-force and equal-spacing residuals are both within tolerance.

[F3] [[alg-improved-tangent-climbing-neb]]: the ordinary NEB force is projected gradient plus a tangential spring term.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
For $n\ge2$ and $1\le r<n$, the set $\mathcal D_r$ of
[[def-admissible-hermitian-density-domain]] is nonempty, closed, and convex in
$\mathbb H_n$, and complete in the Frobenius metric.

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: The diagonal matrix $D_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,\ldots,1,0,\ldots,0)$ with $r$ ones is Hermitian, satisfies $0\preceq D_0\preceq I_n$, and has trace $r$. Thus $D_0\in\mathcal D_r$, so the domain is nonempty. [given, F1, construct]
actualproofparagraphs.2.1: For every fixed $x\in\mathbb C^n$, entrywise convergence gives $x^*D_kx\to x^*Dx$ and $x^*(I_n-D_k)x\to x^*(I_n-D)x$. Since both sequences are nonnegative, their limits are nonnegative, so $0\preceq D\preceq I_n$. Finite sums commute with coordinate limits, hence $\operatorname{tr}D=\lim_k\operatorname{tr}D_k=r$. Therefore $D\in\mathcal D_r$. [step 1.2, F1, algebra]

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ have continuous first and second partial derivatives. Put $g(x):=\nabla f(x)$ and $G(x):=\nabla^2 f(x)$, using the conventions of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]. Let $K\subseteq U$ be convex. Suppose that for every $x\in K$, $G(x)$ is symmetric and, for constants $0<\mu\le\Lambda<\infty$,
$$ \mu\|w\|_2^2\le w^TG(x)w\quad(w\in\mathbb R^n),\qquad \|G(x)\|_2\le\Lambda, $$
where $\|A\|_2:=\sup_{\|w\|_2=1}\|Aw\|_2$. Then for all $u,v\in K$, with $d:=u-v$,
$$ \|g(u)-g(v)\|_2\le\Lambda\|d\|_2, \qquad (g(u)-g(v))^Td\ge\mu\|d\|_2^2, $$
and
$$ \frac\mu2\|d\|_2^2\le f(u)-f(v)-g(v)^Td\le\frac\Lambda2\|d\|_2^2. $$
Separately, let $W\subseteq U$ be convex, let $x_*\in W$, and suppose $G$ is $L_G$-Lipschitz on $W$ in operator norm. Then for all $u,v\in W$, with $d:=u-v$,
$$ \|g(u)-g(v)-G(x_*)d\|_2 \le L_G\max\{\|u-x_*\|_2,\|v-x_*\|_2\}\,\|d\|_2. $$

Let $B$ be SPD, $s\ne0$, and $y$ satisfy $d:=s^Ty>0$. Let $B^+$ be the Hessian update of [[def-bfgs-curvature-pair-and-update-formulas]]. Define
$$ m_s:=\frac{s^Ty}{\|s\|_2^2},\quad M_s:=\frac{\|y\|_2^2}{s^Ty},\quad q:=\frac{s^TBs}{\|s\|_2^2},\quad \eta:=\frac{s^TBs}{\|s\|_2\|Bs\|_2}. $$
Then $\eta>0$, $\eta\le1$, and
$$ \operatorname{tr}(B^+)=\operatorname{tr}(B)-\frac{\|Bs\|_2^2}{s^TBs} +\frac{\|y\|_2^2}{s^Ty}, \qquad \det(B^+)=\det(B)\frac{s^Ty}{s^TBs}. $$
The potential $\psi(B):=\operatorname{tr}(B)-\log\det(B)$ is well-defined and satisfies $\psi(B)\ge n$. With $h(t):=1-t+\log t$ for $t>0$, one has $h(t)\le0$, with equality exactly at $t=1$; $h$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1)$ and strictly decreasing on $(1,\infty)$, and
$$ \psi(B^+)\le\psi(B)+(M_s-\log m_s-1) +h\!\left(\frac{q}{\eta^2}\right)+\log\eta^2. $$

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Assume AC and the usual filtered Brownian conventions of
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. Let $G$ be a predictable
$d\times m$ matrix process on $[0,T]$ with
$$\mathbb E\left(\int_0^T\|G_s\|_F^2\,ds\right)^{p/2}<\infty$$
for some real $p\ge2$, and let $M_t=\int_0^tG_s\,dW_s$ be its continuous
vector Itô integral. There is a finite constant $C_{p,d}$, independent of
$G$ and $T$, such that
$$\mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|M_t|^p\le C_{p,d}\, \mathbb E\left(\int_0^T\|G_s\|_F^2\,ds\right)^{p/2}.$$

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Assume AC and the usual filtered Brownian conventions of
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. Let $G$ be a predictable
$d\times m$ matrix process on $[0,T]$ with
$$\mathbb E\left(\int_0^T\|G_s\|_F^2\,ds\right)^{p/2}<\infty$$
for some real $p\ge2$, and let $M_t=\int_0^tG_s\,dW_s$ be its continuous
vector Itô integral. There is a finite constant $C_{p,d}$, independent of
$G$ and $T$, such that
$$\mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|M_t|^p\le C_{p,d}\, \mathbb E\left(\int_0^T\|G_s\|_F^2\,ds\right)^{p/2}.$$

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $s\ge1$, let $R_1,\ldots,R_s$ be complex matrices of one fixed shape,
and let $C\ge1$. Define
$$\mathcal C_{s,C}:=\{c\in\mathbb R^s:\sum_{i=1}^s c_i=1,\ \sum_{i=1}^s|c_i|\le C\}$$
and $J(c):=\|\sum_{i=1}^s c_iR_i\|_F^2$. Then $J$ attains a minimum on
$\mathcal C_{s,C}$. Among all minimizers there is a unique vector of minimum
Euclidean norm. This rule defines the exact capped DIIS coefficient vector even
when the least-squares Gram matrix is singular.

actualproofparagraphs.2.1: The map $c\mapsto\sum_i c_iR_i$ is linear and continuous in finite dimensions, and its squared Frobenius norm is continuous by [F1]. The extreme-value theorem gives a minimum; its minimizer set is closed as the inverse image of the singleton containing that minimum, hence compact as a closed subset of $\mathcal C_{s,C}$. Thus [F2] gives a nonempty compact set $M=\operatorname*{argmin}_{c\in\mathcal C_{s,C}}J(c)$. [step 1.1, F1, F2]
actualproofparagraphs.3.1: For $c,d\in\mathcal C_{s,C}$ and $0\le t\le1$, the coefficients $e=(1-t)c+td$ satisfy $\sum_i e_i=(1-t)\sum_i c_i+t\sum_i d_i=1$. By [F3], $\sum_i|e_i|\le(1-t)\sum_i|c_i|+t\sum_i|d_i|\le C$, so $\mathcal C_{s,C}$ is convex. The set $M$ is also convex: for matrices $A,B$ the identity $\|(1-t)A+tB\|_F^2=(1-t)\|A\|_F^2+t\|B\|_F^2-t(1-t)\|A-B\|_F^2$ proves convexity of the squared norm. Applying it to $A=\sum_i c_iR_i$ and $B=\sum_i d_iR_i$ shows $J((1-t)c+td)\le(1-t)J(c)+tJ(d)=\min J$, so the convex combination also minimizes. Since $M$ is compact, the continuous function $c\mapsto\|c\|_2^2$ has a minimizer $c_*\in M$. [step 2.1, F1, F3, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.4.1: If distinct $c,d\in M$ both had minimum Euclidean norm, their midpoint would lie in $M$ and satisfy $\left\|\frac{c+d}{2}\right\|_2^2=\frac{\|c\|_2^2+\|d\|_2^2}{2}-\frac{\|c-d\|_2^2}{4}<\frac{\|c\|_2^2+\|d\|_2^2}{2},$ contradicting minimality. Thus $c_*$ is the unique minimum-norm least-squares minimizer. No nonsingularity of the Gram matrix is needed for existence or tie-breaking. [step 3.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $R:J\to\mathbb R^d$ be a unit-speed $C^3$ curve on an open interval $J$ containing $[0,1]$, and suppose $\max_j\sup_{s\in J_0}|R_j'''(s)|\le M_3/\sqrt d$ on the stencil interval $J_0$. For $s-h,s+h\in J_0$, define

$$d_h:=\frac{R(s+h)-R(s-h)}{2h},\qquad \widehat t_h:=\frac{d_h}{\|d_h\|_2}.$$

If $\delta_h:=M_3h^2/6\le1/2$, then $d_h\ne0$ and

$$\|d_h-R'(s)\|_2\le\delta_h,\qquad \|\widehat t_h-R'(s)\|_2\le4\delta_h.$$

For unequal positive steps $h_-,h_+$ with $s-h_-,s+h_+\in J_0$, define

$$d_{h_-,h_+}:=\frac{h_+}{h_-(h_-+h_+)}(R(s)-R(s-h_-))+\frac{h_-}{h_+(h_-+h_+)}(R(s+h_+)-R(s)).$$

If $\delta_{h_-,h_+}:=M_3h_-h_+/6\le1/2$, then it is nonzero and its unit normalization differs from $R'(s)$ by at most $4\delta_{h_-,h_+}$. In particular, equal steps give an $O(h^2)$ unit-tangent error; quasiuniform unequal steps give an $O(h_-h_+)$ error. No second-order claim is made for a one-sided tangent branch.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $R:J\to\mathbb R^d$ be a unit-speed $C^3$ curve on an open interval $J$ containing $[0,1]$, and suppose $\max_j\sup_{s\in J_0}|R_j'''(s)|\le M_3/\sqrt d$ on the stencil interval $J_0$. For $s-h,s+h\in J_0$, define

$$d_h:=\frac{R(s+h)-R(s-h)}{2h},\qquad \widehat t_h:=\frac{d_h}{\|d_h\|_2}.$$

If $\delta_h:=M_3h^2/6\le1/2$, then $d_h\ne0$ and

$$\|d_h-R'(s)\|_2\le\delta_h,\qquad \|\widehat t_h-R'(s)\|_2\le4\delta_h.$$

For unequal positive steps $h_-,h_+$ with $s-h_-,s+h_+\in J_0$, define

$$d_{h_-,h_+}:=\frac{h_+}{h_-(h_-+h_+)}(R(s)-R(s-h_-))+\frac{h_-}{h_+(h_-+h_+)}(R(s+h_+)-R(s)).$$

If $\delta_{h_-,h_+}:=M_3h_-h_+/6\le1/2$, then it is nonzero and its unit normalization differs from $R'(s)$ by at most $4\delta_{h_-,h_+}$. In particular, equal steps give an $O(h^2)$ unit-tangent error; quasiuniform unequal steps give an $O(h_-h_+)$ error. No second-order claim is made for a one-sided tangent branch.

source_anchors.claim: Fix an output coordinate $j$ of $\widehat\lambda$ and put $q_i=B_{ij}c_i$. By success in [F4] and the relative bound in [F5], $p_i=q_i(1+\alpha_i)$ with $|\alpha_i|\le u$; exact-zero products have $\alpha_i=0$. For each addition $i=2,\ldots,n$, write $s_i=(s_{i-1}+p_i)(1+\beta_i)$ with $|\beta_i|\le u$, taking $\beta_i=0$ when the exact sum is zero. Expanding gives $\widehat\lambda_j=s_n=\sum_{i=1}^n q_i(1+\alpha_i)\prod_{k=\max(2,i)}^n(1+\beta_k)$, with an empty product interpreted as $1$. Each coefficient has at most $n$ factors: for $i=1$ it has one product factor and $n-1$ addition factors, while for $i\ge2$ it has one product factor and $n-i+1$ addition factors. Thus [F6], $nu<1$, and monotonicity of $ku/(1-ku)$ imply that each coefficient differs from $1$ by at most $\gamma_n$. Hence $|\widehat\lambda_j-(B^Tc)_j|\le\gamma_n\sum_i|B_{ij}||c_i|$. Stacking these bounds and applying $\||B|^T|c|\|_2\le\|B\|_F\|c\|_2$ gives $\|\widehat\lambda-B^Tc\|_2\le t\|c\|_2$ and then $\|\widehat\lambda\|_2\le(M+t)\|c\|_2$. Each rounded outer-product entry has error at most $u|\widehat\lambda_i\widehat x_j|$, so its Frobenius error is at most $u(M+t)\|\widehat x\|_2\|c\|_2$. Combining these bounds with step 2.1 gives the stated vector and matrix cotangent estimates.

$$\langle T_m,T_n\rangle_C= \begin{cases} \pi,&m=n=0,\\ \pi/2,&m=n\ge1,\\ 0,&m\ne n. \end{cases}$$
The polynomials $T_0,T_1,\ldots$ form a basis of the real polynomial space, and the pairing is positive definite on continuous real functions on $[-1,1]$. If a continuous real function $h$ satisfies $\langle h,T_n\rangle_C=0$ for every $n\ge0$, then $h=0$ on $[-1,1]$.

$$\langle T_m,T_n\rangle_C= \begin{cases} \pi,&m=n=0,\\ \pi/2,&m=n\ge1,\\ 0,&m\ne n. \end{cases}$$

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let $\kappa,\theta,\sigma>0$ satisfy the Feller condition
$2\kappa\theta\ge\sigma^2$, and put
$$a=\frac{4\kappa\theta-\sigma^2}{8}.$$
For a positive local strong solution of the CIR SDE
$$dX_t=\kappa(\theta-X_t)dt+\sigma\sqrt{X_t}\,dW_t$$
on $U=(0,\infty)$, the Lamperti variable $Z_t=\sqrt{X_t}$ satisfies
$$dZ_t=\left(\frac a{Z_t}-\frac\kappa2 Z_t\right)dt+ \frac\sigma2dW_t$$
up to every compact exit time. Moreover, for every $h>0$, $z\ge0$, and
$\Delta W\in\mathbb R$, the drift-implicit step
$$z_+=z+h\left(\frac a{z_+}-\frac\kappa2z_+\right) +\frac\sigma2\Delta W$$
has exactly one positive root. It is the value defined by
[[alg-cir-lamperti-positive-implicit-scheme]]. The boundary input $z=0$ is
included for the numerical root statement; the CIR solution theorem below
uses $X_0>0$.

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let $\kappa,\theta,\sigma>0$ satisfy the Feller condition
$2\kappa\theta\ge\sigma^2$, and put
$$a=\frac{4\kappa\theta-\sigma^2}{8}.$$
For a positive local strong solution of the CIR SDE
$$dX_t=\kappa(\theta-X_t)dt+\sigma\sqrt{X_t}\,dW_t$$
on $U=(0,\infty)$, the Lamperti variable $Z_t=\sqrt{X_t}$ satisfies
$$dZ_t=\left(\frac a{Z_t}-\frac\kappa2 Z_t\right)dt+ \frac\sigma2dW_t$$
up to every compact exit time. Moreover, for every $h>0$, $z\ge0$, and
$\Delta W\in\mathbb R$, the drift-implicit step
$$z_+=z+h\left(\frac a{z_+}-\frac\kappa2z_+\right) +\frac\sigma2\Delta W$$
has exactly one positive root. It is the value defined by
[[alg-cir-lamperti-positive-implicit-scheme]]. The boundary input $z=0$ is
included for the numerical root statement; the CIR solution theorem below
uses $X_0>0$.

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: Fix $c$ with $|c|<r_0$ and choose $R$ with $|c|<R<r_0$. For $0<|h|<R-|c|$ and each $n\ge1$, $$\frac{(c+h)^n-c^n}{h}=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(c+h)^{n-1-j}c^j,$$ so every term has modulus at most $R^{n-1}$ and the quotient has modulus at most $nR^{n-1}$. Therefore the tail after degree $N$ of the difference-quotient series is bounded uniformly in such $h$ by $\sum_{n>N}n|a_n|R^{n-1}$. The tail of the proposed derivative series at $c$ has the same bound. [given, algebra]

abla F(y),x-yangle ig).$$

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $G$ be a semi-infinite pivot grid and $R\in G$. Let $\eta_0$ be a positive grid measure in $\mathcal M_w(E)$ and let $\eta_t$ solve the no-cutoff dynamics of [[def-infinite-fixed-pivot-sectional-dynamics]]. Let $
u_t$ be the finite sectional solution on the initial grid segment $G\cap[a,R]$ from $
u_0=\eta_0|_{[a,R]}$, extended by zero to $G$. Initialize the finite model's reported reservoir with $L_0=\int_{(R,\infty)}x\,\eta_0(dx)$. If $M_1=M_1(\eta_0)$, then for $0\le t\le T$,
$$d_{BL}(
u_t,\eta_t)\le e^{C_Tt}\left[ rac{M_1}{R}+ rac{2K_*M_1^2t}{aR}ight],$$
where $C_T$ is the bounded-number stability constant from [[thm-infinite-fixed-pivot-sectional-global-wellposedness-and-bl-stability]]. The reservoir records the finite model's overflow mass exactly; the estimate allows the unbounded model's above-cutoff particles to coagulate or fragment and return mass to the retained range.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $\mathcal H$, $A$, and $E_t$ be as in [[def-dirichlet-sine-mode-heat-splitting-model]]. The maps $E_t$ for $t\ge0$ satisfy $E_0=I$ and $E_{t+s}=E_tE_s$, are contractions in $\ell^2$, and are strongly continuous at $t=0$. Define the generator domain to consist of those $u\in\mathcal H$ for which the right limit
$$\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{E_tu-u}{t}$$
exists in $\mathcal H$. This domain is exactly $D(A)=\{u:\sum_{k\ge1}k^4|u_k|^2<\infty\}$, and the limit equals $Au=(-k^2u_k)_{k\ge1}$.

actualproofparagraphs.1.2: For every $x\ge0$, [F4] applied to $s\mapsto e^{-s}$ on $[0,x]$ gives $0\le1-e^{-x}\le x$: the difference is $xe^{-\xi}$ for some $\xi\in[0,x]$, and [F3] bounds $e^{-\xi}$ by $1$. For $u\in D(A)$, the $k$th coordinate of $(E_tu-u)/t$ tends to $-k^2u_k$ by the chain rule and exponential derivative in [F4]. Its difference from that limit has absolute value at most $2k^2|u_k|$, by the same bound. The squared tail of these differences is therefore at most $4\sum_{k>K}k^4|u_k|^2$, which tends to zero; on every finite head the coordinate limits give norm convergence. Hence the right limit exists in $\mathcal H$ and equals $Au$. [F1, F3, F4, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.2.1: Fix $u\in\mathcal H$ and $\varepsilon>0$. By convergence of its square sum, choose $K$ so that $\sum_{k>K}|u_k|^2<\varepsilon^2/4$. The squared norm of the tail of $E_tu-u$ is at most this tail because $|e^{-k^2t}-1|\le1$ by [F3]; for the finitely many indices $k\le K$, continuity of the exponential at zero from [F4] makes their squared sum less than $\varepsilon^2/4$ for all sufficiently small $t>0$. Thus $\|E_tu-u\|_2<\varepsilon$, proving strong continuity at zero. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra, choose]

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $V\in C^4(U,\mathbb R)$ on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, let $x\in U$, and let $v\in\mathbb R^d$ satisfy $\|v\|_2=1$ and $x\pm\epsilon v\in U$ for $\epsilon>0$. Assume the segments $x+[-\epsilon,\epsilon]v$ lie in $U$. Define

$$D_\epsilon(x,v):=\frac{\nabla V(x+\epsilon v)-\nabla V(x-\epsilon v)}{2\epsilon}.$$

If approximate gradient evaluations $\widehat g_\pm$ satisfy $\|\widehat g_\pm-\nabla V(x\pm\epsilon v)\|_2\le\eta$, and $M_4$ bounds the third derivatives of each gradient coordinate in the Taylor remainders on these segments, then

$$\left\|\frac{\widehat g_+-\widehat g_-}{2\epsilon}-\nabla^2V(x)v\right\|_2\le\frac{\sqrt d\,M_4}{6}\epsilon^2+\frac{\eta}{\epsilon}.$$

Thus the deterministic truncation error is $O(\epsilon^2)$ and the force-evaluation error contributes $O(\eta/\epsilon)$. This is an error bound for the Hessian action on the supplied direction; it is not an operator-norm bound for a full Hessian approximation.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $V\in C^4(U,\mathbb R)$ on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, let $x\in U$, and let $v\in\mathbb R^d$ satisfy $\|v\|_2=1$ and $x\pm\epsilon v\in U$ for $\epsilon>0$. Assume the segments $x+[-\epsilon,\epsilon]v$ lie in $U$. Define

$$D_\epsilon(x,v):=\frac{\nabla V(x+\epsilon v)-\nabla V(x-\epsilon v)}{2\epsilon}.$$

If approximate gradient evaluations $\widehat g_\pm$ satisfy $\|\widehat g_\pm-\nabla V(x\pm\epsilon v)\|_2\le\eta$, and $M_4$ bounds the third derivatives of each gradient coordinate in the Taylor remainders on these segments, then

$$\left\|\frac{\widehat g_+-\widehat g_-}{2\epsilon}-\nabla^2V(x)v\right\|_2\le\frac{\sqrt d\,M_4}{6}\epsilon^2+\frac{\eta}{\epsilon}.$$

Thus the deterministic truncation error is $O(\epsilon^2)$ and the force-evaluation error contributes $O(\eta/\epsilon)$. This is an error bound for the Hessian action on the supplied direction; it is not an operator-norm bound for a full Hessian approximation.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $V$ be a Hilbert space and let $V_h\subseteq V$ be a subspace. Suppose the exact form $a$ is coercive with constant $\alpha>0$ in the norm $\|\cdot\|_V$. Let $a_h$ be a discrete form on $V_h$ and suppose

$$|a_h(v_h,v_h)-a(v_h,v_h)|\le\eta_h\|v_h\|_V^2\qquad(v_h\in V_h)$$

for some $\eta_h\ge0$. Then $a_h$ is coercive with constant at least $\alpha-\eta_h$ whenever $\eta_h<\alpha$. In particular, if $\eta_h\le\alpha/2$, then its coercivity constant is at least $\alpha/2$.

Assume Countable Choice and the setting of [[def-parameterized-elliptic-variational-problem]]. On an open neighborhood $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, suppose the same constants $M<\infty$ and $\alpha>0$ give boundedness and coercivity for every $a_\theta$, and $\theta\mapsto A_\theta$ and $\theta\mapsto\ell_\theta$ are operator-norm $C^1$. Then each state $u_\theta$ exists uniquely, the map $\theta\mapsto u_\theta\in V$ is $C^1$, and for each direction $\eta\in\mathbb R^m$ its derivative $w_\eta=D_\theta u_\theta[\eta]$ is the unique solution of
$$a_\theta(w_\eta,v)=D_\theta\ell_\theta[\eta](v)-D_\theta a_\theta[\eta](u_\theta,v)\qquad(v\in V).$$
Uniform coercivity is required on the parameter neighborhood; no differentiability conclusion is asserted at a loss of coercivity.

For nearby $\theta,\widetilde\theta$, the identity $A_{\widetilde\theta}^{-1}-A_\theta^{-1} =A_{\widetilde\theta}^{-1}(A_\theta-A_{\widetilde\theta})A_\theta^{-1}$ shows its operator-norm continuity. The formula in step 2.2, together with continuity of $u_\theta$, $D A_\theta$, and $D\ell_\theta$, then shows $D_\theta u_\theta$ is continuous. Hence the state map is $C^1$. source_evidence.fullclaim:
Use the dimensions, exact interval maps $\Phi_n,K_n$, terminal and initial data, and Euclidean conventions of [[lem-local-c1-step-consistency-implies-tangent-adjoint-gradient-order]]. Let $(A,b,c)$ be a fixed explicit $s$-stage tableau with $c_i=\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}$ and $\sum_i b_i=1$. Its weights may be negative or zero. The actual numerical state and cost maps are
$$Y_i=x+h\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}f(t_n+c_jh,Y_j,\theta),$$
$$\Psi_n=x+h\sum_i b_if(t_n+c_ih,Y_i,\theta),\qquad L_n=h\sum_i b_i\ell(t_n+c_ih,Y_i,\theta).$$
These are exact finite-stage maps, not outputs of a stopped implicit solver.

Assume $f:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R^d$ and $\ell:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R$ are $C^2$ on an open convex time-state-parameter domain. On a common compact convex subset with positive margin in $\mathcal D$, their derivatives through order two are uniformly bounded. All admitted local exact trajectories, all numerical trajectories and stages, and all needed joining segments lie in this domain and common tube, uniformly over the fixed parameter neighborhood and $h\le h_0$. Stage times outside $[t_n,t_{n+1}]$ are included when the tableau has such abscissae. Unique admitted local flows are assumed as in the flow-tangent supplier.

Put $r=d+m$, $E=[I_d\ 0]\in\mathbb R^{d\times r}$ and $E_\theta=[0\ I_m]\in\mathbb R^{m\times r}$. Consider the autonomous augmented system, with components $t,u,\vartheta,C,V,g$,
$$t'=1,\quad \vartheta'=0,\quad u'=f(t,u,\vartheta),\quad C'=\ell(t,u,\vartheta),$$
$$V'=f_u(t,u,\vartheta)V+f_\theta(t,u,\vartheta)E_\theta,$$
$$g'=V^T\ell_u(t,u,\vartheta)^T+E_\theta^T\ell_\theta(t,u,\vartheta)^T.$$
For every admitted local start use $(t_n,x,\theta,0,E,0)$. Suppose application of the same tableau to this augmented system has uniform exact-start defect at most $C_a h^{p+1}$, for an integer $p\ge1$, on a common compact convex augmented tube with positive margin. This is a local augmented-order hypothesis, not a global tangent, adjoint or gradient-error assumption.

Then the actual maps $\Psi_n,L_n$ satisfy all local value, first-derivative, $1+Lh$ derivative-stability, $Mh$ derivative-size, and $Hh$ exact-derivative Lipschitz hypotheses of [[lem-local-c1-step-consistency-implies-tangent-adjoint-gradient-order]], with constants independent of $n,N$. Subject to that lemma's initial and terminal hypotheses, their actual differentiated graph tangents, exact reverse adjoints, and reduced gradients consequently have order-$p$ global error.

A concrete sufficient instantiation for $1\le p\le4$ is that this augmented vector field is $C^4$ with bounded derivatives through order four on its admitted compact convex tube and the tableau satisfies the coefficient equations through order $p$ in [[prop-explicit-rk-order-conditions-through-four]]. Jointly $C^5$ base data $f,\ell$ with bounded derivatives through order five on the base tube are sufficient for this augmented $C^4$ condition. The classical RK4 tableau
$$a_{21}=a_{32}=\tfrac12,\quad a_{43}=1,\quad b=(\tfrac16,\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac16),\quad c=(0,\tfrac12,\tfrac12,1),$$
with all other $a_{ij}=0$, therefore gives the claimed order-four tangent, nodal-adjoint and gradient approximation under these hypotheses. For general $p$, retain the explicit local augmented-defect hypothesis above; no higher-order coefficient theorem is being asserted.

actualproofparagraphs.2.1: Differentiate each actual stage, in its explicit order. If $V_i=D_\xi Y_i$, then $$V_i=E+h\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}(f_{u,j}V_j+f_{\theta,j}E_\theta),$$ $$D_\xi\Psi_n=E+h\sum_i b_i(f_{u,i}V_i+f_{\theta,i}E_\theta),$$ $$D_\xi L_n^T=h\sum_i b_i(V_i^T\ell_{u,i}^T+E_\theta^T\ell_{\theta,i}^T).$$ These are exactly the $V$ and $g$ outputs obtained by applying the same RK tableau to the augmented system. Its $C$ output is $L_n$ and its $u$ output is $\Psi_n$. Consequently the assumed augmented local defect bounds $\Psi_n-\Phi_n$, $L_n-K_n$, and all four first-derivative differences by constants times $h^{p+1}$. Projection to a component does not increase the Euclidean norm; a matrix Frobenius bound also bounds its operator norm. [F1, A1, step 1.1]
actualproofparagraphs.7.1: For the displayed RK4 tableau the eight coefficient sums, in the order stated in the source proposition, are $1,1/2,1/3,1/6,1/4,1/12,1/8,1/24$. For example $Ac=(0,0,1/4,1/2)$, $Ac^{[2]}=(0,0,1/8,1/4)$, and $A^2c=(0,0,0,1/4)$, which verify the mixed sums directly. Hence step 3.2 applies with $p=4$. No division by an individual $b_i$ or internal-stage adjoint order condition occurs in this argument. [F3, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

conjugate $f^*$ from [[def-fenchel-conjugate-on-finite-dimensional-euclidean-space]]

used only to prove properness; closedness and convexity follow directly from
the supremum formula.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: For a proper closed convex primal function, the conjugate has the same three properties; the affine minorant is needed only for properness.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 2.1 The epigraph of $f^*$ is the intersection, over $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, of the closed half-spaces $$\{(s,t):t\ge\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)\}.$$ Each half-space is closed because its defining affine function is continuous, and any intersection of closed sets is closed. Hence $f^*$ is closed in the epigraph convention of [F3]. [A1, F1, F3, F4, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Choose $x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f$ by [F3]. The affine minorant [F2] gives $\langle a,x\rangle-f(x)\le-b$ for every $x$ with finite $f(x)$, so $f^*(a)\le-b<+\infty$. The term at $x_0$ gives $f^*(a)\ge\langle a,x_0\rangle-f(x_0)>-\infty$. Thus $f^*$ is proper. [A1, F1, F2, F3, choose]

1.2 For each $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, the map $s\mapsto\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)$ is finite continuous affine by [F4]. A pointwise supremum of these affine functions is convex: apply each affine function to $(1-\theta)s_0+\theta s_1$, bound by $(1-\theta)f^*(s_0)+\theta f^*(s_1)$, then take the supremum. [A1, F1, F4, algebra]

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex. For every
$x,s\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)+f^*(s)\ge\langle s,x\rangle,$$
with extended-real interpretation. Equality holds exactly when
$x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, $f^*(s)<+\infty$, and
$s\in\partial f(x)$; equivalently, for proper convex $f$, equality itself
forces the two finiteness conditions and the subgradient membership.

\nabla F(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\nabla f_i(x).

Let $T:E\to E$ be firmly nonexpansive on $E=\mathbb R^n$, suppose
$\operatorname{Fix}(T)=\{p:T(p)=p\}$ is nonempty, and start at any $w_0$.

source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Firm nonexpansiveness and a supplied fixed point make the finite-dimensional Picard sequence converge; its zero-dimensional space is handled directly as the singleton.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 If $n=0$, [F3] gives $E=\{0\}$ and the nonempty fixed-point set forces $T(0)=0$; since $w_0=0$, every iterate equals the fixed point. It remains to consider $n\ge1$. Firm nonexpansiveness applied to $w_k$ and a fixed point $p$ gives $\|w_{k+1}-p\|_2^2\le\langle w_{k+1}-p,w_k-p\rangle$. Expanding $w_k-p=(w_{k+1}-p)+(w_k-w_{k+1})$ and rearranging yields $$\|w_{k+1}-p\|_2^2+\|w_{k+1}-w_k\|_2^2\le\|w_k-p\|_2^2.$$ Summing this inequality shows that the distances to $p$ are nonincreasing, the sequence is bounded, and $\sum_k\|w_{k+1}-w_k\|_2^2<\infty$, so the increments tend to zero. [A1, given, F1, F3, algebra]

Assume the hypotheses of [[thm-full-memory-bfgs-global-linear-convergence]] and consider an infinite, nonstationary exact-undamped BFGS run with successful strong Wolfe searches. Suppose $G(x)=\nabla^2 f(x)$ is $L_G$-Lipschitz in operator norm on a neighborhood of $x_*$. With $B_k:=H_k^{-1}$ and $s_k:=x_{k+1}-x_k$, the iterates satisfy
$$ \frac{\|(B_k-G_*)s_k\|_2}{\|s_k\|_2}\longrightarrow0,\qquad G_*:=G(x_*). $$
Since $s_k=\alpha_kp_k$ with $\alpha_k>0$, the same limit holds with $p_k$ in place of $s_k$. This is the Dennis–Moré condition used by the local full-memory superlinear convergence result.

For every $X\in U$ at which the response map of
[[def-self-consistent-projector-response-map]] has a strict $r$th gap,
$\Phi(X)$ is a uniquely defined member of $\mathcal P_r$. Degeneracies among
the first $r$ eigenvalues or among the remaining eigenvalues do not affect it.

The strict gap prevents an eigenspace for one eigenvalue from straddling positions $r$ and $r+1$, so the sum of the first $r$ eigenspaces is the span of exactly the first $r$ basis vectors. [given, F1, algebra]

actualproofparagraphs.2.1: Changing the orthonormal basis within a repeated eigenspace below the gap leaves that entire eigenspace in the sum; changing one within a repeated eigenspace above the gap leaves that entire eigenspace out. Thus the selected subspace does not depend on the eigenbasis chosen in step 1.1. Its orthogonal projector is $P=\sum_{j=1}^r u_ju_j^*$, which satisfies $P=P^*$ and $P^2=P$ by orthonormality. By [F3], $\operatorname{tr}P=\sum_{a=1}^n P_{aa}=\sum_{a=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^r (u_j)_a\overline{(u_j)_a}=\sum_{j=1}^r\sum_{a=1}^n|(u_j)_a|^2=\sum_{j=1}^r1=r$, since each $u_j$ is a unit vector. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, L1, algebra]

abla v\|_{L^2(K)}\|

For the cubic model $m_\sigma$ of [[def-adaptive-cubic-regularization-model]],
with $\sigma>0$ and symmetric $B$, a global minimizer exists. If $g\ne0$ and
$s_*$ is any global minimizer, then $s_*\ne0$ and
$$g+Bs_*+\sigma\|s_*\|_2s_*=0,$$
$$m_\sigma(0)-m_\sigma(s_*)\ge\frac{\sigma}{6}\|s_*\|_2^3.$$

More generally, every $s$ satisfying
$$g^Ts+s^TBs+\sigma\|s\|_2^3=0,\qquad s^TBs+\sigma\|s\|_2^3\ge0$$
has $m_\sigma(0)-m_\sigma(s)\ge\frac{\sigma}{6}\|s\|_2^3$.
For $g\ne0$, put $a=\|g\|_2$ and $q=g^TBg$. The unique minimizer of
the cubic model on the negative-gradient ray $\{-tg:t\ge0\}$ is
$$s_C=-t_Cg,\qquad t_C=\frac{-q+\sqrt{q^2+4\sigma a^5}}{2\sigma a^3}>0.$$

$$
\operatorname{inertia}(H)=\operatorname{inertia}(D)+\operatorname{inertia}(S),
$$
where the triples are added coordinatewise.

Let $c\in\mathbb R^d$, $R>0$, $h>0$, and let $b$ be defined on the closed Euclidean ball $\overline B(c,R)$. Suppose $\|b(z)\|_2\le M$ and $\|b(z)-b(w)\|_2\le L\|z-w\|_2$ there, with $hM\le R$ and $hL<1$. Then the IMEX Euler equation $Y=c+h b(Y)$ has exactly one solution in $\overline B(c,R)$. Every $\widetilde Y$ in that ball satisfies
$$\|\widetilde Y-Y\|_2\le\frac{\|\widetilde Y-c-hb(\widetilde Y)\|_2}{1-hL}.$$
In the algorithm [[alg-imex-euler-step]], $c=y+h a(y)$; this is a local branch result and gives no root outside the selected ball.

source_evidence.fullclaim: Use the implicit Runge–Kutta residual $G(Y)=Y-\mathbf1\otimes u-h(A\otimes I_d)F(Y)$ from [[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]] on a convex open neighborhood of an invariant stage ball. Suppose $F$ is $C^1$ there and $\|D_YF(Y)Z\|_{\infty,2}\le L\|Z\|_{\infty,2}$ for every $Y$ in the ball and every block vector $Z$. If $q=h\|A\|_\infty L<1$, then $D_YG(Y)$ is invertible at every point of the selected stage branch. The contraction hypotheses of [[lem-small-step-implicit-rk-branch-and-residual-error]] provide existence and uniqueness of the root in that ball; this lemma supplies nonsingularity for implicit differentiation.

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: Let $Y,W$ belong to the invariant ball. Its convexity puts $Y+t(W-Y)$ in the ball for $0\le t\le1$. For each block $i$, the curve $\gamma_i(t)=F_i(Y+t(W-Y))$ is continuous on $[0,1]$ and differentiable inside because $F$ is $C^1$ on an open neighborhood. Its derivative obeys $$\|\gamma_i'(t)\|_2\le\|D_YF(Y+t(W-Y))(W-Y)\|_{\infty,2}\le L\|W-Y\|_{\infty,2}.$$ Apply [F3] to each block and take the maximum. This gives $\|F(W)-F(Y)\|_{\infty,2}\le L\|W-Y\|_{\infty,2}$ using only the derivative bound on the ball. Hence [F2] applies with its invariant-ball hypotheses and the selected root exists uniquely. [given, F2, F3]

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let $K$ be a compact set of base points $(t,x)$ in a selected branch chart from [[thm-index-one-dae-implicit-function-reduction]], and put $z_*=\psi(t,x)$. Suppose $g(t,x,\cdot)$ is $C^2$ on $B(z_*,\rho)$ for every $(t,x)\in K$. Let $G_*(t,x)=g_z(t,x,\psi(t,x))$. Assume common constants $\gamma>0$, $\Lambda\ge0$, and $\rho>0$ satisfy

$$
\|G_*(t,x)v\|_2\ge\gamma\|v\|_2\quad(v\in\mathbb R^m),\qquad \|g_z(t,x,z)-G_*(t,x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\Lambda\|z-\psi(t,x)\|_2
$$

for every $(t,x)\in K$ and $z\in B(\psi(t,x),\rho)$; if $\Lambda>0$, assume $\rho\le\gamma/(\sqrt m\,\Lambda)$. Then, uniformly for all such base points and candidates,

$$
\|z-z_*\|_2\le \frac{2}{\gamma}\|g(t,x,z)\|_2.
$$

The estimate is local: it applies only to candidates in the specified branch ball and does not turn a residual into a global branch or uniqueness certificate.

Let $K$ be a compact set of base points $(t,x)$ in a selected branch chart from [[thm-index-one-dae-implicit-function-reduction]], and put $z_*=\psi(t,x)$. Suppose $g(t,x,\cdot)$ is $C^2$ on $B(z_*,\rho)$ for every $(t,x)\in K$. Let $G_*(t,x)=g_z(t,x,\psi(t,x))$. Assume common constants $\gamma>0$, $\Lambda\ge0$, and $\rho>0$ satisfy

$$
\|G_*(t,x)v\|_2\ge\gamma\|v\|_2\quad(v\in\mathbb R^m),\qquad \|g_z(t,x,z)-G_*(t,x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\Lambda\|z-\psi(t,x)\|_2
$$

for every $(t,x)\in K$ and $z\in B(\psi(t,x),\rho)$; if $\Lambda>0$, assume $\rho\le\gamma/(\sqrt m\,\Lambda)$. Then, uniformly for all such base points and candidates,

$$
\|z-z_*\|_2\le \frac{2}{\gamma}\|g(t,x,z)\|_2.
$$

The estimate is local: it applies only to candidates in the specified branch ball and does not turn a residual into a global branch or uniqueness certificate.

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Fix $n,m\ge1$, constants $0<a\le b<\infty$, $C>0$, and $0<\gamma_{\min}\le\gamma_{\max}<\infty$. Suppose every stored pair in a limited-memory BFGS state satisfies
$$ a\|s_i\|_2^2\le s_i^Ty_i\le b\|s_i\|_2^2, \qquad \frac{\|y_i\|_2^2}{s_i^Ty_i}\le C, $$
and each base scale satisfies $\gamma_{\min}\le\gamma\le\gamma_{\max}$. Then the implicit SPD matrix $H_k$ represented by the two-loop recursion of [[alg-lbfgs-two-loop-with-curvature-filter]] has uniform bounds
$$ \underline\lambda I\preceq H_k\preceq\overline\lambda I, \quad T:=\frac n{\gamma_{\min}}+mC,\quad r:=\min\{1,a/T\},\quad D:=\gamma_{\max}^{-n}r^m, \quad \underline\lambda:=\frac1T,\quad \overline\lambda:=\frac{T^{n-1}}{D}. $$
Here $A\preceq B$ means $z^TAz\le z^TBz$ for all $z$. If the stored list is nonempty, the usual scale $(s_{\rm last}^Ty_{\rm last})/\|y_{\rm last}\|_2^2$ lies in $[1/C,b/a^2]$.

$$ a\|s_i\|_2^2\le s_i^Ty_i\le b\|s_i\|_2^2, \qquad \frac{\|y_i\|_2^2}{s_i^Ty_i}\le C, $$
and each base scale satisfies $\gamma_{\min}\le\gamma\le\gamma_{\max}$. Then the implicit SPD matrix $H_k$ represented by the two-loop recursion of [[alg-lbfgs-two-loop-with-curvature-filter]] has uniform bounds
$$ \underline\lambda I\preceq H_k\preceq\overline\lambda I, \quad T:=\frac n{\gamma_{\min}}+mC,\quad r:=\min\{1,a/T\},\quad D:=\gamma_{\max}^{-n}r^m, \quad \underline\lambda:=\frac1T,\quad \overline\lambda:=\frac{T^{n-1}}{D}. $$
Here $A\preceq B$ means $z^TAz\le z^TBz$ for all $z$. If the stored list is nonempty, the usual scale $(s_{\rm last}^Ty_{\rm last})/\|y_{\rm last}\|_2^2$ lies in $[1/C,b/a^2]$.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $a,b\in C^3(U,\mathbb R^d)$ on an open set and let $K_0\subset K\subset U$, where $K_0$ is compact and $K$ is compact and convex. Assume the exact subflows and their compositions from $K_0$ remain in $K$ for all sufficiently small $h>0$, and the fields and derivatives through order three are bounded on $K$. Uniformly for $y\in K_0$,
$$L_h(y)-\Phi_{a+b}^h(y)=\frac{h^2}{2}[a,b](y)+O(h^3),$$
and the Strang expansion, pointwise in $y$, is
$$S_h(y)-\Phi_{a+b}^h(y)=-\frac{h^3}{24}[a,[a,b]](y)-\frac{h^3}{12}[b,[a,b]](y)+o(h^3).$$
The Strang defect is also uniformly $O(h^3)$ on $K_0$. The maps and bracket use [[def-exact-split-flows-lie-strang-and-bracket]]; the claim is finite-dimensional.

actualproofparagraphs.3.1: For any $C^2$ scalar $q$, the chain rule gives $[L_a,L_b]q=D^2q(a,b)+Dq\,Db\,a-D^2q(b,a)-Dq\,Da\,b=Dq\,(Db\,a-Da\,b),$ where [F4] cancels the Hessian terms. Thus $[X,Y]q=L_{[a,b]}q$. Applying this to each coordinate function in step 2.1 gives the stated Lie map expansion. [F1, F4, step 2.1, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.4.1: Step 3.1 also applies with the second field equal to $[a,b]$, which is $C^2$ under the $C^3$ hypotheses. Hence $[X,[X,Y]]=L_{[a,[a,b]]}$ and $[Y,[X,Y]]=L_{[b,[a,b]]}$. Applying step 3.2 to each coordinate yields the stated Strang coefficient and pointwise $o(h^3)$ remainder. The uniform $O(h^3)$ defect follows already from the uniform degree-two remainder in step 1.1 and the equality of all coefficients through degree two. [F1, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

The Strang defect is also uniformly $O(h^3)$ on $K_0$. The maps and bracket use [[def-exact-split-flows-lie-strang-and-bracket]]; the claim is finite-dimensional.

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: For a $C^3$ field $c$ and a smooth scalar coordinate function $q(y)=y_j$, define $L_cq:=Dq\,c$. By [F2], differentiating $q(\Phi_c^t(y))$ successively in $t$ gives $L_cq$, $L_c^2q$, and $L_c^3q$, evaluated along the flow. Three uses of [F3] give the expansion through degree two with integral remainder $\frac12\int_0^h(h-s)^2(L_c^3q)(\Phi_c^s(y))\,ds$; [A1] bounds this remainder uniformly by $C h^3$ and continuity at $s=0$ gives cubic coefficient $\frac16L_c^3q(y)$ with pointwise remainder $o(h^3)$. The same reasoning applies successively to the finite flow compositions. [A1, F2, F3, algebra]

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $p\ge1$ be an integer, $T>0$, $h=T/N\le h_0\le1$, and $t_n=nh$. The state dimension $d$ and parameter dimension $m$ are fixed. All vector norms are Euclidean and all matrix norms are their induced operator norms; gradients are columns.

Consider the continuous objective
$$J(\theta)=\phi(u(T,\theta),\theta)+\int_0^T\ell(t,u(t,\theta),\theta)\,dt,$$
and the actual finite graph
$$x_{n+1}=\Psi_n(x_n,\theta),\qquad J_h(\theta)=\phi_h(x_N,\theta)+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}L_n(x_n,\theta).$$
Assume the hypotheses of the continuous flow-tangent and adjoint-gradient results hold on a common tube. Write $\Phi_n(x,\theta)$ for the exact flow from $t_n$ to $t_{n+1}$ and
$$K_n(x,\theta)=\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}\ell(t,u(t;t_n,x,\theta),\theta)\,dt.$$
These exact maps and the actual numerical maps are $C^1$ on open neighborhoods of the admitted state and parameter sets. For every relevant $n$, all states $x_n,u(t_n)$ and the segment joining them belong to a convex admitted state set. All estimates below hold uniformly on those sets and a fixed parameter neighborhood, independently of $N,n$.

For $r=e,h$, define
$$A_n^e=D_x\Phi_n,\quad B_n^e=D_\theta\Phi_n,\quad c_n^e=D_xK_n^T,\quad d_n^e=D_\theta K_n^T,$$
$$A_n^h=D_x\Psi_n,\quad B_n^h=D_\theta\Psi_n,\quad c_n^h=D_xL_n^T,\quad d_n^h=D_\theta L_n^T.$$
Suppose constants $c_v,c_1,L,M,H\ge0$ satisfy, at each admitted $(x,\theta)$,
$$\|\Psi_n-\Phi_n\|\le c_vh^{p+1},$$
$$\|A_n^h-A_n^e\|,\ \|B_n^h-B_n^e\|,\ \|c_n^h-c_n^e\|,\ \|d_n^h-d_n^e\|\le c_1h^{p+1},$$
$$\|A_n^r\|\le1+Lh,\qquad \|B_n^r\|,\ \|c_n^r\|,\ \|d_n^r\|\le Mh.$$
Each of $A_n^e,B_n^e,c_n^e,d_n^e$ is Lipschitz in $x$, with constant at most $Hh$.

Let $S_0=D_\theta u(0,\theta)$ and $S_0^h=D_\theta x_0(\theta)$. Assume
$$\|x_0-u(0)\|\le c_0h^p,\qquad \|S_0^h-S_0\|\le c_{s0}h^p,\qquad \|S_0\|\le M_0.$$
The terminal costs are $C^1$. The exact columns $D_x\phi^T,D_\theta\phi^T$ have norm at most $M_\phi$ and are Lipschitz in $x$ with constant $H_\phi$; at the same admitted $(x,\theta)$,
$$\|D_x\phi_h^T-D_x\phi^T\|,\ \|D_\theta\phi_h^T-D_\theta\phi^T\|\le C_\phi h^p.$$
No terminal value-error hypothesis is needed for the gradient conclusion.

Let $S_n^h=D_\theta x_n$, and let $p_n^h$ be the exact discrete adjoint of this numerical graph. Let $S(t)=D_\theta u(t)$ and let $p(t)$ be the continuous adjoint with terminal value $D_x\phi(u(T),\theta)^T$. Define
$$E=e^{LT},\quad X=E(c_0+Tc_v),\quad \overline S=E(M_0+TM),\quad \overline P=E(M_\phi+TM),$$
$$R=c_1+HX,\quad C_S=E\{c_{s0}+TR(\overline S+1)\},\quad D=C_\phi+H_\phi X,$$
$$C_P=E\{D+TR(\overline P+1)\},$$
$$C_G=D+c_{s0}\overline P+(M_0+c_{s0})C_P+T\{R(1+\overline P)+MC_P\}.$$
Then
$$\max_n\|x_n-u(t_n)\|\le Xh^p,\qquad \max_n\|S_n^h-S(t_n)\|\le C_Sh^p,$$
$$\max_n\|p_n^h-p(t_n)\|\le C_Ph^p,\qquad \|\nabla J_h-\nabla J\|\le C_Gh^p.$$
These conclusions assume local value and first-derivative consistency, rather than a global adjoint-error estimate. They require no representation by nonnegative quadrature weights.

actualproofparagraphs.1.2: Write $u_n=u(t_n)$ and $e_n=\|x_n-u_n\|$. For $d\ge1$, parameterize the admitted segment by $s\mapsto u_n+s(x_n-u_n)$, $0\le s\le1$. The chain rule and the derivative bound for $\Psi_n$ bound the derivative of its composition with this segment by $(1+Lh)\|x_n-u_n\|$; the vector mean value inequality [F1] therefore gives its endpoint Lipschitz bound with constant $1+Lh$. For $d=0$, the state difference and both endpoint values lie in the zero vector space, so the same bound is immediate. Consequently $$e_{n+1}\le(1+Lh)e_n+c_vh^{p+1}.$$ By [F3], $e_n\le Xh^p$. [A1, F1, F3]
actualproofparagraphs.3.2: At the terminal node, the difference of adjoint seeds is at most $Dh^p$. Subtract the two backward recurrences, splitting $A_h^Tp_h-A_e^Tp_e=A_h^T(p_h-p_e)+(A_h-A_e)^Tp_e$. The Euclidean operator norm of a transpose equals that of the matrix. For every finite-dimensional Euclidean vector $v$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|v\|=\sup_{\|w\|\le1}|w^Tv|$: if $v\ne0$, equality is attained at $w=v/\|v\|$, while for $v=0$ both sides vanish, including in dimension zero. Applying this closed-unit-ball formula to both sides of the pairing gives the transpose identity in all finite dimensions. Therefore $$\|p_n^h-p(t_n)\|\le(1+Lh)\|p_{n+1}^h-p(t_{n+1})\|+R(\overline P+1)h^{p+1}.$$ Reverse the indices and apply [F3]. This gives $C_Ph^p$. [F2, A1, step 2.1]
actualproofparagraphs.4.1: Apply the finite-graph gradient formula to both graphs: $$\nabla J_h=D_\theta\phi_h(x_N)^T+(S_0^h)^Tp_0^h+\sum_{n<N}\{d_n^h(x_n)+(B_n^h(x_n))^Tp_{n+1}^h\},$$ $$\nabla J=D_\theta\phi(u_N)^T+S_0^Tp(0)+\sum_{n<N}\{d_n^e(u_n)+(B_n^e(u_n))^Tp(t_{n+1})\}.$$ The terminal direct-derivative difference is at most $Dh^p$.
