source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $p\ge1$ be an integer, $T>0$, $h=T/N\le h_0\le1$, and $t_n=nh$. The state dimension $d$ and parameter dimension $m$ are fixed. All vector norms are Euclidean and all matrix norms are their induced operator norms; gradients are columns.

Consider the continuous objective
$$J(\theta)=\phi(u(T,\theta),\theta)+\int_0^T\ell(t,u(t,\theta),\theta)\,dt,$$
and the actual finite graph
$$x_{n+1}=\Psi_n(x_n,\theta),\qquad J_h(\theta)=\phi_h(x_N,\theta)+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}L_n(x_n,\theta).$$
Assume the hypotheses of the continuous flow-tangent and adjoint-gradient results hold on a common tube. Write $\Phi_n(x,\theta)$ for the exact flow from $t_n$ to $t_{n+1}$ and
$$K_n(x,\theta)=\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}\ell(t,u(t;t_n,x,\theta),\theta)\,dt.$$
These exact maps and the actual numerical maps are $C^1$ on open neighborhoods of the admitted state and parameter sets. For every relevant $n$, all states $x_n,u(t_n)$ and the segment joining them belong to a convex admitted state set. All estimates below hold uniformly on those sets and a fixed parameter neighborhood, independently of $N,n$.

For $r=e,h$, define
$$A_n^e=D_x\Phi_n,\quad B_n^e=D_\theta\Phi_n,\quad c_n^e=D_xK_n^T,\quad d_n^e=D_\theta K_n^T,$$
$$A_n^h=D_x\Psi_n,\quad B_n^h=D_\theta\Psi_n,\quad c_n^h=D_xL_n^T,\quad d_n^h=D_\theta L_n^T.$$
Suppose constants $c_v,c_1,L,M,H\ge0$ satisfy, at each admitted $(x,\theta)$,
$$\|\Psi_n-\Phi_n\|\le c_vh^{p+1},$$
$$\|A_n^h-A_n^e\|,\ \|B_n^h-B_n^e\|,\ \|c_n^h-c_n^e\|,\ \|d_n^h-d_n^e\|\le c_1h^{p+1},$$
$$\|A_n^r\|\le1+Lh,\qquad \|B_n^r\|,\ \|c_n^r\|,\ \|d_n^r\|\le Mh.$$
Each of $A_n^e,B_n^e,c_n^e,d_n^e$ is Lipschitz in $x$, with constant at most $Hh$.

Let $S_0=D_\theta u(0,\theta)$ and $S_0^h=D_\theta x_0(\theta)$. Assume
$$\|x_0-u(0)\|\le c_0h^p,\qquad \|S_0^h-S_0\|\le c_{s0}h^p,\qquad \|S_0\|\le M_0.$$
The terminal costs are $C^1$. The exact columns $D_x\phi^T,D_\theta\phi^T$ have norm at most $M_\phi$ and are Lipschitz in $x$ with constant $H_\phi$; at the same admitted $(x,\theta)$,
$$\|D_x\phi_h^T-D_x\phi^T\|,\ \|D_\theta\phi_h^T-D_\theta\phi^T\|\le C_\phi h^p.$$
No terminal value-error hypothesis is needed for the gradient conclusion.

Let $S_n^h=D_\theta x_n$, and let $p_n^h$ be the exact discrete adjoint of this numerical graph. Let $S(t)=D_\theta u(t)$ and let $p(t)$ be the continuous adjoint with terminal value $D_x\phi(u(T),\theta)^T$. Define
$$E=e^{LT},\quad X=E(c_0+Tc_v),\quad \overline S=E(M_0+TM),\quad \overline P=E(M_\phi+TM),$$
$$R=c_1+HX,\quad C_S=E\{c_{s0}+TR(\overline S+1)\},\quad D=C_\phi+H_\phi X,$$
$$C_P=E\{D+TR(\overline P+1)\},$$
$$C_G=D+c_{s0}\overline P+(M_0+c_{s0})C_P+T\{R(1+\overline P)+MC_P\}.$$
Then
$$\max_n\|x_n-u(t_n)\|\le Xh^p,\qquad \max_n\|S_n^h-S(t_n)\|\le C_Sh^p,$$
$$\max_n\|p_n^h-p(t_n)\|\le C_Ph^p,\qquad \|\nabla J_h-\nabla J\|\le C_Gh^p.$$
These conclusions assume local value and first-derivative consistency, rather than a global adjoint-error estimate. They require no representation by nonnegative quadrature weights.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ with Jacobian $J=DF$. Take $x_0\in U$ such that $A:=J(x_0)$ is invertible, and let $\beta>0$ be any bound with $\|A^{-1}\|_{\rm op}\le\beta$. Suppose $\epsilon:=\|F(x_0)\|_2>0$, set $r:=2\beta\epsilon$, and assume the open ball $B_2(x_0,2r)$ lies in $U$ and

$$\|J(x)-J(y)\|_{\rm op}\le L\|x-y\|_2\qquad(x,y\in B_2(x_0,2r))$$

for some $L\ge0$ with $\beta Lr\le\tfrac12$. Then $F$ has exactly one zero $x_*$ in the closed ball $\overline B_2(x_0,r)$, and

$$\|x_*-x_0\|_2\le2\beta\|F(x_0)\|_2.$$

If $F(x_0)=0$, then $x_0$ itself is a zero; this separate case makes no local uniqueness assertion.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ with Jacobian $J=DF$. Take $x_0\in U$ such that $A:=J(x_0)$ is invertible, and let $\beta>0$ be any bound with $\|A^{-1}\|_{\rm op}\le\beta$. Suppose $\epsilon:=\|F(x_0)\|_2>0$, set $r:=2\beta\epsilon$, and assume the open ball $B_2(x_0,2r)$ lies in $U$ and

$$\|J(x)-J(y)\|_{\rm op}\le L\|x-y\|_2\qquad(x,y\in B_2(x_0,2r))$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$. For $x\in\mathbb R^n$ define $\|x\|_\infty:=\max_{j<n}|x_j|$, and for a linear map $B:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ define its induced norm by $\|B\|_\infty:=\sup_{z\ne0}\|Bz\|_\infty/\|z\|_\infty$. Let $x_0\in U$, $A:=DF(x_0)$ be invertible, and suppose $\|A^{-1}\|_\infty\le\beta$ for some $\beta>0$. Put $\epsilon:=\|F(x_0)\|_\infty\ge0$, and choose $r>0$ with $\beta\epsilon\le r/2$. Assume $B_\infty(x_0,2r)\subset U$ and

$$\|DF(x)-DF(y)\|_\infty\le L\|x-y\|_\infty\qquad(x,y\in B_\infty(x_0,2r))$$

for some $L\ge0$ with $\beta Lr\le\tfrac12$. Then $F$ has exactly one zero $x_*$ in $\overline B_\infty(x_0,r)$, and

$$\|x_*-x_0\|_\infty\le2\beta\|F(x_0)\|_\infty.$$

In particular, when $F(x_0)=0$ the unique zero in this ball is $x_0$.

Let $x_0\in U$, $A:=DF(x_0)$ be invertible, and suppose $\|A^{-1}\|_\infty\le\beta$ for some $\beta>0$. Put $\epsilon:=\|F(x_0)\|_\infty\ge0$, and choose $r>0$ with $\beta\epsilon\le r/2$. Assume $B_\infty(x_0,2r)\subset U$ and

$$\|DF(x)-DF(y)\|_\infty\le L\|x-y\|_\infty\qquad(x,y\in B_\infty(x_0,2r))$$

for some $L\ge0$ with $\beta Lr\le\tfrac12$. Then $F$ has exactly one zero $x_*$ in $\overline B_\infty(x_0,r)$, and

$$\|x_*-x_0\|_\infty\le2\beta\|F(x_0)\|_\infty.$$

selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Since $\|{-E}\|_2=\|E\|_2\le q<1$, [F1] gives that $T=(I-E)^{-1}$ exists. [given, F1]

2.1 Put $S_N=\sum_{k=0}^N E^k$. By induction and [F2], $\|E^k\|_2\le q^k$, so $\|S_N\|_2\le\sum_{k=0}^Nq^k=(1-q^{N+1})/(1-q)$ by [F3]. The finite identity $(I-E)S_N=I-E^{N+1}$, multiplied on the left by $T$, gives $S_N=T-TE^{N+1}$ and hence $T=S_N+TE^{N+1}$. By the triangle inequality from [F3] and submultiplicativity [F2], $(1-q^{N+1})\|T\|_2\le\|S_N\|_2\le(1-q^{N+1})/(1-q)$. Since $q^{N+1}<1$, division gives $\|T\|_2\le(1-q)^{-1}$. This proves the inverse norm bound without taking a limit of matrices. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $E\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, and let $0\le q<1$ satisfy $\|E\|_2\le q$. Then $I-E$ is invertible and
$$
\|(I-E)^{-1}\|_2\le \frac1{1-q}.
$$
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: An induced Euclidean perturbation norm below one gives invertibility of identity minus the matrix and the reciprocal-one-minus-q norm bound.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Since $\|{-E}\|_2=\|E\|_2\le q<1$, [F1] gives that $T=(I-E)^{-1}$ exists. [given, F1]

2.1 Put $S_N=\sum_{k=0}^N E^k$. By induction and [F2], $\|E^k\|_2\le q^k$, so $\|S_N\|_2\le\sum_{k=0}^Nq^k=(1-q^{N+1})/(1-q)$ by [F3]. The finite identity $(I-E)S_N=I-E^{N+1}$, multiplied on the left by $T$, gives $S_N=T-TE^{N+1}$ and hence $T=S_N+TE^{N+1}$. By the triangle inequality from [F3] and submultiplicativity [F2], $(1-q^{N+1})\|T\|_2\le\|S_N\|_2\le(1-q^{N+1})/(1-q)$. Since $q^{N+1}<1$, division gives $\|T\|_2\le(1-q)^{-1}$. This proves the inverse norm bound without taking a limit of matrices. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $S\in C^1([0,T];\mathbb R^{d\times m})$ and $p\in C^1([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy $S'=A S+B$ and $p'=-A^T p-g$, where $A,B,g$ are continuous and have compatible dimensions. Then
$$p(T)^T S(T)-p(0)^T S(0)=\int_0^T\bigl(-g(t)^T S(t)+p(t)^T B(t)\bigr)\,dt.$$

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: Write $p^T S=\sum_{i=1}^d p_i S_{i,\cdot}$. By [F2] coordinatewise, $(p^TS)'=(p')^TS+p^TS'$. Substituting the two equations yields $(-A^Tp-g)^TS+p^T(AS+B)=-g^TS+p^TB$, because $(A^Tp)^TS=p^TAS$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

Let $S\in C^1([0,T];\mathbb R^{d\times m})$ and $p\in C^1([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy $S'=A S+B$ and $p'=-A^T p-g$, where $A,B,g$ are continuous and have compatible dimensions. Then
$$p(T)^T S(T)-p(0)^T S(0)=\int_0^T\bigl(-g(t)^T S(t)+p(t)^T B(t)\bigr)\,dt.$$

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: Write $p^T S=\sum_{i=1}^d p_i S_{i,\cdot}$. By [F2] coordinatewise, $(p^TS)'=(p')^TS+p^TS'$. Substituting the two equations yields $(-A^Tp-g)^TS+p^T(AS+B)=-g^TS+p^TB$, because $(A^Tp)^TS=p^TAS$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.2.1: The right-hand side in step 1.1 is continuous and hence integrable. Apply [F3] to the scalar function $p^TS$ and integrate step 1.1 over $[0,T]$. This gives the stated endpoint identity. [F3, step 1.1] ∎

$T:D\to E$ satisfy $\|T(p)-T(p')\|_2\le\|p-p'\|_2$ for all $p,p'\in D$.

$$\|q-T(p)\|_2\le\|y-p\|_2\qquad(p\in D).$$

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ and $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta$ be open, and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be continuously differentiable. Let $V_\theta\subseteq\Theta$ be open and $u_0:V_\theta\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^1$. Assume there is a bounded convex open set $O\subset D$ with compact closure in $D$ such that for every $\theta\in V_\theta$ the unique solution of $u'=f(t,u,\theta)$, $u(0)=u_0(\theta)$, exists on $[0,T]$, and all triples $(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)$ lie in $O$. Then $\theta\mapsto u_\theta$ is $C^1$ as a map to $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$. For any $\theta_0\in V_\theta$, its tangent matrix $S(t)=D_\theta u_\theta(t)|_{\theta=\theta_0}$ is the unique solution of
$$S'(t)=D_u f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)S(t)+D_\theta f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0),\qquad S(0)=D u_0(\theta_0).$$
The result is local to the stated common compact tube and claims no differentiability outside it.

actualproofparagraphs.1.2: Put $A(t)=D_u f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)$ and let $B_j(t)$ be column $j$ of $D_\theta f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)$. For each parameter coordinate $j$, the augmented vector $Z_j=(S_{\cdot j},1)$ solves the homogeneous linear system $$Z_j'(t)=\begin{pmatrix}A(t)&B_j(t)\\0&0\end{pmatrix}Z_j(t),\qquad Z_j(0)=\begin{pmatrix}D u_0(\theta_0)_{\cdot j}\\1\end{pmatrix}.$$ Embed $Z_j(0)$ as one column of a square $(d+1)\times(d+1)$ initial matrix, with all other columns zero. The unique linear matrix solution supplied by [F5] has that vector solution as the selected column. Thus the tangent equation has a unique solution for each of the finitely many columns. [A1, F5, construct]

The $B$ terms telescope, $B_0=0$, and the $X$ terms satisfy $\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(X_{k+1}-\kappa X_k)=(1-\kappa)\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}X_k+X_N\ge0$. selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 For each positive-dimensional proximal space, the optimality condition [F2] and extended-real subgradient definition [F3] give the relevant inequality. If a proximal space is zero-dimensional, [F6] says its only point is $0$; its update and test point are both $0$, so the same inequality is equality in that coordinate. Therefore in every dimension the two inequalities are $$g^*(y)-g^*(y^{k+1})\ge\left\langle\frac{y^k-y^{k+1}}\sigma+K\bar x^k,y-y^{k+1}\right\rangle,$$ $$f(x)-f(x^{k+1})\ge\left\langle\frac{x^k-x^{k+1}}\tau-K^*y^{k+1},x-x^{k+1}\right\rangle.$$ The identity $-\langle a-b,c-b\rangle=(\|c-a\|^2-\|c-b\|^2-\|b-a\|^2)/2$ applied to the primal and dual displacement terms gives the two distance differences $E_k-E_{k+1}-X_{k+1}$ and $E_k-E_{k+1}-Y_{k+1}$ in their respective coordinates. The bilinear terms from the primal inequality and the gap expand as $\langle y^{k+1},K(x-x^{k+1})\rangle+\langle Kx^{k+1},y\rangle-\langle Kx,y^{k+1}\rangle=\langle Kx^{k+1},y-y^{k+1}\rangle$. Adding the dual update term $\langle K\bar x^k,y^{k+1}-y\rangle$ gives $\langle K(\bar x^k-x^{k+1}),y^{k+1}-y\rangle$ in the upper bound for $G_{k+1}$. Moving this term to the other side yields $$E_k\ge G_{k+1}+E_{k+1}+X_{k+1}+Y_{k+1}+\langle K(x^{k+1}-\bar x^k),y^{k+1}-y\rangle,$$ where $G_{k+1}=\Phi(x^{k+1},y)-\Phi(x,y^{k+1})$, $E_j=\|x-x^j\|^2/(2\tau)+\|y-y^j\|^2/(2\sigma)$, $X_j=\|x^j-x^{j-1}\|^2/(2\tau)$, and $Y_j=\|y^j-y^{j-1}\|^2/(2\sigma)$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, algebra]

after.reason:
The source retains exactly the model, pairing, grid, or example displayed below. This row asserts no substitute construction for an undefined or collapsed model and does not exclude vanishing data already covered by its formulas. Actual Statement clause: Let $N\ge2$ and $x_j=2\pi j/N$. If integers $k,r$ satisfy $k\equiv r\pmod N$, then
$$
e^{ikx_j}=e^{irx_j}\qquad(0\le j<N).
$$
Consequently, sampling a product of Fourier modes with frequencies $k_1,\ldots,k_s$ gives the same nodal data as the single mode whose frequency is the sum $\sum_{\ell=1}^s k_\ell$ reduced modulo $N$.

The frequency space in [[def-periodic-fourier-collocation-grid]] is real-valued. For complex data, let $\mathcal T_N^{\mathbb C}$ be the space obtained by allowing complex coefficients in that same real basis, and extend its cardinal formula by
$$
I_N^{\mathbb C}V(x):=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}V_jL_j(x),\qquad V\in\mathbb C^N.
$$
Then $I_N^{\mathbb C}V$ is the unique member of $\mathcal T_N^{\mathbb C}$ with nodal data $V$. On real data this formula agrees with $I_N$; in the even case the complex Nyquist samples are interpolated by the real basis function $\cos(Nx/2)$.

$$
e^{ikx_j}=e^{irx_j}\qquad(0\le j<N).
$$

$$

$$

$$

The frequency space in [[def-periodic-fourier-collocation-grid]] is real-valued. For complex data, let $\mathcal T_N^{\mathbb C}$ be the space obtained by allowing complex coefficients in that same real basis, and extend its cardinal formula by
$$
I_N^{\mathbb C}V(x):=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}V_jL_j(x),\qquad V\in\mathbb C^N.

By [F4], there is a local return-time function $\tau(x)$ on the section with $\tau(x_*)=T$ and $\Psi(\tau(x),x)=0$. Differentiating this identity at $x_*$ in a tangent direction $v\in S:=\ker c^\top$ gives $D\tau(x_*)v=-c^\top Mv/(c^\top f(x_*))$. [F1, F2, F4, F5, given, construct]

2.1 The local return map is $P(x)=\phi_{\tau(x)}(x)$. The chain rule and step 1.1 give, for $v\in S$, $ DP(x_*)v=Mv-\frac{f(x_*)c^\top Mv}{c^\top f(x_*)}=\Pi Mv,\qquad \Pi=I-\frac{f(x_*)c^\top}{c^\top f(x_*)}. $ The map $\Pi$ identifies the quotient $\mathbb C^d/\operatorname{span}\{f(x_*)\}$ with $S$: it kills the phase direction and is the identity on $S$. Since $M f(x_*)=f(x_*)$ by [F3], it induces a linear map on this quotient, and $DP(x_*)$ is its conjugate under that identification. [F1, F3, F5, step 1.1, given, algebra]

Let $u_*(s)=(\gamma(Ts),T)$, $0\le s\le1$, be the augmented solution from [[def-phase-bordered-periodic-orbit-bvp]] for a nonconstant $C^2$ autonomous periodic orbit of period $T>0$. Assume its phase multiplier $1$ is algebraically simple and its affine phase covector $c$ satisfies $c^\top f(\gamma(0))\ne0$. For the continuous linearized BVP operator $\mathcal L:X\to Z$ of [[def-linearized-two-point-bvp-operator-and-conditioning]], define
$$ A(s)=D\widetilde f(u_*(s)),\quad a_0=\sup_{0\le s\le1}\|A(s)\|_2, \quad B_2=D_2B(u_*(0),u_*(1)),\quad K_J\ge\|J^{-1}\|_{2\to2}, $$
where $J=\begin{bmatrix}M-I&f(\gamma(0))\\c^\top&0\end{bmatrix}$ and $M=D\phi_T(\gamma(0))$. Put $E=e^{a_0}$ and
$$ K_{\mathcal L}:=(1+a_0)\left[E K_J(1+\|B_2\|_2E)+E\right]+1. $$
Then $\mathcal L$ is bijective and $\|\mathcal L^{-1}\|_{Z\to X}\le K_{\mathcal L}$, with the spaces and norms defined in [[def-linearized-two-point-bvp-operator-and-conditioning]]. All constants are finite and explicit once the stated coefficient and shooting-inverse bounds are supplied.

selected_current_proof_blocks: 2.1 The homogeneous solution with initial value $\xi$ is $U(t,0)\xi$. Its endpoint variation is the derivative of the augmented flow. The first $d$ endpoint coordinates differentiate to $Mv+f(\gamma(0))\tau$ in initial variation $(v,\tau)$: the $v$ column is monodromy, and the period column is $\partial_T\phi_T(\gamma(0))=f(\gamma(0))$ by [F5] and periodicity. Differentiating $B(u_0,u_1)=(x_1-x_0,\psi(x_0))$ by [F7] therefore gives $B_1+B_2U(1,0)=J$. [F1, F2, F5, F7, step 1.1]

2.2 For data $(g,q)\in Z$, let $p$ be the unique solution of $p'=Ap+g$, $p(0)=0$. Local existence and uniqueness follow from [F3]; integrating this equation by [F6] gives $\|p(t)\|_2\le\|g\|_\infty+a_0\int_0^t\|p(s)\|_2ds$, hence $\|p\|_\infty\le E\|g\|_\infty$ by [F4]. This bound extends $p$ through the full interval by [F3]. Every solution with initial value $\xi$ equals $U(t,0)\xi+p(t)$, since their difference solves the homogeneous linear IVP with initial value $\xi$ and uniqueness [F3] applies. [F1, F3, F4, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

All vector and matrix norms below are Euclidean and induced Euclidean norms, and the product norm on $(u,\tau)\in\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R$ is Euclidean. Then
$$ \|J^{-1}\|_{2\to2}\le K_W\|Q\|_2+\|w\|_2+ \frac{\|f_*\|_2\bigl(1+\|c\|_2K_W\|Q\|_2\bigr)}{|c^\top f_*|}. $$

Choose a real basis $v_1,\ldots,v_{d-1}$ of $\operatorname{range}(M-I_d)$. The $d-1$ real linear forms $w\mapsto v_j^\top w$ are independent: if a linear combination vanishes for every $w$, then the row $\bigl(\sum_j a_jv_j\bigr)^\top$ is zero, so $\sum_j a_jv_j=0$ and basis independence forces every coefficient $a_j$ to vanish. Rank-nullity therefore gives a nonzero real $w_0$ with $v_j^\top w_0=0$ for every $j$. Thus $w_0^\top(M-I_d)=0$. It is a compatible left eigenvector with the real right eigenvector $f_*$, so [F3], applied over $\mathbb C$, gives $w_0^\top f_*\ne0$. This pairing is real; normalize $w=w_0/(w_0^\top f_*)$, so $w$ is real, $w^\top M=w^\top$, and $w^\top f_*=1$. This pairing is real; normalize $w=w_0/(w_0^\top f_*)$, so $w$ is real, $w^\top M=w^\top$, and $w^\top f_*=1$. For $Q=I-f_*w^\top$ and $W=\ker w^\top$, one has $Qf_*=0$, $Q|_W=I_W$, and $QM=M-f_*w^\top M=M-f_*w^\top=M-Mf_*w^\top=MQ$. Hence $Q$ is the projection onto $W$, $M$ preserves $W$, and $M-I_d$ maps $W$ into $W$. Its restriction to $W$ is injective: a kernel vector there would be an eigenvector independent of $f_*$, contrary to simplicity. Since $W$ is finite dimensional, [F7] makes the restriction invertible. For $J(u,\tau)=(r,s)$, left multiplication of the first row by $w^\top$ gives $\tau=w^\top r$. source_anchors.claim: By [F1], the evaluation function of $p$ is $\sum_{k=0}^{m}a_kX^k$; zero padding changes this finite sum by zero terms only. For $0\le r\le m$, define the real function $Q_r(X)=\sum_{k=r}^{m}a_k\bigl(\prod_{s=0}^{r-1}(k-s)\bigr)X^{k-r}$, with the empty product equal to $1$; each factor $k-s$ is natural because $k\ge r>s$.

At $r=0$, $Q_0=p=p^{(0)}$ by [F2]. If $r<m$ and $p^{(r)}=Q_r$, termwise differentiation in [F3] kills the $k=r$ constant term and multiplies each term with $k>r$ by its exponent $k-r$; for each $k>r$, the resulting real coefficient is $a_k\bigl(\prod_{s=0}^{r-1}(k-s)\bigr)(k-r)=a_k\prod_{s=0}^{r}(k-s)$. Indeed the finite natural product extends by its last factor, and [F7] carries that natural identity to the product of canonical real images. The new exponent is $(k-r)-1=k-(r+1)$, so the differentiated sum is exactly $Q_{r+1}$. Hence $p^{(r+1)}=Q_{r+1}$.

selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Fix an exterior point $q\notin P$. Compactness gives a nearest point $p\in P$. For every $u\in P$, convexity puts $p+t(u-p)$ in $P$ for $0\le t\le1$; minimality of $p$ gives $\|q-p\|_2^2\le\|q-p-t(u-p)\|_2^2$. Expanding, dividing by $t>0$, and letting $t\downarrow0$ yields $\langle q-p,u-p\rangle\le0$. Hence the ray $q+s(q-p)$, $s\ge0$, remains strictly in the separating half-plane and avoids $P$. Each exterior point can therefore be joined outside $P$ to a circle containing $P$ in its interior; that circle is connected, so $\mathbb C\setminus P$ is connected and unbounded. [given, construct]

3.1 Fix $z\in\operatorname{int}P$. Choose a ray from $z$ whose direction is not aimed at a vertex. Its intersection with the convex polygon is a bounded interval starting at $z$, so the ray exits at the interior $p$ of a single edge with directed tangent $v\ne0$. The polygon interior lies locally to the left of this positively oriented edge. Apply the orientation-preserving similarity $\rho(w)=\overline v(w-p)/|v|$, which sends $p$ to $0$ and the edge tangent to the positive real direction. For every $a\notin\Gamma$, put $c=\overline v/|v|$. Parametrizing the transformed contour and using [F1] gives $\int_{\rho\circ\Gamma}\frac{d\zeta}{\zeta-\rho(a)}=\int_\Gamma\frac{c\,dw}{c(w-a)}=\int_\Gamma\frac{dw}{w-a}$, so $n(\rho\circ\Gamma,\rho(a))=n(\Gamma,a)$. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, the points $\rho^{-1}(i\varepsilon)$ and $\rho^{-1}(-i\varepsilon)$ lie respectively on the interior and exterior local sides of the edge. Applying [F4] to $\rho\circ\Gamma$ gives $n(\rho\circ\Gamma,i\varepsilon)-n(\rho\circ\Gamma,-i\varepsilon)=1$; the just-proved invariance rewrites this as $n(\Gamma,\rho^{-1}(i\varepsilon))-n(\Gamma,\rho^{-1}(-i\varepsilon))=1$. The exterior-side index is zero by step 2.1. Thus an interior point near that edge has winding number one. [F1, F4, step 2.1, choose, algebra]

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $C$ be a compact subset of the regular phase manifold whose configuration projection lies in a compact regular chart. For each $(q,p)\in C$, the two scaled RATTLE equations in [[def-regular-classical-rattle-step-map]] have unique local roots in neighborhoods of
$$\lambda_0=\mu_0=\frac12A(q)^{-1}\bigl(D^2c(q)[v,v]-J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)\bigr),\qquad v=M^{-1}p.$$
In local phase coordinates the position root depends smoothly on $(h,q,p)$, and the momentum root depends smoothly on $(h,q,p,\lambda)$ when the position multiplier is treated as a parameter near its selected root. The local branches agree on overlaps after shrinking their neighborhoods. A finite cover of $C$ therefore gives a common $h_0(C)>0$ for $|h|<h_0(C)$; the derivatives of each fixed finite order are uniformly bounded on this cover, and the two multiplier Jacobians remain uniformly invertible there. The exact position roots can also be kept in an ambient neighborhood of the compact regular configuration projection where $J$ has full row rank, so their constrained positions remain in $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$. At $h=0$ both Jacobians equal $-A(q)$.

proofparagraphs.text: Put $v=M^{-1}p$ and $w(\lambda)=-M^{-1}(\frac12\nabla V(q)+J(q)^T\lambda)$. Then $q_1=q+hv+h^2w(\lambda)$. Since $c(q)=0$ and $J(q)v=0$, [F3] extends $h^{-2}c(q_1)$ smoothly, with value $F_q(0,q,p,\lambda)=\frac12D^2c(q)[v,v]-\frac12J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)-A(q)\lambda$. Its $\lambda$ derivative is $-A(q)$, which is invertible. Since $A$ is smooth and invertible, $A^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(A)/\det A$ is smooth locally, so the center $\lambda_0$ varies smoothly with the phase input. Thus [F4] gives the unique local position multiplier branch at that center. [F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

The branch equations are smooth in local phase coordinates, and $A^{-1}$ is uniformly bounded on the compact configuration projection of $C$. Since $J$ has full row rank on that compact projection, continuity gives an ambient neighborhood where it remains full row rank. Around each point of $C$, shrink the phase and multiplier neighborhoods so both roots remain in common IFT uniqueness neighborhoods on overlaps and exact $q_1$ remains in this regular neighborhood. These neighborhoods cover $C$; compactness gives a finite subcover and the minimum of their positive step radii is a common $h_0(C)$. The smooth branch derivatives are bounded on smaller compact neighborhoods covering $C$ for $|h|\le h_0(C)$, and continuity of the multiplier Jacobians preserves uniform invertibility after a further shrink. [F2, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, choose] ∎

additional_source_clauses.text:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $c:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be smooth (that is, $C^\infty$) with $1\le m<d$, let $M$ be a constant symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix, and let $V:U\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. A **holonomic constraint** is the position condition $c(q)=0$. Write $J(q)=Dc(q)$, let $Q=\{q\in U:c(q)=0\}$, and define its regular part by $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}=\{q\in Q:\operatorname{rank}J(q)=m\}$. For $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A(q)=J(q)M^{-1}J(q)^T$ is positive definite. On a compact regular chart $K\subset Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A^{-1}$ is uniformly bounded: $\sup_{q\in K}\|A(q)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty$.

A position-momentum pair $(q,p)$ is **consistent** when $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$. The **regular constrained phase manifold** is
$$\mathcal M=\{(q,p)\in U\times\mathbb R^d:c(q)=0,\ J(q)M^{-1}p=0,\ q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}\}.$$
The ambient canonical two-form is $\omega_0=\sum_{i=1}^d dq_i\wedge dp_i$; its restriction to $\mathcal M$ is denoted $\omega_{\mathcal M}$.

For $v=M^{-1}p$, the constrained Hamilton equations are
$$\dot q=v,\qquad \dot p=-\nabla V(q)-J(q)^T\lambda,$$
with multiplier
$$\lambda=A(q)^{-1}\bigl(D^2c(q)[v,v]-J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)\bigr).$$
Here $D^2c(q)[v,v]\in\mathbb R^m$ has components $v^TD^2c_j(q)v$. This multiplier is the one that keeps both $c(q)=0$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$ satisfied.

Holonomic phase residuals control distance to the consistent phase manifold: The regularity, nonzero denominator, spectral gap, or explicit failure clause relevant to degeneracy is stated in Statement: Fix a compact regular configuration chart from [[def-regular-holonomic-phase-space-and-dynamics]] and a compact momentum set. Use the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^{2d}$ for phase-state differences. Each point of its consistent phase set has a neighborhood $U_j$ with a smooth retraction $\Pi_j:U_j\to\mathcal M$ such that $\Pi_j$ is the identity on $U_j\cap\mathcal M$ and
$$\|\Pi_j(q,p)-(q,p)\|\le C_j\bigl(\|c(q)\|_2+\|J(q)M^{-1}p\|_2\bigr).$$
A finite number of these neighborhoods cover the compact phase set, so one constant works for all of them. In particular, residuals of sizes $O(h^4)$ and $O(h^3)$ admit a consistent restoration at distance $O(h^3)$, uniformly on the chart. The existing argument records step 1.1: At a point of the compact regular chart $K\subset Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, permute coordinates as $q=(x,y)$ so $D_yc$ is an invertible $m\times m$ block. Apply [F2] for each finite regularity order; uniqueness makes these graphs agree locally, so the graph $y=\psi(x)$ is smooth. Write $\phi(x)=(x,\psi(x))$ and $T(x)=D\phi(x)$. Since $J(\phi(x))T(x)=0$ and both kernels have dimension $d-m$, $\operatorname{im}T=\ker J$. [F1, F2, algebra]; step 2.1: After shrinking to a convex coordinate neighborhood, $B(x)=D_yc(x,\psi(x))$ remains invertible and $\|B(x)^{-1}(D_yc(x,y)-B(x))\|\le\frac12$. Set $R_x(y)=c(x,y)-B(x)(y-\psi(x))$. Then $R_x(\psi(x))=0$ and the derivative of $B(x)^{-1}R_x$ has norm at most $\frac12$. The mean-value inequality [F4] gives $\|B(x)^{-1}R_x(y)\|\le\frac12\|y-\psi(x)\|$. Since $B^{-1}c=(y-\psi)+B^{-1}R_x(y)$, it follows that $\|q-\phi(x)\|=\|y-\psi(x)\|\le 2\|B(x)^{-1}\|\,\|c(q)\|$. Compactness makes the constant uniform on a finite chart cover. [F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Fix a compact regular configuration chart from [[def-regular-holonomic-phase-space-and-dynamics]] and a compact momentum set. Use the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^{2d}$ for phase-state differences. Each point of its consistent phase set has a neighborhood $U_j$ with a smooth retraction $\Pi_j:U_j\to\mathcal M$ such that $\Pi_j$ is the identity on $U_j\cap\mathcal M$ and
$$\|\Pi_j(q,p)-(q,p)\|\le C_j\bigl(\|c(q)\|_2+\|J(q)M^{-1}p\|_2\bigr).$$
A finite number of these neighborhoods cover the compact phase set, so one constant works for all of them. In particular, residuals of sizes $O(h^4)$ and $O(h^3)$ admit a consistent restoration at distance $O(h^3)$, uniformly on the chart.

after.evidence: The regular holonomic phase space is a symplectic cotangent bundle: The regularity, nonzero denominator, spectral gap, or explicit failure clause relevant to degeneracy is stated in Statement: Under the hypotheses of [[def-regular-holonomic-phase-space-and-dynamics]], let $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}=\{q\in Q:\operatorname{rank}J(q)=m\}$. It is a smooth manifold of dimension $d-m$. Choose a local configuration chart $\phi:O\subseteq\mathbb R^{d-m}\to Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and write $T=D\phi$, $G=T^TMT$. The cotangent coordinates $\pi=T^Tp$ identify the part of $\mathcal M$ over this chart locally with $T^*Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$: the unique consistent ambient momentum representing $\pi$ is $p=MTG^{-1}\pi$. In these coordinates the restricted canonical one-form $p^Tdq$ is $\pi^Tdx$, so the restricted two-form is $\omega_{\mathcal M}=\sum_{j=1}^{d-m}dx_j\wedge d\pi_j$. It is closed and nondegenerate, hence is symplectic on the regular phase manifold. The existing argument records step 1.1: At any $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, full row rank of $J(q)$ gives a permutation of coordinates $q=(x,y)$ for which the $m\times m$ block $D_yc(q)$ is invertible. Apply [F2] to the smooth map $c$ for each finite $k\ge1$. The resulting local graphs agree with the unique $C^1$ graph on overlaps, so that graph is $C^k$ locally for every $k$ and hence smooth. Thus locally $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is $y=\psi(x)$; $\phi(x)=(x,\psi(x))$ parametrizes it, and $D\phi$ has rank $d-m$ with image $\ker J$. [F1, F2, construct]; step 2.1: Define $G(x)=D\phi(x)^TMD\phi(x)$. For every nonzero $\xi$, $D\phi\,\xi\ne0$ and $\xi^TG(x)\xi=(D\phi\,\xi)^TM(D\phi\,\xi)>0$, so $G$ is invertible. Its entries are smooth, and $G^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(G)/\det G$ is smooth because $\det G>0$. For a cotangent coordinate $\pi\in\mathbb R^{d-m}$, put $p=MD\phi\,G^{-1}\pi$. Then $JM^{-1}p=JD\phi\,G^{-1}\pi=0$ and $D\phi^Tp=G G^{-1}\pi=\pi$. Conversely, if $JM^{-1}p=0$, then $M^{-1}p=D\phi\,\xi$ for a unique $\xi$, and $D\phi^Tp=G\xi$; hence the displayed formula gives the unique ambient $p$ representing $\pi$. Both this map and its inverse $(q,p)\mapsto(x,D\phi(x)^Tp)$ are smooth, so $(x,\pi)\mapsto(\phi(x),p)$ is a local diffeomorphism from $T^*Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ onto the part of $\mathcal M$ over this chart. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

Thus locally $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is $y=\psi(x)$; $\phi(x)=(x,\psi(x))$ parametrizes it, and $D\phi$ has rank $d-m$ with image $\ker J$. [F1, F2, construct]
actualproofparagraphs.3.1: Let $\theta_0=p^Tdq$ be the ambient canonical one-form. Under the chart just constructed, $dq=D\phi\,dx$ and $D\phi^Tp=\pi$, so its pullback is $\pi^Tdx$. Therefore the pullback of $\omega_0=-d\theta_0$ is $\sum_{j=1}^{d-m}dx_j\wedge d\pi_j$, which is closed and nondegenerate. [F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

source_anchors.claim: If $\alpha>0$, maxima and minima of $\alpha f$ on every partition piece are $\alpha$ times those of $f$, so both Darboux sums scale by $\alpha$ and their infimum/supremum do as well. If $\alpha=0$, every sum is zero. If $\alpha<0$, multiplication reverses order, giving $U(\alpha f,P)=\alpha L(f,P)$ and $L(\alpha f,P)=\alpha U(f,P)$; taking the infimum and supremum, which reverse under multiplication by negative $\alpha$, again gives $\int_a^b\alpha f=\alpha\int_a^b f$. Combine this homogeneity with step 1.1 to obtain the displayed formula. For reversed endpoints use $\int_b^a=-\int_a^b$; for $a=b$ use the zero-length definition.

space as real, let $x\in M$, and let $g=\operatorname{grad}f(x)\ne0$.

$\widehat f_x(s)=f(R_x(s))$ on the tangent (or horizontal) space, equipped
with its real Frobenius inner product. Suppose $\nabla\widehat f_x$ is
$L_R$-Lipschitz on the ball $\|s\|\le\Delta$, and let
$m_x(s)=f(x)+\langle g,s\rangle+\tfrac12\langle s,B_xs\rangle$ with
$B_x$ self-adjoint and real-linear. Define its induced operator norm by
$$\|B_x\|_{\rm op}:=\sup_{s\ne0}\frac{\|B_xs\|}{\|s\|},$$
and assume $\|B_x\|_{\rm op}\le M_B$. Let $p_C$ be the negative-gradient
Cauchy step, and let a feasible trial $p$ satisfy
$m_x(0)-m_x(p)\ge\theta_C[m_x(0)-m_x(p_C)]$ for $0<\theta_C\le1$.
With a zero denominator interpreted as $+\infty$, if
$\Delta\le\|g\|/(2M_B)$, then its predicted decrease $P$ is positive and
$$|\rho-1|\le\frac{2(L_R+M_B)\Delta}{\theta_C\|g\|},\qquad \rho=\frac{f(x)-f(R_x(p))}{P}.$$
Consequently, for $0<\eta_2<1$, if
$$\Delta\le \min\left\{\frac{\|g\|}{2M_B}, \frac{\theta_C(1-\eta_2)\|g\|}{2(L_R+M_B)}\right\},$$
then $\rho\ge\eta_2$. If $L_R+M_B=0$, the ratio equals $1$.

source_evidence.fullclaim: Let $T(z)=\sum_{k\ge1}k^{k-1}z^k/k!$ and $U(z)=T(z)-T(z)^2/2$. These series converge absolutely for $|z|<e^{-1}$. On that disk they satisfy $T=ze^T$, $zT'=T/(1-T)$, and $zU'=T$. Consequently $U(z)=\sum_{k\ge1}k^{k-2}z^k/k!$. For real $0\le z<e^{-1}$, $T(z)$ is the unique $u\in[0,1)$ satisfying $u e^{-u}=z$.

actualproofparagraphs.2.1: Differentiate $T=ze^T$ formally using [F2]. Since $T(0)=0$, the series $1-T$ is a unit by [F3], and rearrangement yields $zT'=T/(1-T)$. Therefore $zU'=zT'(1-T)=T$, so $[z^k]U=[z^k]T/k=k^{k-2}/k!$. [step 1.1, F2, F3, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.3.1: For real $0\le z<e^{-1}$, the coefficients of $T$ are nonnegative, so $T(z)\ge0$. If $T(z)\ge1$, continuity and $T(0)=0$ give $z_0\le z$ with $T(z_0)=1$, but step 1.1 implies $z_0=T(z_0)e^{-T(z_0)}=e^{-1}$, a contradiction. Thus $T(z)<1$. Since $u\mapsto ue^{-u}$ is strictly increasing on $[0,1)$, step 1.1 identifies $T(z)$ with its unique inverse-branch value. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open and $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^2$ (componentwise, as in [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Let $y(s)$ solve $y'=f(s,y)$ on $[t,t+h]$, $h>0$, and set $J=D_yf(t,y(t))$. Suppose the trajectory lies in a region where $\|f\|_2\le F$, $\|D_yf\|_2\le L$, and $\|f_t+D_yf\,f\|_2\le M_1$. Fix $\gamma>0$ and a real matrix $\widetilde J$. Suppose $A=I-\gamma hJ$ and $\widetilde A=I-\gamma h\widetilde J$ are invertible with $\|A^{-1}\|_2\le\kappa_0$ and $\|\widetilde A^{-1}\|_2\le\kappa_1$. Write $\delta=\|\widetilde J-J\|_2$.

For the exact-arithmetic Rosenbrock stage map $\Phi_{\gamma,h}^{\widetilde J}$, and a computed stage $\widehat k$ whose update residual obeys $\|\widetilde A\widehat k-f(t,y(t))\|_2\le\rho$, the update $\widehat y_+=y(t)+h\widehat k$ satisfies
$$\|\widehat y_+-y(t+h)\|_2\le C_Eh^2+\kappa_1h\rho, \qquad C_E:=\gamma\kappa_0LF+\frac{M_1}{2}+\gamma\kappa_0\kappa_1\delta F.$$
The last term is the separate Jacobian-approximation allowance. The residual is an equation residual in the units of [[def-implicit-residual-and-algebraic-error-units]], not a forward-error estimate by itself.

$$\widehat v_i:=\operatorname{fl}\Bigl(\sum_{j<d}M_{ij}x_j\Bigr),\qquad \widehat r:=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat v-b),\qquad \gamma_d:=\frac{du}{1-du}.$$

$$W:=\gamma_d\|M\|_F\|x\|_2+u(\|\widehat v\|_2+\|b\|_2).$$
Then
$$\|\widehat r-(Mx-b)\|_2\le W,\qquad \|Mx-b\|_2\le\|\widehat r\|_2+W.$$
If a norm in these formulas is replaced by an exact or certified upper bound, the resulting value of $\|\widehat r\|_2+W$ remains a certified upper bound for the exact residual.

Zeros cause no difficulty in this expansion.

Expand the rounded dot to obtain $s_i=\sum_{j>i}R_{ij}\widehat x_j(1+\theta_{ij})$, with $|\theta_{ij}|\le\gamma_{n-i}$, and use $s_n=0$. Write subtraction and division errors as $\alpha_i,\beta_i\in[-u,u]$. The computed row identity is then $R_{ii}\widehat x_i/((1+\alpha_i)(1+\beta_i))+\sum_{j>i}R_{ij}\widehat x_j(1+\theta_{ij})=y_i$. These identities also hold for zero intermediates by taking the corresponding error zero.

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let f_i:R^d->R be convex and continuously differentiable with L-Lipschitz gradients, set F=n^{-1}sum_i f_i, and let x* satisfy grad F(x*)=0. Conditional on the current iterate x_k and table alpha_i^k, assume an independent uniform index I_k and finite second moments. Put

$$S_k=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\|\alpha_i^k-\nabla f_i(x^*)\|_2^2,\quad \bar\alpha_k=\frac1n\sum_i\alpha_i^k,\quad v_k=\nabla f_{I_k}(x_k)-\alpha_{I_k}^k+\bar\alpha_k.$$

Then

$$\mathbb E[v_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla F(x_k),\qquad \mathbb E[\|v_k\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le6L(F(x_k)-F(x^*))+6S_k,$$

and, for the SAGA table replacement in [[alg-saga-finite-sum-method]],

$$
\mathbb E[S_{k+1}\mid\mathcal F_k]\le(1-1/n)S_k+\frac{2L}{n}(F(x_k)-F(x^*)).
$$

source_anchors.claim: If $x=0$, the algorithm copies $B$ and the zero column; take $H=I$ and $E=0$. Otherwise put $N=\|x\|_2$, $\alpha_0=-\sigma N$, $v_0=x-\alpha_0e_1$ and $V_0=\|v_0\|_2\ge N$. The nonnegative scaled squared-norm sum has each exact squared input multiplied by at most $r+2$ factors $1+\delta$, $|\delta|\le u$: two from scaling and at most $r$ from squaring and subsequent additions. Thus the computed norm divided by $N$ lies between $(1-u)^{r/2+3}$ and $(1+u)^{r/2+3}$ after square root and rescaling. For exponent $p\ge1$, convexity of $t^p$ on $t>0$ gives $1-(1-u)^p\le(1+u)^p-1$. Hence $|\widehat\alpha-\alpha_0|\le e_rN$. Only the first stored coordinate can differ from $v_0$, and subtraction gives $\|v-v_0\|_2\le(e_r+u(2+e_r))N=d_rN$. Success gives nonzero stored $v$.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $p(z)=z^n+a_{n-1}z^{n-1}+\cdots+a_0$ be a real monic polynomial of
degree $n\ge1$ with $|a_0|<1$. Define the reversed polynomial
$p^\#(z)=z^np(1/z)$ and
$$q(z)=\frac{p(z)-a_0p^\#(z)}{z(1-a_0^2)}.$$
If every zero of $p$ lies strictly inside the unit disk, then every zero of
$q$ does too.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: The real monic polynomial reduction divides by a positive one-minus-constant-square factor and transfers strict unit-disk root inclusion to the reduced degree.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 On $|z|=1$, real coefficients give $p^\#(z)=z^n\overline{p(z)}$, so $|p^\#(z)|=|p(z)|$. The strict root hypothesis makes $p$ nonzero on the unit circle, and $|a_0p^\#(z)|<|p(z)|$. Apply [F1] to $p$ and $-a_0p^\#$; $p-a_0p^\#$ has the same $n$ zeros in the disk as $p$. [A1, given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The polynomial $p-a_0p^\#$ has constant term zero and leading coefficient $1-a_0^2\ne0$, so it is $z$ times a degree-$(n-1)$ polynomial. source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ have an algebraically simple eigenvalue $\lambda_0$, with right vector $v$ normalized by $\|v\|_2=1$ and compatible left vector $w$ normalized by $w^*v=1$. Put $Q=I-vw^*$, $W=\ker w^*$, $q=\|Q\|_2$, and $\kappa=\|w\|_2$. The restriction $A_W=A|_W$ is well-defined. Let $D=\{\lambda:|\lambda-\lambda_0|\le\rho\}$ be a disk such that every $\lambda\in D$ makes $\lambda I_W-A_W$ invertible and
$$R\ge\sup_{\lambda\in D}\| (\lambda I_W-A_W)^{-1}\|_2<\infty.$$
If $n\ge2$, $\|E\|_2\le\delta$, and $Rq^2\delta<1$, then every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $A+E$ in $D$ satisfies
$$
|\lambda-\lambda_0|\le \kappa\delta+\frac{\kappa qR\delta^2}{1-Rq^2\delta}.
$$
When $A$ is a monodromy matrix, this bounds the corresponding Floquet multiplier. The formula is a finite nonnormal perturbation enclosure; an unseparated cluster requires the contour-count route instead.

selected_current_proof_blocks: 2.1 Let $\lambda\in D$ be an eigenvalue of $A+E$ with eigenvector $x=\alpha v+y$, $y\in W$. If $\alpha=0$, projection onto $W$ gives $y=(\lambda I_W-A_W)^{-1}QE y$. Thus $\|y\|_2\le Rq\delta\|y\|_2$, while $Rq\delta\le Rq^2\delta<1$, forcing $y=0$, contrary to $x\ne0$. Hence $\alpha\ne0$; rescale the eigenvector so $\alpha=1$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

4.1 Applying $w^*$ to the same eigen-equation gives $\lambda-\lambda_0=w^*Ev+w^*Ey$. The first term is the first-order eigenvalue derivative [F3]; its modulus is at most $\kappa\delta$, while the second is at most $\kappa\delta\|y\|_2$. Substituting step 3.1 gives the stronger denominator $1-Rq\delta$. Since $q\ge1$, $1-Rq^2\delta\le1-Rq\delta$ and both are positive, so replacing by the smaller denominator yields the stated bound. If $A$ is monodromy, [F5] identifies $\lambda$ as a Floquet multiplier. [F3, F5, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Use the dyadic composite-Simpson hierarchy of
[[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]]. Let $d\ge1$. For
$S=\{j_1<\cdots<j_k\}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$, define
$$D_Sf:=\partial_{x_{j_k}}^4\cdots\partial_{x_{j_1}}^4f,$$
so these derivatives are applied in increasing coordinate order; set
$D_\varnothing f=f$. Assume every $D_Sf$ is continuous on the closed cube,
with the one-sided endpoint convention of
[[def-higher-derivatives-and-smoothness]], and choose finite bounds $M_S\ge0$
such that $|D_Sf(x)|\le M_S$ on $[0,1]^d$. For
$\ell\in\mathbb N_0^d$, put $S(\ell):=\{j:\ell_j\ge1\}$ and
$$\delta_\ell(f):=(\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)})(f).$$
Then
$$|\delta_\ell(f)|\le M_{S(\ell)}\left(\frac{17}{2880}\right)^{|S(\ell)|}16^{-\sum_{j\in S(\ell)}\ell_j}.$$
Moreover, for every finite $F\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d$,
$$\sum_{\ell\in F}|\delta_\ell(f)|\le\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}}M_S\left(\frac{17}{43200}\right)^{|S|}<\infty.$$

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: For $\ell\ge1$, use [F2] on levels $\ell$ and $\ell-1$, inserting the exact integral between their values. With panel counts $2^{\ell+1}$ and $2^\ell$, [F5] gives $|\Delta_\ell g|\le(2^{-4(\ell+1)}/180+2^{-4\ell}/180)\|g^{(4)}\|_\infty=(17/2880)16^{-\ell}\|g^{(4)}\|_\infty$. For $\ell=0$, [F3] gives $|\Delta_0g|=|Q_0g|\le\|g\|_\infty$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F5, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.3.1: Fix finite $F$ and group indices by $S=S(\ell)$. For a fixed nonempty $S$, enlarge its levels to the finite box $1\le\ell_j\le R_j$ where $R_j$ is the largest such coordinate level in that group. By step 2.1 and [F6], the sum over that box is at most $M_S\prod_{j\in S}((17/2880)\sum_{r=1}^{R_j}16^{-r})\le M_S(17/43200)^{|S|}$, using [F7]. For $S=\varnothing$, the only possible index is $0$ and its term is at most $M_\varnothing$. Summing over all subsets proves the finite-subsum claim; the right side is finite. [given, step 2.1, F6, F7, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $d\ge1$ and $m=(m_1,\ldots,m_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$. For
$R_m:=\{\ell\in\mathbb N_0^d:0\le\ell_j\le m_j\text{ for every }j\}$ and
the details of [[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]],
$$\sum_{\ell\in R_m}\Delta_\ell=Q_{m_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes Q_{m_d}^{(d)}.$$

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: Fix any one-dimensional input $g$ and coordinate $j$, and put $c_r:=Q_r(g)$. By [F3], $\sum_{r=1}^{m_j}(c_r-c_{r-1})=c_{m_j}-c_0$; for $m_j=0$ this is the empty-sum identity. Adding $Q_0(g)$ and using [F1] yields $\sum_{r=0}^{m_j}\Delta_r(g)=Q_{m_j}(g)$. Since $g$ was arbitrary, this is equality of functionals. [given, F1, F3, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.2.1: Expand $\bigotimes_{j=1}^d\left(\sum_{r=0}^{m_j}\Delta_r^{(j)}\right)$ by distributing each finite coordinate sum. By [F3]–[F4] the resulting terms are exactly the tensor details indexed once by $R_m$, which is the Smolyak sum $Q_{R_m}$ by [F2]. Applying step 1.1 in every coordinate identifies this expansion with $Q_{m_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes Q_{m_d}^{(d)}$, as claimed. [given, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $H_0\in\mathbb H_n$ have eigenvalues with multiplicity
$\lambda_1(H_0)\le\cdots\le\lambda_n(H_0)$ and gap
$g=\lambda_{r+1}(H_0)-\lambda_r(H_0)>0$. Put
$$c=\lambda_1(H_0),\qquad R=\frac{\lambda_r(H_0)+\lambda_{r+1}(H_0)}2-c,$$
and let $\Gamma=\{c+Re^{it}:0\le t\le2\pi\}$ be positively oriented.
For Hermitian $H$, write $\sigma(H)=\{\lambda_j(H):1\le j\le n\}$.
Then
$R\ge g/2$. For every Hermitian $H$ with $\|H-H_0\|_{op}\le g/4$, exactly
the $r$ lowest eigenvalues of $H$, counted with multiplicity, lie inside $\Gamma$;
the gap is at least $g/2$, and
$$\operatorname{dist}(\Gamma,\sigma(H))\ge g/4,\qquad \|(zI-H)^{-1}\|_{op}\le4/g\quad(z\in\Gamma).$$

with $\lambda_i>0$ are linearly independent. This KKT tuple certifies the
global minimizer.

Integrating against that finite measure bounds the telescoping term by $\epsilon_j$; summing yields $\sum_j\epsilon_j$.

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let f_i:R^d->R be convex and continuously differentiable with L-Lipschitz gradients, set F=n^{-1}sum_i f_i, and let x* satisfy grad F(x*)=0. Conditional on a filtration \mathcal F_t, suppose x_t and the snapshot \tilde x are measurable, the uniform index I_t is independent of \mathcal F_t, and the relevant second moments are finite. For

$$
v_t=\nabla f_{I_t}(x_t)-\nabla f_{I_t}(\tilde x)+\nabla F(\tilde x),
$$

one has

$$\mathbb E[v_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=\nabla F(x_t),\qquad \mathbb E[\|v_t\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_t] \le4L(F(x_t)-F(x^*))+4L(F(\tilde x)-F(x^*)).$$

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Assume AC. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, $T>0$, and let $b,\sigma,\xi,W$ satisfy
the coefficient, Brownian, and initial-moment hypotheses of
[[thm-superlinear-sde-global-existence-and-moments]]. For each integer
$N\ge\max(1,\lceil T\rceil)$, put $h=T/N$ and define $Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$ by
[[alg-tamed-euler-superlinear-drift]]. Then for every finite $p\ge1$,
$$\sup_{N\ge\max(1,\lceil T\rceil)}\ \max_{0\le n\le N}\mathbb E|Y_n|^p<\infty.$$
The bound may depend on $p,T$, the coefficient constants, and the initial
moments, but not on $N$ or $n$.

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Assume AC. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, $T>0$, and let $b,\sigma,\xi,W$ satisfy
the coefficient, Brownian, and initial-moment hypotheses of
[[thm-superlinear-sde-global-existence-and-moments]]. For each integer
$N\ge\max(1,\lceil T\rceil)$, put $h=T/N$ and define $Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$ by
[[alg-tamed-euler-superlinear-drift]]. Then for every finite $p\ge1$,
$$\sup_{N\ge\max(1,\lceil T\rceil)}\ \max_{0\le n\le N}\mathbb E|Y_n|^p<\infty.$$
The bound may depend on $p,T$, the coefficient constants, and the initial
moments, but not on $N$ or $n$.

source_anchors.claim: For fixed $f,c,x$, define $I_m=\frac1{m!}\int_c^x f^{(m+1)}(t)(x-t)^m\,dt$ for $0\le m\le n$. For $m=0$, [L1] gives $I_0=f(x)-f(c)$. For $m\ge1$, apply integration by parts [L1] to $u(t)=f^{(m)}(t)$ and $v(t)=(x-t)^m/m!$. Since $v(x)=0$, $v(c)=(x-c)^m/m!$, and $v'(t)=-(x-t)^{m-1}/(m-1)!$, it gives $$ I_m=I_{m-1}-\frac{f^{(m)}(c)(x-c)^m}{m!}. $$ Induction from $I_0$ yields $I_n=f(x)-\sum_{j=0}^n f^{(j)}(c)(x-c)^j/j!=f(x)-P_n(x)$. The oriented integration-by-parts identity makes the same recurrence valid when $x<c$; if $x=c$, both sides are zero.

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let $B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric, let $g\in\mathbb R^n$, and
let $\Delta>0$. Every global minimizer $p_*$ of
$$q(p):=\langle g,p\rangle+\tfrac12p^TBp\quad\text{over }\|p\|_2\le\Delta$$
has a multiplier $\lambda\ge0$ such that
$$(B+\lambda I)p_*=-g,\qquad B+\lambda I\succeq0,\qquad \lambda(\Delta-\|p_*\|_2)=0.$$
Conversely, every feasible $p_*$ satisfying these conditions is a global
minimizer. A global minimizer always exists.

The singular hard case is included as follows. Let $\mu$ be the least
eigenvalue of $B$ and $E_\mu$ its eigenspace. If $\mu<0$, $g\perp E_\mu$,
and the solution $p_0$ of
$(B-\mu I)p_0=-g$, $p_0\perp E_\mu$, has $\|p_0\|_2\le\Delta$, then
$$p_*=p_0+z,\qquad z\in E_\mu,\qquad \|z\|_2^2=\Delta^2-\|p_0\|_2^2$$
is a global minimizer with the singular multiplier $\lambda=-\mu$. If
$\|p_0\|_2<\Delta$, both signs of any chosen nonzero $z$ of the required
length give distinct minimizers.

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let $B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric, let $g\in\mathbb R^n$, and
let $\Delta>0$. Every global minimizer $p_*$ of
$$q(p):=\langle g,p\rangle+\tfrac12p^TBp\quad\text{over }\|p\|_2\le\Delta$$
has a multiplier $\lambda\ge0$ such that
$$(B+\lambda I)p_*=-g,\qquad B+\lambda I\succeq0,\qquad \lambda(\Delta-\|p_*\|_2)=0.$$
Conversely, every feasible $p_*$ satisfying these conditions is a global
minimizer. A global minimizer always exists.

The singular hard case is included as follows. Let $\mu$ be the least
eigenvalue of $B$ and $E_\mu$ its eigenspace. If $\mu<0$, $g\perp E_\mu$,
and the solution $p_0$ of
$(B-\mu I)p_0=-g$, $p_0\perp E_\mu$, has $\|p_0\|_2\le\Delta$, then
$$p_*=p_0+z,\qquad z\in E_\mu,\qquad \|z\|_2^2=\Delta^2-\|p_0\|_2^2$$
is a global minimizer with the singular multiplier $\lambda=-\mu$. If
$\|p_0\|_2<\Delta$, both signs of any chosen nonzero $z$ of the required
length give distinct minimizers.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Suppose proper closed convex $f,g$ have a saddle point $(x_*,z_*,y_*)$ for the
Lagrangian in [[alg-two-block-admm-scaled]], with $Kx_*+Lz_*=c$, and every
subproblem in the exact ADMM sequence is attained. Put
$\Delta z^{k+1}=z^{k+1}-z^k$ and
$$V^k=\frac1\rho\|y^k-y_*\|_2^2+\rho\|L(z^k-z_*)\|_2^2.$$
For every $k\ge1$,
$$V^{k+1}\le V^k-\rho\|r^{k+1}\|_2^2-\rho\|L\Delta z^{k+1}\|_2^2.$$
The index begins at $k=1$: an arbitrary initial $z^0$ need not satisfy a
previous $z$-subproblem optimality condition. Also, with $p_k=f(x^k)+g(z^k)$
and $p_*=f(x_*)+g(z_*)$, every exact sweep satisfies
$$p_{k+1}-p_*\le-\langle y^{k+1},r^{k+1}\rangle+ \rho\langle L\Delta z^{k+1},r^{k+1}-L(z^{k+1}-z_*)\rangle,$$
$$p_*-p_{k+1}\le\langle y_*,r^{k+1}\rangle.$$

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^2$, and $y(s)$ solve $y'=f(s,y)$ on $[t,t+h]$. Assume a compact convex tube $Q\subset D$ contains the trajectory, the stage midpoint segments, and all vectors used below. On $Q$, suppose
$$
\|f\|_2\le F,\quad \|D_yf\|_2\le L,\quad \|f_t\|_2\le T_0,\quad \|D^2f\|_{\rm op}\le H,
$$
where $D^2f$ is the second total derivative on the joint variable $(t,y)$, and $\|D^2f\|_{\rm op}:=\sup_{\|u\|=\|v\|=1}\|D^2f[u,v]\|_2$ for the Euclidean product norm. Fix $\alpha=1-1/\sqrt2$, and suppose $\|\widetilde J\|_2\le B_J$, $\|\widetilde T\|_2\le B_T$, and $\|\alpha h\widetilde J\|_2\le q<1$. Put $\kappa=(1-q)^{-1}$ and $M=T_0+LF$. The shifted inverse has norm at most $\kappa$ by [[lem-rosenbrock-shifted-matrix-invertibility-bound]].

For exact-arithmetic stages $k_1,q_2,k_2$ of [[alg-two-stage-rosenbrock-w-method]] (with its exact-storage checks successful), define
$$C_1=B_JF+B_T,\quad K_1=F+\alpha h\kappa C_1,\quad C_F=\frac{\alpha\kappa L C_1}{2}+\frac{H(1+K_1^2)}{8}.$$
$$C_K=\alpha^2\kappa^2B_JC_1+\frac{\alpha\kappa B_JM}{2}+\kappa C_F, \qquad M_2=H(1+F^2)+LT_0+L^2F.$$
Then the exact one-step defect is at most
$$
\|y(t)+hk_2-y(t+h)\|_2\le (C_K+M_2/6)h^3.
$$
If the computed first and second shifted solves have certified update-residual bounds $\rho_1$ and $\rho_2$, then the computed update satisfies
$$\|\widehat y_+-y(t+h)\|_2\le (C_K+M_2/6)h^3+C_rh^2\rho_1+\kappa h\rho_2, \qquad C_r:=\kappa^2(L/2+\alpha B_J).$$
Thus $\rho_1=O(h)$ and $\rho_2=O(h^2)$ preserve a cubic local defect. These are equation-residual conditions, not stage forward-error claims without the inverse bound.

At any base point in the tube, the same two-stage residual perturbation argument gives the solver-to-exact-map bound $\|\widehat\Phi_h(t,y)-\Phi_h(t,y)\|_2\le C_rh^2\rho_1+\kappa h\rho_2$, whenever both midpoint evaluations lie in $Q$.

Define $\eta(A)$ by that sum. If $(A_k)$ are disjoint, the double series of absolute values is bounded by $\|\eta_{n_1}\|_{TV}+\sum_j\|\eta_{n_{j+1}}-\eta_{n_j}\|_{TV}$, so the two countable sums may be interchanged; hence $\eta$ is countably additive. The same tail bound gives $\|\eta-\eta_{n_j}\|_{TV}\le\sum_{r\ge j}2^{-r}\to0$. source_evidence.fullclaim:
Apply [[def-ars222-additive-tableau-and-stages]] to the scalar split test equation $y'=\lambda_a y+\lambda_b y$, with $z_a=h\lambda_a$ and $z_b=h\lambda_b$ in $\mathbb C$. If $1-\gamma z_b\ne0$, the one-step amplification factor is
$$R(z_a,z_b)=\frac{1+z_a+(1-2\gamma)z_b+\frac12z_a^2+(\frac12-\gamma^2)z_az_b}{(1-\gamma z_b)^2}.$$
The exact scalar absolute-stability region for this tableau is
$$\mathcal S=\left\{(z_a,z_b)\in\mathbb C^2:1-\gamma z_b\ne0,\ \left|1+z_a+(1-2\gamma)z_b+\frac12z_a^2+(\frac12-\gamma^2)z_az_b\right|\le|1-\gamma z_b|^2\right\}.$$
On $z_b=0$ this reduces to $|1+z_a+z_a^2/2|\le1$; on $z_a=0$ it reduces to $|1+(1-2\gamma)z_b|\le|1-\gamma z_b|^2$. This is a scalar, two-variable region; it makes no matrix-nonnormality or PDE stability claim.

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: Substituting $a(y)=\lambda_a y$ and $b(y)=\lambda_b y$ into [F1] gives $Y_2/y=(1+\gamma z_a)/(1-\gamma z_b)$ whenever the denominator is nonzero. The third stage then satisfies $\frac{Y_3}{y}=\frac{1+\delta z_a+[(1-\delta)z_a+(1-\gamma)z_b](Y_2/y)}{1-\gamma z_b}.$ These formulas are linear coefficient identities, so they also define the amplification when $y=0$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.4.1: Repeated application to the scalar test equation multiplies its state by $R$ at each step, so nonincrease of the absolute value is exactly $|R|\le1$. Since $| (1-\gamma z_b)^2|=|1-\gamma z_b|^2$, this is precisely the displayed set $\mathcal S$, with the pole excluded because the implicit stage equation is singular there. Setting either variable to zero gives the stated axis sections by substitution. [F3, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $L>0$, let $M\ge2$ be an integer, and let $R$ be a regular MEP as in [[def-regular-minimum-energy-path-in-a-collision-free-tube]], now parameterized by arc length on $[0,L]$, with $R\in C^3$ under the endpoint convention of [[lem-arc-length-polyline-interpolation-error]] and the bounds of [[lem-centered-chord-and-unequal-step-tangent-error]] and [[lem-arc-length-polyline-interpolation-error]]. Let $R_i=R(ih)$ for $i=0,\ldots,M$, $Mh=L$, and assume every interior centered chord is nonzero. Suppose $\|\nabla V(R(s))\|_2\le G$ along the curve and $0<h\le1$. Use the centered unit tangent $\widehat t_i=(R_{i+1}-R_{i-1})/\|R_{i+1}-R_{i-1}\|_2$. Then the projected string force at each interior sample satisfies

$$\|(I-\widehat t_i\widehat t_i^T)\nabla V(R_i)\|_2\le C_Fh^2.$$

If the equal-spacing spring residual $k(\ell_i^+-\ell_i^-)\widehat t_i$ is also evaluated on these samples, then its norm is at most $C_Sh^3$ for fixed $k$. Equal-length polyline redistribution of the exact samples changes each image by at most $C_Rh^2$. The constants depend on the stated derivative bounds, $G$, $k$, and the path, not on $M$. The projected-force conclusion is for the centered-tangent string residual; it does not assert second-order consistency for the improved energy-selected NEB tangent.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
For the data of [[def-finite-basis-projector-energy-model]], $E(P)$ is real
and $C^2$ on its stated neighborhood. For every Hermitian $P$ in that
neighborhood and every Hermitian direction $H$,
$$DE(P)[H]=\operatorname{tr}\big((h+G(P)+\nabla E_{xc}(P))H\big)=\langle F(P),H\rangle_F.$$
Thus $F(P)$ is the Hermitian Frobenius gradient of $E$.

actualproofparagraphs.1.2: For real $t$, real-linearity gives $G(P+tH)=G(P)+tG(H)$. Expanding and collecting the coefficient of $t$ yields $\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}((P+tH)G(P+tH))=\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(H G(P)) +\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(P G(H))$. The linear trace term differentiates to $\operatorname{tr}(hH)$ by [F1], and the $E_{xc}$ term differentiates to $\langle\nabla E_{xc}(P),H\rangle_F$ by its gradient definition. [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

For $0\prec D\prec I$ and every Hermitian direction $H$, let
$\mathcal S(D)=\operatorname{tr}(D\log D+(I-D)\log(I-D))$. Then
$$D\mathcal S(D)[H]=\operatorname{tr}\big(H(\log D-\log(I-D))\big).$$

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: For positive scalars the integral in [F1] converges and equals $\log x$ by integrating over $[0,R]$ and taking $R\to\infty$. Diagonalizing a positive-definite Hermitian $X$ by [F4] gives the same identity for $\log X$. If $X\succeq mI$ for some $m>0$, the resolvent $R_s=(X+sI)^{-1}$ has norm at most $(m+s)^{-1}$. [F1, F4, given, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.2.1: In the neighborhood $X\succeq (m/2)I$, the resolvent identity gives $\frac{R_s(X+tH)-R_s(X)}{t}=-R_s(X+tH)H R_s(X)$. On every bounded interval of $s$, [F2] and continuity give uniform convergence of these difference quotients to $-R_sHR_s$. For $s\ge R\ge1$, their norm is at most $\|H\|_2/s^2$, so the integral of the tail is at most $\|H\|_2/R$, uniformly for small $t$. First differentiating on $[0,R]$ and then letting $R\to\infty$ proves $D\log(X)[H]=\int_0^\infty R_sHR_s\,ds$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, given]

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let $n\ge1$, and let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ and bounded
below by $f_{inf}$.
Run [[alg-adaptive-cubic-regularization]] with exact Hessians and parameters
$0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1$, $\gamma_{up}>1$, $0<\gamma_{down}<1$,
$0<\kappa<1$, $0<\kappa_\theta<1$, and
$0<\sigma_{min}\le\sigma_k\le\sigma_{max}$ with $\sigma_{max}\ge3L$.
Suppose the Hessian is $L$-Lipschitz on every trial segment, and let
$0<\varepsilon\le1$. Let $R\in\mathbb N_0$ satisfy
$\gamma_{up}^R\sigma_{min}\ge3L$ (take $R=0$ if
$\sigma_{min}\ge3L$).

The algorithm has two complexity guarantees.

1. **Exact model minimizers.** If every solver call returns an exact global
   minimizer, define
   $$C_g:=\sigma_{max}+\sqrt n\,L,\qquad c_g:=\frac{\eta_1\sigma_{min}}{6C_g^{3/2}}.$$
   Through the first iterate with gradient norm at most $\varepsilon$, the
   numbers $N_s$ of accepted steps and $N_u$ of rejected trials satisfy
   $$N_s\le [f(x_0)-f_{inf}]c_g^{-1}\varepsilon^{-3/2}+1,\qquad N_u\le R N_s.$$

2. **Admissible inexact model steps.** Suppose each solver-success candidate
   passes the cubic solution, residual, and Cauchy-decrease checks in
   [[alg-adaptive-cubic-regularization]], and $\nabla f$ is $K$-Lipschitz
   on every trial segment. If the solver succeeds at every nonterminal
   trial, define
   $$D_g:=\frac{\sigma_{max}+\sqrt n\,L+\kappa_\theta K} {1-\kappa_\theta},\qquad c_a:=\frac{\eta_1\sigma_{min}}{6D_g^{3/2}}.$$
   Then the same counts satisfy
   $$N_s\le [f(x_0)-f_{inf}]c_a^{-1}\varepsilon^{-3/2}+1,\qquad N_u\le R N_s.$$

In either case the uncapped process reaches a stationary or target-achieved
iterate with gradient norm at most $\varepsilon$. For the finite-cap
algorithm, an outer cap at least
$$(R+1)\left(\frac{f(x_0)-f_{inf}}{c\,\varepsilon^{3/2}}+1\right)$$
suffices, where $c=c_g$ in case 1 and $c=c_a$ in case 2. The resulting
number of outer trials, and their function, gradient, and Hessian evaluation
counts, are $O(\varepsilon^{-3/2})$. These counts do not bound the internal
work of the model solver.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Use the tableau and stage equations in [[def-ars222-additive-tableau-and-stages]], with $F=a+b$. Let $a,b\in C^2(U,\mathbb R^d)$ on an open set, and suppose the exact solution, exact stages, approximate candidates, and all joining line segments remain in a common compact convex tube on which $a,b$ and their first two derivatives are bounded and $a,b$ are Lipschitz with constants $L_a,L_b$. At each implicit stage assume the selected branch hypotheses of [[lem-ars222-stage-branch-and-residual-control]] hold, with $|\gamma|hL_b\le1/2$.

For exact stage roots, the exact-start one-step defect is at most $C h^3$, and the exact-root one-step map is Lipschitz with constant $1+Lh$ on the tube, for constants independent of sufficiently small $h$. If computed stages have unscaled update residuals $r_2,r_3$ satisfying
$$\|r_2\|_2\le C_2h^2,\qquad \|r_3\|_2\le C_3h^3,$$
then their output differs from the exact-root output at the same input by at most $C_{\rm alg}h^3$. Consequently, for $h=T/N$ and initial error $\|y_0-y(0)\|_2\le C_0h^2$, the computed method satisfies
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le C_T h^2.$$
The second-stage residual has the weaker $O(h^2)$ budget because its stage error is multiplied by $h$ in the last stage; the final-stage residual must be $O(h^3)$. All residuals are in update units.

actualproofparagraphs.1.3: Let $e_2=\|\widetilde Y_2-Y_2\|_2$. By $\gamma>0$ from [F6] and $|\gamma|hL_b\le1/2$ from [A1], subtracting the second-stage equations and using its residual gives $(1-\gamma hL_b)e_2\le\|r_2\|_2$, hence $e_2\le2\|r_2\|_2$. For the final stage, subtract the equations with the same initial input; the terms depending on $Y_2$ are bounded by $hK_s e_2$, where $K_s=|1-\delta|L_a+|1-\gamma|L_b$. The final-stage residual therefore gives $\|\widetilde Y_3-Y_3\|_2\le2\|r_3\|_2+4K_s h\|r_2\|_2.$ This is at most $C_{\rm alg}h^3$ under the two stated residual budgets. [A1, F1, F3, F6, algebra]

actualproofparagraphs.3.1: By [F2] and [A1], the selected third-stage root exists after $Y_2$ is selected. The second-stage residual has the weaker $O(h^2)$ budget because its stage error is multiplied by $h$ in the last stage; the final-stage residual must be $O(h^3)$. All residuals are in update units.

Applying [F5] to $b(Y_2)$ then gives $b(Y_2)=b(y)+\gamma h\,Db(y)F(y)+O(h^2)$, and substitution into [F1] yields $Y_2=y+\gamma hF(y)+\gamma^2h^2Db(y)F(y)+O(h^3).$ [A1, F1, F2, F5, step 1.1, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.3.1: By [F2] and [A1], the selected third-stage root exists after $Y_2$ is selected. Since $Y_2-y=O(h)$ and the stage equations give $Y_3-y=O(h)$, Lipschitz continuity and the weight sums $\delta+(1-\delta)=1$ and $(1-\gamma)+\gamma=1$ imply $Y_3-y=hF(y)+O(h^2)$. Taylor's formula applied to the last-stage terms gives $a(Y_2)=a(y)+\gamma h\,Da(y)F(y)+O(h^2),\quad b(Y_2)=b(y)+\gamma h\,Db(y)F(y)+O(h^2),\quad b(Y_3)=b(y)+h\,Db(y)F(y)+O(h^2).$ Substituting these expansions into [F1] and collecting the coefficients gives $Y_3=y+hF(y)+h^2\{\gamma(1-\delta)Da(y)F(y)+\gamma(2-\gamma)Db(y)F(y)\}+O(h^3).$ [A1, F1, F2, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

source_anchors.claim: Split the product for $\omega_n(x)$ before and after index $j$ using [F4]: it is $A(x-x_j)B$, where $A=\prod_{k<j}(x-x_k)$ and $B=\prod_{j<k\le n}(x-x_k)$. Since $x\ne x_j$, division by $x-x_j$ gives $AB=\prod_{k\ne j}(x-x_k)$ in the increasing omitted-index order of [F1]. Multiplying by $w_j$ therefore gives $\ell_j(x)=\omega_n(x)w_j/(x-x_j)$.

By [F1], $S(X):=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\ell_j(X)=I_n(1,\ldots,1)(X)$, so it has degree at most $n$ by [F2]. At each node $x_i$, [F3] gives $S(x_i)=1$. The constant polynomial $1$ is another degree-at-most-$n$ interpolant of these data; uniqueness in [F2] gives $S(X)=1$.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $H_0\in\mathbb H_n$ have an occupied/unoccupied gap
$g=\lambda_{r+1}(H_0)-\lambda_r(H_0)>0$, and let $c,R,\Gamma$ be the circle
from [[lem-spectral-gap-persistence-and-uniform-resolvent-bound]]. For Hermitian
$H$ in the open operator-norm ball $\|H-H_0\|_{op}<g/4$, let $\Pi_r(H)$ be its
projector onto the $r$ lowest eigenvalues. Then $H\mapsto\Pi_r(H)$ is real
Frechet $C^1$ in the Frobenius norm and
$$D\Pi_r(H)[E]=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma (zI-H)^{-1}E(zI-H)^{-1}\,dz$$
for each Hermitian direction $E$. With $\ell(\Gamma)=2\pi R$,
$$\|D\Pi_r(H)[E]\|_F\le\frac{16R}{g^2}\|E\|_F.$$
This is a block/cluster statement: no gap between eigenvalues inside either
cluster is required.

actualproofparagraphs.2.1: Integrating each diagonal entry and using [F3], linearity in [F4], and the finite spectral expansion gives $\frac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma R_H(z)\,dz=U\operatorname{diag}(1,\ldots,1,0,\ldots,0)U^*=\Pi_r(H).$ Thus the contour expression represents the full occupied cluster projector, including repeated eigenvalues within that cluster. [step 1.1, F3, F4, algebra]

Let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^2$ on an open set $U$. Let $T_+>0$, let $W\subset U$ be open, and suppose every solution from $x\in W$ exists on an open time interval containing $[0,T_+]$ and stays in one compact convex set $K\subset U$ for all $t\in[0,T_+]$. Write $\Phi(t,x)=\phi_t(x)$. Then $\Phi$ is $C^2$ jointly in $(t,x)$ on $(0,T_+)\times W$, locally on every common-tube neighborhood in $W$, and its derivatives extend continuously in time to $[0,T_+]$. Its first state derivative $S(t,x)=D_x\Phi(t,x)$ solves
$$
\partial_t S=Df(\Phi)S,\qquad S(0,x)=I_n,
$$
and its second state derivative is the bilinear map $H(t,x)$ determined by
$$
\partial_t H[u,v]=Df(\Phi)H[u,v]+D^2f(\Phi)[S u,S v],\qquad H(0,x)[u,v]=0.
$$
In particular $\partial_t\Phi=f(\Phi)$, $\partial_{tx}\Phi=Df(\Phi)S$, and $\partial_{tt}\Phi=Df(\Phi)f(\Phi)$. The assertion is local to the stated common tube.

Let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^2$ on an open set $U$. Let $T_+>0$, let $W\subset U$ be open, and suppose every solution from $x\in W$ exists on an open time interval containing $[0,T_+]$ and stays in one compact convex set $K\subset U$ for all $t\in[0,T_+]$. Write $\Phi(t,x)=\phi_t(x)$. Then $\Phi$ is $C^2$ jointly in $(t,x)$ on $(0,T_+)\times W$, locally on every common-tube neighborhood in $W$, and its derivatives extend continuously in time to $[0,T_+]$. Its first state derivative $S(t,x)=D_x\Phi(t,x)$ solves
$$
\partial_t S=Df(\Phi)S,\qquad S(0,x)=I_n,
$$
and its second state derivative is the bilinear map $H(t,x)$ determined by
$$
\partial_t H[u,v]=Df(\Phi)H[u,v]+D^2f(\Phi)[S u,S v],\qquad H(0,x)[u,v]=0.
$$
In particular $\partial_t\Phi=f(\Phi)$, $\partial_{tx}\Phi=Df(\Phi)S$, and $\partial_{tt}\Phi=Df(\Phi)f(\Phi)$. The assertion is local to the stated common tube.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Assume the hypotheses and certificates in
[[alg-certified-scf-with-diis-safeguard]]: $\Phi$ is a $q$-contraction on the
complete invariant set $K$, its fixed point is $P_*$, the starting error is at
most $E_0$, and every baseline response error is at most $\eta_k$. Let $E_k$
be updated by that algorithm. Then every produced iterate obeys
$$\|P_k-P_*\|_F\le E_k\le q^kE_0+\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}q^{k-1-j}\eta_j.$$
An accepted DIIS candidate has certified error at most $qE_k$; the commutator
least-squares residual alone is not used as an error bound. If the procedure is
continued indefinitely with successful certificates and $\eta_k\to0$, then
$P_k\to P_*$; a finite update cap still may return budget exhaustion.
Use the convention $q^0=1$, including when $q=0$.

Assume the hypotheses and certificates in
[[alg-certified-scf-with-diis-safeguard]]: $\Phi$ is a $q$-contraction on the
complete invariant set $K$, its fixed point is $P_*$, the starting error is at
most $E_0$, and every baseline response error is at most $\eta_k$. Let $E_k$
be updated by that algorithm. Then every produced iterate obeys
$$\|P_k-P_*\|_F\le E_k\le q^kE_0+\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}q^{k-1-j}\eta_j.$$
An accepted DIIS candidate has certified error at most $qE_k$; the commutator
least-squares residual alone is not used as an error bound. If the procedure is

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: Initially $\|P_0-P_*\|_F\le E_0$ by input. Suppose $\|P_k-P_*\|_F\le E_k$. If the algorithm accepts candidate $Y=P_{k+1}$, [F2] gives a certified upper bound $\bar\rho(Y)$ for $\|Y-\Phi(Y)\|_F$ with $\bar\rho(Y)/(1-q)\le qE_k$. Applying [F1] at $Y$ proves $\|P_{k+1}-P_*\|_F\le qE_k=E_{k+1}$. [given, F1, F2]
actualproofparagraphs.2.1: If the baseline is used, its evaluator certifies $\|P_{k+1}-\Phi(P_k)\|_F\le\eta_k$. The triangle inequality and contraction give $\|P_{k+1}-P_*\|_F\le\eta_k+\|\Phi(P_k)-\Phi(P_*)\|_F\le\eta_k+q\|P_k-P_*\|_F\le qE_k+\eta_k=E_{k+1}.$ Thus induction proves $\|P_k-P_*\|_F\le E_k$ at every step. [given, step 1.1, F2, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.3.1: By [F2], both update branches obey $E_{k+1}\le qE_k+\eta_k$ (accepted DIIS uses $\eta_k=0$ for this upper estimate). Iterating this scalar recurrence by induction gives $E_k\le q^kE_0+\sum_{j<k}q^{k-1-j}\eta_j$. [step 2.1, F2, induction, algebra]

$$
E_\rho=\left\{\frac{\rho e^{it}+\rho^{-1}e^{-it}}2:0\le t\le2\pi\right\}

$$
\|f-I_N^Lf\|_C\le \frac{4\sqrt{\pi}M}{\rho-1}\rho^{-N}.
$$

source_anchors.claim: Induct on $N$. For $N=0$, the empty interval has terminal state $x_{a+N}=x_a$ and unchanged cotangent, exactly the returned pair. For $N=1$, the single evaluation returns its exact output state and its local reverse rule returns the exact input cotangent. For $N\ge2$, midpoint replay produces the exact $x_{a+L}$ by [F3]. By induction the right child returns terminal state $x_{a+N}$ and the exact cotangent at that midpoint; the left child returns terminal state $x_{a+L}$ and, after the earlier transitions, the exact cotangent at $x_a$. The parent returns the right child's terminal state and the left child's starting cotangent, so both outputs are correct. Every interval is split into disjoint left and right steps and each base step is recorded and reversed once. Therefore the terminal value and initial cotangent agree with the ordinary reverse sweep.

[[def-locally-lipschitz-ito-sde-and-maximal-solution]]. Let
$\kappa,\theta,\sigma>0$, let $x_0>0$ be deterministic, and suppose
$2\kappa\theta\ge\sigma^2$. Then the CIR SDE
$$dX_t=\kappa(\theta-X_t)dt+\sigma\sqrt{X_t}\,dW_t, \qquad X_0=x_0,$$
has a unique global strong solution on every finite horizon. Its paths remain
strictly positive and finite, and for every finite $p\ge1$,
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\mathbb E X_t^p<\infty.$$
No negative-moment bound or strong numerical convergence rate is asserted.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $n\ge1$, let $\Gamma$ be a nonempty finite union of closed line segments in $\mathbb C$, let $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ be nonempty, and let $A_0\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$. Each segment of $\Gamma$ is assigned to one of finitely many disks $D_j=\{z:|z-z_j|\le r_j\}$ whose radius is $r_j\ge0$ and whose disk contains both endpoints of that segment. For each disk there are $R_j\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ and nonnegative bounds $e_j,\delta_A,s_j$ satisfying
$$e_j\ge\|I-R_j(z_jI-A_0)\|_{\infty,\mathbb C},\quad \delta_A\ge\sup_{A\in\mathcal A}\|A-A_0\|_{\infty,\mathbb C},\quad s_j\ge\|R_j\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}.$$
If $q_j=e_j+s_j(r_j+\delta_A)<1$ for each $j$, then every $z\in\Gamma$ and $A\in\mathcal A$ make $zI-A$ invertible, and
$$\|(zI-A)^{-1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le \max_j\frac{s_j}{1-q_j}.$$
The theorem bounds the resolvent on the supplied contour cover; it does not count enclosed eigenvalues or certify a nonnormal eigenvalue disk from a residual.

Then $(zI-A)^{-1}=M^{-1}R_j$, so [F2] gives $\|(zI-A)^{-1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le s_j/(1-q_j)$. The disk cover from step 1.1 yields the maximum bound on all of $\Gamma$, uniformly in $A$. source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $n\ge1$, let $\Gamma$ be a nonempty finite union of closed line segments in $\mathbb C$, let $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ be nonempty, and let $A_0\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$. Each segment of $\Gamma$ is assigned to one of finitely many disks $D_j=\{z:|z-z_j|\le r_j\}$ whose radius is $r_j\ge0$ and whose disk contains both endpoints of that segment. For each disk there are $R_j\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ and nonnegative bounds $e_j,\delta_A,s_j$ satisfying
$$e_j\ge\|I-R_j(z_jI-A_0)\|_{\infty,\mathbb C},\quad \delta_A\ge\sup_{A\in\mathcal A}\|A-A_0\|_{\infty,\mathbb C},\quad s_j\ge\|R_j\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}.$$
If $q_j=e_j+s_j(r_j+\delta_A)<1$ for each $j$, then every $z\in\Gamma$ and $A\in\mathcal A$ make $zI-A$ invertible, and
$$\|(zI-A)^{-1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le \max_j\frac{s_j}{1-q_j}.$$
The theorem bounds the resolvent on the supplied contour cover; it does not count enclosed eigenvalues or certify a nonnormal eigenvalue disk from a residual.

source_anchors.claim: Under the stated nonsingularity hypothesis, $\widetilde A=\widehat Q(\widehat R+\Delta R)$ has full column rank, and [F3] identifies $\widehat x$ as its unique least-squares minimizer for $b+\delta b$. Finally $\|\widehat R\|_F=\|A+\Delta_Q\|_F\le(1+\beta_Q)\|A\|_F$, and $\widetilde A-A=\Delta_Q+\widehat Q\Delta R$ gives the stated relative matrix bound. At fixed dimensions, [F1] gives $\beta_Q=O(u)$, and $\gamma_m=O(u)$ gives $\beta_b=O(u)$ in either right-hand-side branch, so the displayed coefficients are $O(u)$. Under the additional coefficient checks, write $g=\gamma_{n+3}$; then $\beta_Q+g(1+\beta_Q)=(1+g)\beta_Q+g\le19g+g=20g$, while the assumed $\beta_b\le20g$ gives the right-hand bound. No comparison between $\beta_Q$ and $g$ is inferred from arithmetic success alone.

source_anchors.claim: For stored-reflector evaluation, [F1] bounds $\|\widehat y-\widehat Q^Tb\|_2$ by $\beta_Q\|b\|_2$. In the explicit admissible-input alternative, dot expansion by [F4] gives coordinate errors at most $\gamma_m\sum_i|\widehat q_{ij}b_i|\le\gamma_m\|b\|_2$ by Cauchy-Schwarz and unit column norms; combining coordinates gives $\sqrt n\gamma_m\|b\|_2$. In either case put $z=\widehat y-\widehat Q^Tb$ and $\delta b=\widehat Qz$. Exact orthonormality gives $\widehat Q^T\delta b=z$ and $\|\delta b\|_2=\|z\|_2$.

Apply [F2] to the actual rounded back substitution. It supplies upper triangular $\Delta R$ with $(\widehat R+\Delta R)\widehat x=\widehat y$ and the displayed Frobenius estimate. This holds also when $\widehat x=0$, since the same row identities force $\widehat y=0$. Combined with step 1.1 this proves the perturbed normal-coordinate equation.

The coagulation integrand $H_\varphi(x,y)=\frac12K(x,y)[\varphi(x+y)-\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)]$ has a uniform supremum bound and uniform Lipschitz bounds in each variable: the bracket is bounded by $3$ and changes by at most $2|x-x'|$ when only $x$ changes, so the product rule for differences gives a bound depending only on $K_*,L_K$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

The function $J_\varphi(x)=\beta(x)[\int\varphi\,dB_x-\varphi(x)]$ is bounded by $\beta_*(D+1)$ and Lipschitz with constant at most $L_\beta(D+1)+\beta_*(L_B+1)$, by the assumed boundedness and $d_{BL}(B_x,B_y)\le L_B|x-y|$. Thus its fragmentation derivative difference is bounded by a constant times $d_{BL}(\mu_t,\nu_t)$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

Integrating the weak equations, steps 2.1 and 1.2 give for every admissible $\varphi$ the bound $|\langle\varphi,\mu_t-

u_s)\,ds$, where [F3] makes $C_T$ uniform on $[0,T]$. Taking the supremum gives $d(t)\le d(0)+C_T\int_0^t d(s)\,ds$. Put $g(t)=d(0)+C_T\int_0^t d(s)\,ds$; then $d\le g$ and $g'\le C_Tg$ almost everywhere, so $(e^{-C_Tt}g(t))'\le0$ and $d(t)\le g(t)\le e^{C_Tt}d(0)$. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $u_\theta$ solve the parameter-dependent ODE of [[lem-parameter-ode-flow-tangent-on-common-tube]] on $[0,T]$. Let
$$J(\theta)=\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)+\int_0^T\ell(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)\,dt,$$
where $\phi$ and $\ell$ are $C^1$ on a neighborhood of the trajectory tube and their first derivatives are bounded and uniformly continuous there. Let $S=D_\theta u_\theta$ be the tangent from that lemma. Let $p$ solve the terminal adjoint problem
$$-p'(t)=D_u f(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^Tp(t)+D_u\ell(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^T,\qquad p(T)=D_u\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)^T.$$
Then
$$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)^T+D_\theta u_0(\theta)^Tp(0)+\int_0^T\bigl(D_\theta\ell(t,u_\theta,\theta)^T+D_\theta f(t,u_\theta,\theta)^Tp(t)\bigr)\,dt.$$
This formula separates initial, terminal, running-cost and vector-field parameter terms. It applies only while the common-tube and differentiability hypotheses hold.

The chain rule gives the column gradient of the running integrand as $D_\theta\ell(t,u_\theta,\theta)^T+S(t)^TD_u\ell(t,u_\theta,\theta)^T$. The mean-value integral formula, boundedness and uniform continuity of the objective derivatives on the common compact tube, and the uniform first-order state remainder from [F1] make the running first-order remainder $o(\|h\|)$ uniformly in $t$ for a parameter increment $h$. Integration therefore gives its derivative by integrating that column gradient. The terminal chain rule gives $D_\theta\phi^T+S(T)^TD_u\phi^T$. source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $(K,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space and let $\Phi:K\to K$ be a
contraction with constant $0\le q<1$. In the SCF application, $K$ is a
complete invariant subset of the response-map domain from
[[def-self-consistent-projector-response-map]], with $d(X,Y)=\|X-Y\|_F$.
Then $\Phi$ has a unique fixed point $X_*$ and exact iterates
$X_{k+1}=\Phi(X_k)$ satisfy
$$d(X_k,X_*)\le q^k d(X_0,X_*).$$
For every $X\in K$,
$$d(X,X_*)\le\frac{d(X,\Phi(X))}{1-q}.$$
If computed updates $X_{k+1}\in K$ obey
$d(X_{k+1},\Phi(X_k))\le\eta_k$, then
$$e_{k+1}\le q e_k+\eta_k,\qquad e_k\le q^k e_0+\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}q^{k-1-j}\eta_j,$$
where $e_k=d(X_k,X_*)$ and $X_0$ is the supplied initial point.
Use the convention $q^0=1$, including when $q=0$.

source_anchors.claim: Fix $n\ge\max\{1,V(x_0)\}$ and set $K_n=\{x\in E:V(x)\le n\}$. This is finite by properness. The set $D_n=\{x+\nu_j:x\in K_n,\ a_j(x)>0,\ 1\le j\le R\}\setminus K_n$ of one-reaction exit states is finite, and $F_n=K_n\cup D_n$ is finite. The rate bound $M_n:=\max_{x\in K_n}\lambda(x)$ is therefore finite. For fixed ordered channel labels $j_1,\ldots,j_m$, the density of event times $0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T$ before the first exit is the product of the successive channel rates and exponential no-event factors. Summing over channel labels bounds this density by $M_n^m$, since at each event the sum of active channel rates is at most $M_n$. The ordered simplex has volume $T^m/m!$, so the probability of at least $m$ events before exit by $T$ is at most $(M_nT)^m/m!$, which tends to zero. Thus infinitely many jumps cannot occur in finite time while the process remains in $K_n$.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $K\subseteq\mathcal D_r$ be nonempty, closed, and convex in Frobenius norm.
Suppose $F$ is $C^1$ on an open neighborhood of $K$, every matrix $F(D)$ there
has a strict $r$th gap so the gapped projector map $\Phi$ is defined, and for a
fixed $\alpha\in[0,1]$ the relaxed map
$$T_\alpha(D)=(1-\alpha)D+\alpha\Phi(D)$$
satisfies $T_\alpha(K)\subseteq K$. If a certified induced-norm bound
$$\|DT_\alpha(D)\|_{F\to F}\le q\qquad(D\in K),\qquad 0\le q<1,$$
holds, where $\|A\|_{F\to F}:=\sup_{\|H\|_F=1}\|A[H]\|_F$, then
$T_\alpha$ is a contraction on $K$ and its iterates converge to a unique fixed
point. The derivative is
$$DT_\alpha(D)=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha D\Phi(D).$$
The derivative bound is a separate hypothesis; $\alpha>0$ alone does not imply
contraction.

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: For $D,E\in K$, convexity puts the segment $Z(t)=E+t(D-E)$ in $K$ for $t\in[0,1]$. By [F1] and [L1], $\Phi$ is defined along this segment; [F2] gives its local $C^1$ regularity. For an increment $H$, $T_\alpha(D+H)-T_\alpha(D)=(1-\alpha)H+\alpha(\Phi(D+H)-\Phi(D))$, so Frechet differentiability of $\Phi$ gives $DT_\alpha(D)=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha D\Phi(D)$. The chain rule [F5] on the segment gives $\frac d{dt}T_\alpha(Z(t))=DT_\alpha(Z(t))[D-E]$. Its norm is at most $q\|D-E\|_F$ by the assumed induced-norm bound; continuity follows from [F2] and [F6]. [given, F1, L1, F2, F5, F6, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.2.1: Apply [F3] on $[0,1]$ to this path. It yields $\|T_\alpha(D)-T_\alpha(E)\|_F\le q\|D-E\|_F$, so $T_\alpha$ is a contraction on $K$. [step 1.1, F3]

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and suppose its coordinate diameters
$$D_j=\sup\{|x_j-u_j|:x,u\in C\}$$
are finite. Run diagonal AdaGrad [[alg-diagonal-adagrad-online-regret]] for $T\ge1$ rounds on convex losses $\ell_t:C\to\mathbb R$, with $g_t\in\partial\ell_t(x_t)$, step size $\eta>0$, and accumulator $s_{t,j}=\sqrt{\epsilon^2+\sum_{k=1}^t g_{k,j}^2}$ for $\epsilon>0$. For every comparator $u\in C$,

$$\sum_{t=1}^T(\ell_t(x_t)-\ell_t(u))\le\sum_{j=1}^d\left(\frac{D_j^2}{2\eta}+\eta\right)s_{T,j}.$$

$$\lambda_1(H_*)\le-2\gamma,\qquad \lambda_j(H_*)\ge2\gamma\ (j\ge2),\qquad \|H_*\|_{\rm op}\le\Lambda$$

for $\gamma>0$ and $\Lambda\ge2\gamma$. Let the closed ball $\overline B_2(x_*,r)$ lie in $U$, let the Hessian be $L$-Lipschitz there, and assume $Lr\le\gamma$. At every iterate $x$ in this ball, suppose a validated Hessian enclosure gives $\lambda_1(H(x))\le-\gamma$ and $\lambda_j(H(x))\ge\gamma$ for $j\ge2$, and accepted dimer data satisfy the hypotheses of [[thm-dimer-mode-perturbation-and-local-saddle-error]] with uniform rotation residual $\tau_{\rm rot}$ and HVP error bound $\delta\le\gamma/4$. $$\alpha:=\frac{4(\tau_{\rm rot}+\delta)}{5\gamma},\qquad q:=\max\left\{|1+\sigma\lambda_1(H_*)|,\ \max_{2\le j\le d}|1-\sigma\lambda_j(H_*)|\right\},$$

where $0<\sigma<2/\Lambda$. Suppose the finite dimer saddle translation of [[alg-finite-budget-dimer-mode-following]] uses a unit direction $v$ from those accepted data and a computed gradient $\widehat g(x)$ with $\|\widehat g(x)-\nabla V(x)\|_2\le\eta$. Put

$$\kappa:=q+\frac{\sigma Lr}{2}+2\sigma\left(\alpha+\frac{Lr}{3\gamma}\right)\left(\Lambda+\frac{Lr}{2}\right).$$
